1517.title: Aktualizace firmware
1517.content: Keep your Meshtastic node up to date with the latest firmware for new features, bug fixes, and security improvements.

1518.title: Checking for Updates
1518.content: . | Open Settings for the connected node and, under Advanced, tap Firmware Update. The entry appears only for OTA-capable nodes. | The app checks for available firmware versions. | Available updates show the version number and release notes. | . The app also tells you when the connected node is behind the latest stable release. The Connect tab shows a Firmware update available card naming the installed and the stable version, and a notification says the same once per node and release. Its button reads Open Firmware Updates when the app can update the node over the current connection, or Open Meshtastic Flasher when it can’t.

1519.title: Update Methods
1519.content: The Firmware Update screen picks the method from how the node is connected, and its update button names it: Update via BLE OTA, Update via Wi-Fi OTA, or Update via USB File Transfer. | Připojení | nRF52 | ESP32 | RP2040 | . | Bluetooth | BLE OTA | BLE OTA | — | . | Síť | — | Wi-Fi OTA | — | . | USB | Přenos souborů přes USB | — | Přenos souborů přes USB | . Where the table has no method, the screen says firmware updates are not supported over this connection. Connect another way, or use the Web Flasher. OTA (Over-The-Air) via Bluetooth . The most common update method for Android users: . ⚠️ Warning: Interrupting a firmware update can leave the node unable to boot. Keep the phone nearby and both devices powered until the update completes. | Ensure your node is connected via Bluetooth. | Navigate to the Firmware Update screen. | Select the desired firmware version. | Tap Update via BLE OTA. An Update Warning dialog lists the pre-flight checks — read it, then tap I know what I’m doing. to start. This dialog appears for every update method, including Wi-Fi OTA, USB, and a local firmware file. | Wait for the update to complete. Do not disconnect during the update. | . While the update downloads, uploads or verifies, you can tap Play Chirpy Hop to play a short runner game: tap to jump, swipe down to crouch. The update’s progress stays visible above the game, and back returns to the update screen. When the update finishes or fails, the game stops and offers Back to update. Your best score is kept on this device. Some boards ship with a bootloader that cannot take a Bluetooth update. For these, the screen shows a warning card before you start, with a hint for the board where one exists. Don’t show again for this device hides it for that node. When a stock nRF bootloader limits how fast the upload can run, the screen says so during the upload, and again on the success screen, with a link to the Meshtastic nRF52 Bootloader, which makes Bluetooth updates much faster. Vymazat zařízení během aktualizace . Where the app offers it, an Erase device during update switch appears above the update button. It is a per-update opt-in and is never remembered. | Method | What erasing does | . | BLE / Wi-Fi OTA | Factory-resets the device once the update is verified. All settings and Bluetooth pairing are removed. | . | USB | Úplně vymaže paměť zařízení a poté od začátku nainstaluje vybraný firmware. | . It is not offered for a local firmware file, during a recovery update, or over USB in the desktop app — the USB erase runs the Android-only maintenance sequence below. Over USB it is offered for nRF52 and RP2040 nodes only, and when the app can’t erase one safely, the switch is shown disabled with the reason. Afterwards the device needs setting up — and pairing — again. OTA via Wi-Fi (network-connected ESP32) . When an ESP32 node is connected over the network rather than Bluetooth, the app offers Wi-Fi OTA, which pushes the same update over TCP: . | Connect to the node over the network (see Connections). | Open the Firmware Update screen and pick a version. | Tap Update via Wi-Fi OTA. Keep the node and phone on the same network for the whole transfer. | . Wi-Fi OTA installs the ESP32 app image, a .bin file, rather than the .uf2 a USB update uses. The app selects the right file from the release for you. In-App USB Update . When your nRF52 or RP2040 node is connected over USB/serial (rather than Bluetooth), the Firmware Update screen offers USB File Transfer. The app reboots the device into DFU mode, then prompts you to save the .uf2 file to the device’s DFU drive using the system file picker. This option appears only on a USB/serial connection. It is not available over Bluetooth, and ESP32 nodes have no USB update path in the app. A vendor nRF bootloader supplied as a .zip (e.g. RAK WisBlock RAK4631) has to be flashed with a serial DFU tool such as adafruit-nrfutil — copying that .zip to the drive won’t work. A bootloader supplied as an update-....uf2 can be installed by copying it to the drive; that is how the app’s own bootloader upgrade works. The app surfaces a hint when the serial-only route applies. Factory Erase and Bootloader Upgrade . On a USB/serial connection, nRF52 and RP2040 devices can be wiped as part of an update — that is the Erase device during update opt-in described earlier on this page. nRF52 devices additionally offer Upgrade bootloader where an upgraded bootloader is published for the board; RP2040 devices run no Adafruit bootloader, so they never see it. The upgrade installs the Meshtastic nRF52 Bootloader release named on the card. Both are Android-only. They depend on Android’s update-drive checks, so the desktop app does not show them — use the Web Flasher there instead. Select a firmware version before either one: the app hides both until a release is chosen, because the firmware is reinstalled after the device is wiped or the new bootloader is written. Both a USB erase and a bootloader upgrade write two files in turn, so you are asked to select the device’s update drive twice: once for the erase or bootloader image, then again for the firmware. The app reads INFO_UF2.TXT from the drive you select to confirm it really is the device’s update drive and to identify the board before writing anything. For a bootloader upgrade, the app also reads the installed bootloader version from INFO_UF2.TXT and shows it next to the latest release before writing anything. The running firmware doesn’t report its bootloader, so the installed version appears only once the device has restarted into update mode, never on the firmware screen while connected. If the two match, the bootloader is left as it is and the app moves straight on to reinstalling the firmware. Otherwise choose Upgrade bootloader to write it, or Skip to reinstall the firmware without changing it. On nRF52 the app must already know which Bluetooth stack your device uses before it starts, because it can’t read the bootloader until the device has rebooted. If it can’t confirm the stack, it refuses to erase and points you at the Web Flasher instead. In the Web Flasher, choosing the wrong Bluetooth stack can leave the node recoverable only with a hardware programmer. Once the drive is readable, how an nRF52 device is erased depends on its bootloader: . | Newer bootloaders erase themselves. A bootloader that advertises factory-erase support in INFO_UF2.TXT (OTAFIX 2.4 and later) takes a single, board-agnostic erase file. The bootloader wipes your settings, channels, keys and the stored node list itself, leaves the installed firmware in place, and comes back as an update drive a second or two later for the firmware file. There is no Bluetooth-stack choice to get wrong on this path. | Older bootloaders need a Bluetooth-stack-specific erase. On these the app writes a small erase program matched to your device’s Bluetooth stack, then starts it over the serial port. If the drive reports a different stack than expected, the app refuses rather than guessing. | . The app picks the path from what the drive reports; you don’t choose it. What the nRF52 bootloader does . Version 2.6.0 and later of the Meshtastic nRF52 Bootloader does the following while the update drive is up. | Backup. CURRENT.UF2 on the drive is a copy of the installed firmware. Copy it off to back up, or back onto the drive to reinstall. | Screen. On a node with a screen, the title reads BOOTLOADER, ERASE, WRONG FILE or NO FIRMWARE, and a progress bar shows the copy. | Wrong file. A firmware file the board cannot take is refused as WRONG FILE. | Interrupted copy. If the cable is pulled mid-copy, the node has no firmware. Plug it in again and copy the firmware once more. | Idle. After 6 minutes with no update activity, a node with firmware boots it. A node with no firmware keeps waiting. | Single-button boards. The T1000-E and the MeshTracker X1 have no reset button. Hold the button for about 3 seconds while the node powers on to enter update mode. 1527.title: Update Methods
1527.content: The Firmware Update screen picks the method from how the node is connected, and its update button names it: Update via BLE OTA, Update via Wi-Fi OTA, or Update via USB File Transfer. | Connection | nRF52 | ESP32 | RP2040 | . | Bluetooth | BLE OTA | BLE OTA | — | . | Rede | — | Wi-Fi OTA | — | . | USB | USB File Transfer | — | USB File Transfer | . Where the table has no method, the screen says firmware updates are not supported over this connection. Connect another way, or use the Web Flasher. OTA (Over-The-Air) via Bluetooth . The most common update method for Android users: . ⚠️ Warning: Interrupting a firmware update can leave the node unable to boot. Keep the phone nearby and both devices powered until the update completes. | Ensure your node is connected via Bluetooth. | Navigate to the Firmware Update screen. | Select the desired firmware version. | Tap Update via BLE OTA. An Update Warning dialog lists the pre-flight checks — read it, then tap I know what I’m doing. to start. This dialog appears for every update method, including Wi-Fi OTA, USB, and a local firmware file. | Wait for the update to complete. Do not disconnect during the update. | . While the update downloads, uploads or verifies, you can tap Play Chirpy Hop to play a short runner game: tap to jump, swipe down to crouch. The update’s progress stays visible above the game, and back returns to the update screen. When the update finishes or fails, the game stops and offers Back to update. Your best score is kept on this device. Some boards ship with a bootloader that cannot take a Bluetooth update. For these, the screen shows a warning card before you start, with a hint for the board where one exists. Don’t show again for this device hides it for that node. When a stock nRF bootloader limits how fast the upload can run, the screen says so during the upload, and again on the success screen, with a link to the Meshtastic nRF52 Bootloader, which makes Bluetooth updates much faster. Erase device during update . Where the app offers it, an Erase device during update switch appears above the update button. It is a per-update opt-in and is never remembered. | Method | What erasing does | . | BLE / Wi-Fi OTA | Factory-resets the device once the update is verified. All settings and Bluetooth pairing are removed. | . | USB | Wipes the device’s flash completely, then installs the selected firmware from scratch. | . It is not offered for a local firmware file, during a recovery update, or over USB in the desktop app — the USB erase runs the Android-only maintenance sequence below. Over USB it is offered for nRF52 and RP2040 nodes only, and when the app can’t erase one safely, the switch is shown disabled with the reason. Afterwards the device needs setting up — and pairing — again. OTA via Wi-Fi (network-connected ESP32) . When an ESP32 node is connected over the network rather than Bluetooth, the app offers Wi-Fi OTA, which pushes the same update over TCP: . | Connect to the node over the network (see Connections). | Open the Firmware Update screen and pick a version. | Tap Update via Wi-Fi OTA. Keep the node and phone on the same network for the whole transfer. | . Wi-Fi OTA installs the ESP32 app image, a .bin file, rather than the .uf2 a USB update uses. The app selects the right file from the release for you. In-App USB Update . When your nRF52 or RP2040 node is connected over USB/serial (rather than Bluetooth), the Firmware Update screen offers USB File Transfer. The app reboots the device into DFU mode, then prompts you to save the .uf2 file to the device’s DFU drive using the system file picker. This option appears only on a USB/serial connection. It is not available over Bluetooth, and ESP32 nodes have no USB update path in the app. A vendor nRF bootloader supplied as a .zip (e.g. RAK WisBlock RAK4631) has to be flashed with a serial DFU tool such as adafruit-nrfutil — copying that .zip to the drive won’t work. A bootloader supplied as an update-....uf2 can be installed by copying it to the drive; that is how the app’s own bootloader upgrade works. The app surfaces a hint when the serial-only route applies. Factory Erase and Bootloader Upgrade . On a USB/serial connection, nRF52 and RP2040 devices can be wiped as part of an update — that is the Erase device during update opt-in described earlier on this page. nRF52 devices additionally offer Upgrade bootloader where an upgraded bootloader is published for the board; RP2040 devices run no Adafruit bootloader, so they never see it. The upgrade installs the Meshtastic nRF52 Bootloader release named on the card. Both are Android-only. They depend on Android’s update-drive checks, so the desktop app does not show them — use the Web Flasher there instead. Select a firmware version before either one: the app hides both until a release is chosen, because the firmware is reinstalled after the device is wiped or the new bootloader is written. Both a USB erase and a bootloader upgrade write two files in turn, so you are asked to select the device’s update drive twice: once for the erase or bootloader image, then again for the firmware. The app reads INFO_UF2.TXT from the drive you select to confirm it really is the device’s update drive and to identify the board before writing anything. For a bootloader upgrade, the app also reads the installed bootloader version from INFO_UF2.TXT and shows it next to the latest release before writing anything. The running firmware doesn’t report its bootloader, so the installed version appears only once the device has restarted into update mode, never on the firmware screen while connected. If the two match, the bootloader is left as it is and the app moves straight on to reinstalling the firmware. Otherwise choose Upgrade bootloader to write it, or Skip to reinstall the firmware without changing it. On nRF52 the app must already know which Bluetooth stack your device uses before it starts, because it can’t read the bootloader until the device has rebooted. If it can’t confirm the stack, it refuses to erase and points you at the Web Flasher instead. In the Web Flasher, choosing the wrong Bluetooth stack can leave the node recoverable only with a hardware programmer. Once the drive is readable, how an nRF52 device is erased depends on its bootloader: . | Newer bootloaders erase themselves. A bootloader that advertises factory-erase support in INFO_UF2.TXT (OTAFIX 2.4 and later) takes a single, board-agnostic erase file. The bootloader wipes your settings, channels, keys and the stored node list itself, leaves the installed firmware in place, and comes back as an update drive a second or two later for the firmware file. There is no Bluetooth-stack choice to get wrong on this path. | Older bootloaders need a Bluetooth-stack-specific erase. On these the app writes a small erase program matched to your device’s Bluetooth stack, then starts it over the serial port. If the drive reports a different stack than expected, the app refuses rather than guessing. | . The app picks the path from what the drive reports; you don’t choose it. CURRENT.UF2 on the drive is a copy of the installed firmware. Copy it off to back up, or back onto the drive to reinstall. | Screen. On a node with a screen, the title reads BOOTLOADER, ERASE, WRONG FILE or NO FIRMWARE, and a progress bar shows the copy. | Wrong file. A firmware file the board cannot take is refused as WRONG FILE. | Interrupted copy. If the cable is pulled mid-copy, the node has no firmware. Plug it in again and copy the firmware once more. | Idle. After 6 minutes with no update activity, a node with firmware boots it. A node with no firmware keeps waiting. | Single-button boards. The T1000-E and the MeshTracker X1 have no reset button. Hold the button for about 3 seconds while the node powers on to enter update mode. Eject the drive from the computer to leave without copying a file. The app’s USB update needs no button. | . Other Flashing Options . For recovery or when neither OTA nor in-app USB is available: . | Use the Meshtastic Web Flasher | Or the Meshtastic CLI tool on desktop | .

1543.content: The Firmware Update screen picks the method from how the node is connected, and its update button names it: Update via BLE OTA, Update via Wi-Fi OTA, or Update via USB File Transfer. | Connection | nRF52 | ESP32 | RP2040 | . | Bluetooth | BLE OTA | BLE OTA | — | . | Network | — | Wi-Fi OTA | — | . | USB | USB File Transfer | — | USB File Transfer | . Where the table has no method, the screen says firmware updates are not supported over this connection. Connect another way, or use the Web Flasher. OTA (Over-The-Air) via Bluetooth . The most common update method for Android users: . ⚠️ Warning: Interrupting a firmware update can leave the node unable to boot. Keep the phone nearby and both devices powered until the update completes. | Ensure your node is connected via Bluetooth. | Navigate to the Firmware Update screen. | Select the desired firmware version. | Tap Update via BLE OTA. An Update Warning dialog lists the pre-flight checks — read it, then tap I know what I’m doing. to start. This dialog appears for every update method, including Wi-Fi OTA, USB, and a local firmware file. | Wait for the update to complete. Do not disconnect during the update. | . While the update downloads, uploads or verifies, you can tap Play Chirpy Hop to play a short runner game: tap to jump, swipe down to crouch. The update’s progress stays visible above the game, and back returns to the update screen. When the update finishes or fails, the game stops and offers Back to update. Your best score is kept on this device. Some boards ship with a bootloader that cannot take a Bluetooth update. For these, the screen shows a warning card before you start, with a hint for the board where one exists. Don’t show again for this device hides it for that node. When a stock nRF bootloader limits how fast the upload can run, the screen says so during the upload, and again on the success screen, with a link to the Meshtastic nRF52 Bootloader, which makes Bluetooth updates much faster. Erase device during update . Where the app offers it, an Erase device during update switch appears above the update button. It is a per-update opt-in and is never remembered. | Method | What erasing does | . | BLE / Wi-Fi OTA | Factory-resets the device once the update is verified. All settings and Bluetooth pairing are removed. | . | USB | Wipes the device’s flash completely, then installs the selected firmware from scratch. | . It is not offered for a local firmware file, during a recovery update, or over USB in the desktop app — the USB erase runs the Android-only maintenance sequence below. Over USB it is offered for nRF52 and RP2040 nodes only, and when the app can’t erase one safely, the switch is shown disabled with the reason. Afterwards the device needs setting up — and pairing — again. OTA via Wi-Fi (network-connected ESP32) . When an ESP32 node is connected over the network rather than Bluetooth, the app offers Wi-Fi OTA, which pushes the same update over TCP: . | Connect to the node over the network (see Connections). | Open the Firmware Update screen and pick a version. | Tap Update via Wi-Fi OTA. Keep the node and phone on the same network for the whole transfer. | . Wi-Fi OTA installs the ESP32 app image, a .bin file, rather than the .uf2 a USB update uses. The app selects the right file from the release for you. In-App USB Update . When your nRF52 or RP2040 node is connected over USB/serial (rather than Bluetooth), the Firmware Update screen offers USB File Transfer. The app reboots the device into DFU mode, then prompts you to save the .uf2 file to the device’s DFU drive using the system file picker. This option appears only on a USB/serial connection. It is not available over Bluetooth, and ESP32 nodes have no USB update path in the app. A vendor nRF bootloader supplied as a .zip (e.g. RAK WisBlock RAK4631) has to be flashed with a serial DFU tool such as adafruit-nrfutil — copying that .zip to the drive won’t work. A bootloader supplied as an update-....uf2 can be installed by copying it to the drive; that is how the app’s own bootloader upgrade works. The app surfaces a hint when the serial-only route applies. Factory Erase and Bootloader Upgrade . On a USB/serial connection, nRF52 and RP2040 devices can be wiped as part of an update — that is the Erase device during update opt-in described earlier on this page. nRF52 devices additionally offer Upgrade bootloader where an upgraded bootloader is published for the board; RP2040 devices run no Adafruit bootloader, so they never see it. The upgrade installs the Meshtastic nRF52 Bootloader release named on the card. Both are Android-only. They depend on Android’s update-drive checks, so the desktop app does not show them — use the Web Flasher there instead. Select a firmware version before either one: the app hides both until a release is chosen, because the firmware is reinstalled after the device is wiped or the new bootloader is written. Both a USB erase and a bootloader upgrade write two files in turn, so you are asked to select the device’s update drive twice: once for the erase or bootloader image, then again for the firmware. The app reads INFO_UF2.TXT from the drive you select to confirm it really is the device’s update drive and to identify the board before writing anything. For a bootloader upgrade, the app also reads the installed bootloader version from INFO_UF2.TXT and shows it next to the latest release before writing anything. The running firmware doesn’t report its bootloader, so the installed version appears only once the device has restarted into update mode, never on the firmware screen while connected. If the two match, the bootloader is left as it is and the app moves straight on to reinstalling the firmware. Otherwise choose Upgrade bootloader to write it, or Skip to reinstall the firmware without changing it. On nRF52 the app must already know which Bluetooth stack your device uses before it starts, because it can’t read the bootloader until the device has rebooted. If it can’t confirm the stack, it refuses to erase and points you at the Web Flasher instead. In the Web Flasher, choosing the wrong Bluetooth stack can leave the node recoverable only with a hardware programmer. Once the drive is readable, how an nRF52 device is erased depends on its bootloader: . | Newer bootloaders erase themselves. A bootloader that advertises factory-erase support in INFO_UF2.TXT (OTAFIX 2.4 and later) takes a single, board-agnostic erase file. The bootloader wipes your settings, channels, keys and the stored node list itself, leaves the installed firmware in place, and comes back as an update drive a second or two later for the firmware file. There is no Bluetooth-stack choice to get wrong on this path. | Older bootloaders need a Bluetooth-stack-specific erase. On these the app writes a small erase program matched to your device’s Bluetooth stack, then starts it over the serial port. If the drive reports a different stack than expected, the app refuses rather than guessing. | . The app picks the path from what the drive reports; you don’t choose it. What the nRF52 bootloader does . Version 2.6.0 and later of the Meshtastic nRF52 Bootloader does the following while the update drive is up. | Backup. CURRENT.UF2 on the drive is a copy of the installed firmware. Copy it off to back up, or back onto the drive to reinstall. | Screen. On a node with a screen, the title reads BOOTLOADER, ERASE, WRONG FILE or NO FIRMWARE, and a progress bar shows the copy. | Wrong file. A firmware file the board cannot take is refused as WRONG FILE. | Interrupted copy. If the cable is pulled mid-copy, the node has no firmware. Plug it in again and copy the firmware once more. | Idle. After 6 minutes with no update activity, a node with firmware boots it. A node with no firmware keeps waiting. | Single-button boards. The T1000-E and the MeshTracker X1 have no reset button. Hold the button for about 3 seconds while the node powers on to enter update mode. Eject the drive from the computer to leave without copying a file. The app’s USB update needs no button. | . Other Flashing Options . For recovery or when neither OTA nor in-app USB is available: . | Use the Meshtastic Web Flasher | Or the Meshtastic CLI tool on desktop | .

1545.title: Pre-Update Checklist
1545.content: Before updating: . | Battery above 50%, recommended. The app itself refuses to start an update only when the node reports 10% or less | A stable connection over the method you’re updating with: Bluetooth, Wi-Fi, or USB | Note your current settings (they may reset on major version changes) | Check the release notes for breaking changes | Update the Meshtastic app itself, before or alongside firmware updates, to ensure compatibility | .

1546.title: Post-Update
1546.content: After the firmware is written, the app verifies the update and waits for the device to come back online: . Once the update succeeds: . | The node reboots automatically | The Bluetooth connection re-establishes | Verify your settings are intact | Confirm the new version under Currently Installed on the Firmware Update screen — it’s also shown on the node’s detail page and the Connections screen | .

1547.title: Troubleshooting
1547.content: Update Stuck . If the update appears frozen: . | Give it a minute. After writing the image the app waits up to 60 seconds for the node to come back and report its new version, so a pause at the verify step is expected. | If it is still stuck after that, power-cycle the node. | Attempt the update again. | . The message Verification timed out. Device did not reconnect in time. means the image was written but the node did not come back within that window. Power-cycle it and check the version under Currently Installed before re-running the update. Radio Won’t Boot After Update . A Bluetooth update that stops partway can leave the node waiting in bootloader mode. While the app is disconnected, the Connect tab then shows a Finish updating card naming the node. Tap Resume firmware update and keep the node nearby so the app can re-flash it, or dismiss the card if the update can’t be finished from the phone. If the app told you the Bluetooth update could not be finished, follow the instruction it gave: connect the node to a computer over USB and re-flash it with the vendor’s serial DFU tool, such as adafruit-nrfutil. A stock nRF bootloader cannot reliably complete an interrupted over-the-air update. On the Meshtastic nRF52 Bootloader 2.6.0 and later, a dropped Bluetooth update can start over, and where the node waits depends on its power: . | On battery, it waits for the Bluetooth update, so Resume firmware update can reach it. | Plugged into a computer, it shows NO FIRMWARE and comes up as its update drive, not over Bluetooth. Copy your board’s firmware .uf2 onto the drive, or use the Web Flasher. Unplug it to resume over Bluetooth. The app’s USB update cannot start here. | . Otherwise, if your node fails to boot: . | Try connecting via USB to a computer | Use the web flasher in recovery/DFU mode | Flash a known-good firmware version | Check the Meshtastic Discord for device-specific recovery steps | . Compatibility Warnings . On connecting, the app compares the node’s firmware against two thresholds and reacts differently to each: . | Firmware version | What you see | What happens | . | Below 2.3.15 | Firmware update required. | The app disconnects from the node. It does not operate against firmware this old. | . | 2.3.15 up to, but not including, 2.5.14 | Firmware update required | The node stays connected, but the dialog blocks the rest of the app until the firmware is updated. It names the installed, minimum, and latest stable versions. Update firmware opens the Firmware Update screen; Disconnect drops the node. | . | 2.5.14 or newer | Nothing | — | . A version string the app cannot parse is ignored rather than treated as too old, so a transient read never disconnects a working node.

1582.title: Checking for Updates
1582.content: . | Open Settings for the connected node and, under Advanced, tap Firmware Update. The entry appears only for OTA-capable nodes. | The app checks for available firmware versions. | Available updates show the version number and release notes. | . The app also tells you when the connected node is behind the latest stable release. 1583.title: Update Methods
1583.content: The Firmware Update screen picks the method from how the node is connected, and its update button names it: Update via BLE OTA, Update via Wi-Fi OTA, or Update via USB File Transfer. | Connection | nRF52 | ESP32 | RP2040 | . | Bluetooth | BLE OTA | BLE OTA | — | . | Network | — | Wi-Fi OTA | — | . | USB | USB File Transfer | — | USB File Transfer | . Where the table has no method, the screen says firmware updates are not supported over this connection. Connect another way, or use the Web Flasher. OTA (Over-The-Air) via Bluetooth . The most common update method for Android users: . ⚠️ Warning: Interrupting a firmware update can leave the node unable to boot. Keep the phone nearby and both devices powered until the update completes. | Ensure your node is connected via Bluetooth. | Navigate to the Firmware Update screen. | Select the desired firmware version. | Tap Update via BLE OTA. An Update Warning dialog lists the pre-flight checks — read it, then tap I know what I’m doing. to start. This dialog appears for every update method, including Wi-Fi OTA, USB, and a local firmware file. | Wait for the update to complete. Do not disconnect during the update. | . While the update downloads, uploads or verifies, you can tap Play Chirpy Hop to play a short runner game: tap to jump, swipe down to crouch. The update’s progress stays visible above the game, and back returns to the update screen. When the update finishes or fails, the game stops and offers Back to update. Your best score is kept on this device. Some boards ship with a bootloader that cannot take a Bluetooth update. For these, the screen shows a warning card before you start, with a hint for the board where one exists. Don’t show again for this device hides it for that node. When a stock nRF bootloader limits how fast the upload can run, the screen says so during the upload, and again on the success screen, with a link to the Meshtastic nRF52 Bootloader, which makes Bluetooth updates much faster. Erase device during update . Where the app offers it, an Erase device during update switch appears above the update button. It is a per-update opt-in and is never remembered. | Method | What erasing does | . | BLE / Wi-Fi OTA | Factory-resets the device once the update is verified. All settings and Bluetooth pairing are removed. | . | USB | Wipes the device’s flash completely, then installs the selected firmware from scratch. | . It is not offered for a local firmware file, during a recovery update, or over USB in the desktop app — the USB erase runs the Android-only maintenance sequence below. Over USB it is offered for nRF52 and RP2040 nodes only, and when the app can’t erase one safely, the switch is shown disabled with the reason. Afterwards the device needs setting up — and pairing — again. OTA via Wi-Fi (network-connected ESP32) . When an ESP32 node is connected over the network rather than Bluetooth, the app offers Wi-Fi OTA, which pushes the same update over TCP: . | Connect to the node over the network (see Connections). | Open the Firmware Update screen and pick a version. | Tap Update via Wi-Fi OTA. Keep the node and phone on the same network for the whole transfer. | . Wi-Fi OTA installs the ESP32 app image, a .bin file, rather than the .uf2 a USB update uses. The app selects the right file from the release for you. In-App USB Update . When your nRF52 or RP2040 node is connected over USB/serial (rather than Bluetooth), the Firmware Update screen offers USB File Transfer. The app reboots the device into DFU mode, then prompts you to save the .uf2 file to the device’s DFU drive using the system file picker. This option appears only on a USB/serial connection. It is not available over Bluetooth, and ESP32 nodes have no USB update path in the app. A vendor nRF bootloader supplied as a .zip (e.g. RAK WisBlock RAK4631) has to be flashed with a serial DFU tool such as adafruit-nrfutil — copying that .zip to the drive won’t work. A bootloader supplied as an update-....uf2 can be installed by copying it to the drive; that is how the app’s own bootloader upgrade works. The app surfaces a hint when the serial-only route applies. Factory Erase and Bootloader Upgrade . On a USB/serial connection, nRF52 and RP2040 devices can be wiped as part of an update — that is the Erase device during update opt-in described earlier on this page. nRF52 devices additionally offer Upgrade bootloader where an upgraded bootloader is published for the board; RP2040 devices run no Adafruit bootloader, so they never see it. The upgrade installs the Meshtastic nRF52 Bootloader release named on the card. Both are Android-only. They depend on Android’s update-drive checks, so the desktop app does not show them — use the Web Flasher there instead. Select a firmware version before either one: the app hides both until a release is chosen, because the firmware is reinstalled after the device is wiped or the new bootloader is written. Both a USB erase and a bootloader upgrade write two files in turn, so you are asked to select the device’s update drive twice: once for the erase or bootloader image, then again for the firmware. The app reads INFO_UF2.TXT from the drive you select to confirm it really is the device’s update drive and to identify the board before writing anything. For a bootloader upgrade, the app also reads the installed bootloader version from INFO_UF2.TXT and shows it next to the latest release before writing anything. The running firmware doesn’t report its bootloader, so the installed version appears only once the device has restarted into update mode, never on the firmware screen while connected. If the two match, the bootloader is left as it is and the app moves straight on to reinstalling the firmware. Otherwise choose Upgrade bootloader to write it, or Skip to reinstall the firmware without changing it. On nRF52 the app must already know which Bluetooth stack your device uses before it starts, because it can’t read the bootloader until the device has rebooted. If it can’t confirm the stack, it refuses to erase and points you at the Web Flasher instead. In the Web Flasher, choosing the wrong Bluetooth stack can leave the node recoverable only with a hardware programmer. Once the drive is readable, how an nRF52 device is erased depends on its bootloader: . | Newer bootloaders erase themselves. A bootloader that advertises factory-erase support in INFO_UF2.TXT (OTAFIX 2.4 and later) takes a single, board-agnostic erase file. The bootloader wipes your settings, channels, keys and the stored node list itself, leaves the installed firmware in place, and comes back as an update drive a second or two later for the firmware file. There is no Bluetooth-stack choice to get wrong on this path. | Older bootloaders need a Bluetooth-stack-specific erase. On these the app writes a small erase program matched to your device’s Bluetooth stack, then starts it over the serial port. If the drive reports a different stack than expected, the app refuses rather than guessing. | . The app picks the path from what the drive reports; you don’t choose it. What the nRF52 bootloader does . Version 2.6.0 and later of the Meshtastic nRF52 Bootloader does the following while the update drive is up. | Backup. CURRENT.UF2 on the drive is a copy of the installed firmware. Copy it off to back up, or back onto the drive to reinstall. | Screen. On a node with a screen, the title reads BOOTLOADER, ERASE, WRONG FILE or NO FIRMWARE, and a progress bar shows the copy. | Wrong file. A firmware file the board cannot take is refused as WRONG FILE. | Interrupted copy. If the cable is pulled mid-copy, the node has no firmware. Plug it in again and copy the firmware once more. | Idle. After 6 minutes with no update activity, a node with firmware boots it. A node with no firmware keeps waiting. | Single-button boards. The T1000-E and the MeshTracker X1 have no reset button. Hold the button for about 3 seconds while the node powers on to enter update mode. Eject the drive from the computer to leave without copying a file. The app’s USB update needs no button. | . Other Flashing Options . For recovery or when neither OTA nor in-app USB is available: . | Use the Meshtastic Web Flasher | Or the Meshtastic CLI tool on desktop | .

1601.title: Pre-Update Checklist
1601.content: Before updating: . | Battery above 50%, recommended. The app itself refuses to start an update only when the node reports 10% or less | A stable connection over the method you’re updating with: Bluetooth, Wi-Fi, or USB | Note your current settings (they may reset on major version changes) | Check the release notes for breaking changes | Update the Meshtastic app itself, before or alongside firmware updates, to ensure compatibility | .

1602.title: Post-Update
1602.content: After the firmware is written, the app verifies the update and waits for the device to come back online: . Once the update succeeds: . | The node reboots automatically | The Bluetooth connection re-establishes | Verify your settings are intact | Confirm the new version under Currently Installed on the Firmware Update screen — it’s also shown on the node’s detail page and the Connections screen | .

1603.title: Troubleshooting
1603.content: Update Stuck . If the update appears frozen: . | Give it a minute. After writing the image the app waits up to 60 seconds for the node to come back and report its new version, so a pause at the verify step is expected. | If it is still stuck after that, power-cycle the node. | Attempt the update again. | . The message Verification timed out. Device did not reconnect in time. means the image was written but the node did not come back within that window. Power-cycle it and check the version under Currently Installed before re-running the update. Radio Won’t Boot After Update . A Bluetooth update that stops partway can leave the node waiting in bootloader mode. While the app is disconnected, the Connect tab then shows a Finish updating card naming the node. Tap Resume firmware update and keep the node nearby so the app can re-flash it, or dismiss the card if the update can’t be finished from the phone. If the app told you the Bluetooth update could not be finished, follow the instruction it gave: connect the node to a computer over USB and re-flash it with the vendor’s serial DFU tool, such as adafruit-nrfutil. A stock nRF bootloader cannot reliably complete an interrupted over-the-air update. On the Meshtastic nRF52 Bootloader 2.6.0 and later, a dropped Bluetooth update can start over, and where the node waits depends on its power: . | On battery, it waits for the Bluetooth update, so Resume firmware update can reach it. | Plugged into a computer, it shows NO FIRMWARE and comes up as its update drive, not over Bluetooth. Copy your board’s firmware .uf2 onto the drive, or use the Web Flasher. Unplug it to resume over Bluetooth. The app’s USB update cannot start here. | . Otherwise, if your node fails to boot: . | Try connecting via USB to a computer | Use the web flasher in recovery/DFU mode | Flash a known-good firmware version | Check the Meshtastic Discord for device-specific recovery steps | . Compatibility Warnings . On connecting, the app compares the node’s firmware against two thresholds and reacts differently to each: . | Versión del software | What you see | What happens | . | Below 2.3.15 | Firmware update required. | The app disconnects from the node. It does not operate against firmware this old. | . | 2.3.15 up to, but not including, 2.5.14 | Firmware update required | The node stays connected, but the dialog blocks the rest of the app until the firmware is updated. It names the installed, minimum, and latest stable versions. Update firmware opens the Firmware Update screen; Disconnect drops the node. | . | 2.5.14 or newer | Nothing | — | . A version string the app cannot parse is ignored rather than treated as too old, so a transient read never disconnects a working node.

Where the table has no method, the screen says firmware updates are not supported over this connection. Connect another way, or use the Web Flasher. OTA (Over-The-Air) via Bluetooth . The most common update method for Android users: . ⚠️ Warning: Interrupting a firmware update can leave the node unable to boot. Keep the phone nearby and both devices powered until the update completes. | Ensure your node is connected via Bluetooth. | Navigate to the Firmware Update screen. | Select the desired firmware version. | Tap Update via BLE OTA. An Update Warning dialog lists the pre-flight checks — read it, then tap I know what I’m doing. to start. This dialog appears for every update method, including Wi-Fi OTA, USB, and a local firmware file. | Wait for the update to complete. Do not disconnect during the update. | . While the update downloads, uploads or verifies, you can tap Play Chirpy Hop to play a short runner game: tap to jump, swipe down to crouch. The update’s progress stays visible above the game, and back returns to the update screen. When the update finishes or fails, the game stops and offers Back to update. Your best score is kept on this device. Some boards ship with a bootloader that cannot take a Bluetooth update. For these, the screen shows a warning card before you start, with a hint for the board where one exists. Don’t show again for this device hides it for that node. When a stock nRF bootloader limits how fast the upload can run, the screen says so during the upload, and again on the success screen, with a link to the Meshtastic nRF52 Bootloader, which makes Bluetooth updates much faster. Erase device during update . Where the app offers it, an Erase device during update switch appears above the update button. It is a per-update opt-in and is never remembered. | Method | What erasing does | . | BLE / Wi-Fi OTA | Factory-resets the device once the update is verified. All settings and Bluetooth pairing are removed. | . | USB | Wipes the device’s flash completely, then installs the selected firmware from scratch. | . It is not offered for a local firmware file, during a recovery update, or over USB in the desktop app — the USB erase runs the Android-only maintenance sequence below. Over USB it is offered for nRF52 and RP2040 nodes only, and when the app can’t erase one safely, the switch is shown disabled with the reason. Afterwards the device needs setting up — and pairing — again. OTA via Wi-Fi (network-connected ESP32) . When an ESP32 node is connected over the network rather than Bluetooth, the app offers Wi-Fi OTA, which pushes the same update over TCP: . | Connect to the node over the network (see Connections). | Open the Firmware Update screen and pick a version. | Tap Update via Wi-Fi OTA. Keep the node and phone on the same network for the whole transfer. | . Wi-Fi OTA installs the ESP32 app image, a .bin file, rather than the .uf2 a USB update uses. The app selects the right file from the release for you. In-App USB Update . When your nRF52 or RP2040 node is connected over USB/serial (rather than Bluetooth), the Firmware Update screen offers USB File Transfer. The app reboots the device into DFU mode, then prompts you to save the .uf2 file to the device’s DFU drive using the system file picker. This option appears only on a USB/serial connection. It is not available over Bluetooth, and ESP32 nodes have no USB update path in the app. A vendor nRF bootloader supplied as a .zip (e.g. RAK WisBlock RAK4631) has to be flashed with a serial DFU tool such as adafruit-nrfutil — copying that .zip to the drive won’t work. A bootloader supplied as an update-....uf2 can be installed by copying it to the drive; that is how the app’s own bootloader upgrade works. The app surfaces a hint when the serial-only route applies. Factory Erase and Bootloader Upgrade . On a USB/serial connection, nRF52 and RP2040 devices can be wiped as part of an update — that is the Erase device during update opt-in described earlier on this page. nRF52 devices additionally offer Upgrade bootloader where an upgraded bootloader is published for the board; RP2040 devices run no Adafruit bootloader, so they never see it. The upgrade installs the Meshtastic nRF52 Bootloader release named on the card. Both are Android-only. They depend on Android’s update-drive checks, so the desktop app does not show them — use the Web Flasher there instead. Select a firmware version before either one: the app hides both until a release is chosen, because the firmware is reinstalled after the device is wiped or the new bootloader is written. Both a USB erase and a bootloader upgrade write two files in turn, so you are asked to select the device’s update drive twice: once for the erase or bootloader image, then again for the firmware. The running firmware doesn’t report its bootloader, so the installed version appears only once the device has restarted into update mode, never on the firmware screen while connected. If the two match, the bootloader is left as it is and the app moves straight on to reinstalling the firmware. A bootloader that advertises factory-erase support in INFO_UF2.TXT (OTAFIX 2.4 and later) takes a single, board-agnostic erase file. On these the app writes a small erase program matched to your device’s Bluetooth stack, then starts it over the serial port. If the drive reports a different stack than expected, the app refuses rather than guessing. | . The app picks the path from what the drive reports; you don’t choose it. What the nRF52 bootloader does . Version 2.6.0 and later of the Meshtastic nRF52 Bootloader does the following while the update drive is up. | Backup. CURRENT.UF2 on the drive is a copy of the installed firmware. Copy it off to back up, or back onto the drive to reinstall. | Screen. On a node with a screen, the title reads BOOTLOADER, ERASE, WRONG FILE or NO FIRMWARE, and a progress bar shows the copy. | Wrong file. A firmware file the board cannot take is refused as WRONG FILE. | Interrupted copy. If the cable is pulled mid-copy, the node has no firmware. Plug it in again and copy the firmware once more. | Idle. After 6 minutes with no update activity, a node with firmware boots it. A node with no firmware keeps waiting. | Single-button boards. The T1000-E and the MeshTracker X1 have no reset button. Hold the button for about 3 seconds while the node powers on to enter update mode. Eject the drive from the computer to leave without copying a file. The app’s USB update needs no button. | . Other Flashing Options . 1674.title: Post-Update
1674.content: After the firmware is written, the app verifies the update and waits for the device to come back online: . Once the update succeeds: . | The node reboots automatically | The Bluetooth connection re-establishes | Verify your settings are intact | Confirm the new version under Currently Installed on the Firmware Update screen — it’s also shown on the node’s detail page and the Connections screen | .

1675.title: Troubleshooting
1675.content: Update Stuck . If the update appears frozen: . | Give it a minute. After writing the image the app waits up to 60 seconds for the node to come back and report its new version, so a pause at the verify step is expected. | If it is still stuck after that, power-cycle the node. | Attempt the update again. | . The message Verification timed out. Device did not reconnect in time. means the image was written but the node did not come back within that window. Power-cycle it and check the version under Currently Installed before re-running the update. Radio Won’t Boot After Update . A Bluetooth update that stops partway can leave the node waiting in bootloader mode. While the app is disconnected, the Connect tab then shows a Finish updating card naming the node. Tap Resume firmware update and keep the node nearby so the app can re-flash it, or dismiss the card if the update can’t be finished from the phone. If the app told you the Bluetooth update could not be finished, follow the instruction it gave: connect the node to a computer over USB and re-flash it with the vendor’s serial DFU tool, such as adafruit-nrfutil. A stock nRF bootloader cannot reliably complete an interrupted over-the-air update. On the Meshtastic nRF52 Bootloader 2.6.0 and later, a dropped Bluetooth update can start over, and where the node waits depends on its power: . | On battery, it waits for the Bluetooth update, so Resume firmware update can reach it. | Plugged into a computer, it shows NO FIRMWARE and comes up as its update drive, not over Bluetooth. Copy your board’s firmware .uf2 onto the drive, or use the Web Flasher. Unplug it to resume over Bluetooth. The app’s USB update cannot start here. | . Otherwise, if your node fails to boot: . | Try connecting via USB to a computer | Use the web flasher in recovery/DFU mode | Flash a known-good firmware version | Check the Meshtastic Discord for device-specific recovery steps | . Compatibility Warnings . On connecting, the app compares the node’s firmware against two thresholds and reacts differently to each: . | Firmware version | What you see | What happens | . | Below 2.3.15 | Firmware update required. | The app disconnects from the node. It does not operate against firmware this old. | . | 2.3.15 up to, but not including, 2.5.14 | Firmware update required | The node stays connected, but the dialog blocks the rest of the app until the firmware is updated. It names the installed, minimum, and latest stable versions. Update firmware opens the Firmware Update screen; Disconnect drops the node. | . | 2.5.14 or newer | Nothing | — | . 1679.title: Update Methods
1679.content: OTA (Over-The-Air) via Bluetooth . The most common update method for Android users: . ⚠️ Warning: Interrupting a firmware update can leave the radio unable to boot. Keep the phone nearby and both devices powered until the update completes. | Ensure your radio is connected via Bluetooth. | Navigate to the Firmware Update screen. | Select the desired firmware version. | Tap Update. An Update Warning dialog lists the pre-flight checks — read it, then tap I know what I’m doing. to start. This dialog appears for every update method, including Wi-Fi OTA, USB, and a local firmware file. | Wait for the update to complete — do not disconnect during the update. | . While the update downloads, uploads or verifies, you can tap Play Chirpy Hop to play a short runner game: tap to jump, swipe down to crouch. The update’s progress stays visible above the game, and back returns to the update screen. When the update finishes or fails, the game stops and offers Back to update. The app reboots the device into DFU mode, then prompts you to save the .uf2 file to the device’s DFU drive using the system file picker. If the drive reports a different stack than expected, the app refuses rather than guessing. | . The app picks the path from what the drive reports; you don’t choose it. 1698.title: Post-Update
1698.content: After the firmware is written, the app verifies the update and waits for the device to come back online: . Once the update succeeds: . | The node reboots automatically | The Bluetooth connection re-establishes | Verify your settings are intact | Confirm the new version under Currently Installed on the Firmware Update screen — it’s also shown on the node’s detail page and the Connections screen | .

1699.title: Risoluzione problemi

Copy your board’s firmware .uf2 onto the drive, or use the Web Flasher. Unplug it to resume over Bluetooth. The app’s USB update cannot start here. | . Otherwise, if your node fails to boot: . | Try connecting via USB to a computer | Use the web flasher in recovery/DFU mode | Flash a known-good firmware version | Check the Meshtastic Discord for device-specific recovery steps | . Compatibility Warnings . It does not operate against firmware this old. | . | 2.3.15 up to, but not including, 2.5.14 | Firmware update required | The node stays connected, but the dialog blocks the rest of the app until the firmware is updated. It names the installed, minimum, and latest stable versions. Update firmware opens the Firmware Update screen; Disconnect drops the node. | . | 2.5.14 or newer | Nothing | — | . Where the table has no method, the screen says firmware updates are not supported over this connection. Connect another way, or use the Web Flasher. OTA (Over-The-Air) чрез Bluetooth . Keep the phone nearby and both devices powered until the update completes. | Ensure your node is connected via Bluetooth. | Отидете до екрана за актуализация на фърмуера. | Изберете желаната версия на фърмуера. | Tap Update via BLE OTA. An Update Warning dialog lists the pre-flight checks — read it, then tap I know what I’m doing. to start. This dialog appears for every update method, including Wi-Fi OTA, USB, and a local firmware file. | Wait for the update to complete. Do not disconnect during the update. | . While the update downloads, uploads or verifies, you can tap Play Chirpy Hop to play a short runner game: tap to jump, swipe down to crouch. The update’s progress stays visible above the game, and back returns to the update screen. When the update finishes or fails, the game stops and offers Back to update. Your best score is kept on this device. Some boards ship with a bootloader that cannot take a Bluetooth update. For these, the screen shows a warning card before you start, with a hint for the board where one exists. Don’t show again for this device hides it for that node. When a stock nRF bootloader limits how fast the upload can run, the screen says so during the upload, and again on the success screen, with a link to the Meshtastic nRF52 Bootloader, which makes Bluetooth updates much faster. Erase device during update . Where the app offers it, an Erase device during update switch appears above the update button. It is a per-update opt-in and is never remembered. | Method | What erasing does | . | BLE / Wi-Fi OTA | Factory-resets the device once the update is verified. All settings and Bluetooth pairing are removed. | . | USB | Wipes the device’s flash completely, then installs the selected firmware from scratch. | . It is not offered for a local firmware file, during a recovery update, or over USB in the desktop app — the USB erase runs the Android-only maintenance sequence below. Over USB it is offered for nRF52 and RP2040 nodes only, and when the app can’t erase one safely, the switch is shown disabled with the reason. Afterwards the device needs setting up — and pairing — again. OTA via Wi-Fi (network-connected ESP32) . When an ESP32 node is connected over the network rather than Bluetooth, the app offers Wi-Fi OTA, which pushes the same update over TCP: . | Connect to the node over the network (see Connections). | Open the Firmware Update screen and pick a version. | Tap Update via Wi-Fi OTA. The app selects the right file from the release for you. In-App USB Update . When your nRF52 or RP2040 node is connected over USB/serial (rather than Bluetooth), the Firmware Update screen offers USB File Transfer. The app reboots the device into DFU mode, then prompts you to save the .uf2 file to the device’s DFU drive using the system file picker. This option appears only on a USB/serial connection. It is not available over Bluetooth, and ESP32 nodes have no USB update path in the app. A vendor nRF bootloader supplied as a .zip (e.g. RAK WisBlock RAK4631) has to be flashed with a serial DFU tool such as adafruit-nrfutil — copying that .zip to the drive won’t work. A bootloader supplied as an update-....uf2 can be installed by copying it to the drive; that is how the app’s own bootloader upgrade works. The app surfaces a hint when the serial-only route applies. On a USB/serial connection, nRF52 and RP2040 devices can be wiped as part of an update — that is the Erase device during update opt-in described earlier on this page. nRF52 devices additionally offer Upgrade bootloader where an upgraded bootloader is published for the board; RP2040 devices run no Adafruit bootloader, so they never see it. The upgrade installs the Meshtastic nRF52 Bootloader release named on the card. Both are Android-only. Both a USB erase and a bootloader upgrade write two files in turn, so you are asked to select the device’s update drive twice: once for the erase or bootloader image, then again for the firmware. A bootloader that advertises factory-erase support in INFO_UF2.TXT (OTAFIX 2.4 and later) takes a single, board-agnostic erase file. There is no Bluetooth-stack choice to get wrong on this path. | Older bootloaders need a Bluetooth-stack-specific erase. On these the app writes a small erase program matched to your device’s Bluetooth stack, then starts it over the serial port. If the drive reports a different stack than expected, the app refuses rather than guessing. | . The app picks the path from what the drive reports; you don’t choose it. What the nRF52 bootloader does . Version 2.6.0 and later of the Meshtastic nRF52 Bootloader does the following while the update drive is up. | Backup. CURRENT.UF2 on the drive is a copy of the installed firmware. Copy it off to back up, or back onto the drive to reinstall. | Screen. On a node with a screen, the title reads BOOTLOADER, ERASE, WRONG FILE or NO FIRMWARE, and a progress bar shows the copy. | Wrong file. A firmware file the board cannot take is refused as WRONG FILE. | Interrupted copy. If the cable is pulled mid-copy, the node has no firmware. Plug it in again and copy the firmware once more. | Idle. After 6 minutes with no update activity, a node with firmware boots it. A node with no firmware keeps waiting. | Single-button boards. The T1000-E and the MeshTracker X1 have no reset button. Hold the button for about 3 seconds while the node powers on to enter update mode. Eject the drive from the computer to leave without copying a file. The app’s USB update needs no button. | . Other Flashing Options . For recovery or when neither OTA nor in-app USB is available: . | Use the Meshtastic Web Flasher | Or the Meshtastic CLI tool on desktop | .

1734.title: Checking for Updates
1734.content: . | Open Settings for the connected node and, under Advanced, tap Firmware Update. 1735.title: Update Methods
1735.content: The Firmware Update screen picks the method from how the node is connected, and its update button names it: Update via BLE OTA, Update via Wi-Fi OTA, or Update via USB File Transfer. | Connection | nRF52 | ESP32 | RP2040 | . | Bluetooth | BLE OTA | BLE OTA | — | . | Netwerk | — | Wi-Fi OTA | — | . | USB | USB File Transfer | — | USB File Transfer | . Where the table has no method, the screen says firmware updates are not supported over this connection. Connect another way, or use the Web Flasher. OTA (Over-The-Air) via Bluetooth . The most common update method for Android users: . ⚠️ Warning: Interrupting a firmware update can leave the node unable to boot. Keep the phone nearby and both devices powered until the update completes. | Ensure your node is connected via Bluetooth. | Navigate to the Firmware Update screen. | Select the desired firmware version. | Tap Update via BLE OTA. An Update Warning dialog lists the pre-flight checks — read it, then tap I know what I’m doing. to start. This dialog appears for every update method, including Wi-Fi OTA, USB, and a local firmware file. | Wait for the update to complete. Do not disconnect during the update. | . While the update downloads, uploads or verifies, you can tap Play Chirpy Hop to play a short runner game: tap to jump, swipe down to crouch. The update’s progress stays visible above the game, and back returns to the update screen. When the update finishes or fails, the game stops and offers Back to update. Your best score is kept on this device. Some boards ship with a bootloader that cannot take a Bluetooth update. For these, the screen shows a warning card before you start, with a hint for the board where one exists. Don’t show again for this device hides it for that node. When a stock nRF bootloader limits how fast the upload can run, the screen says so during the upload, and again on the success screen, with a link to the Meshtastic nRF52 Bootloader, which makes Bluetooth updates much faster. Erase device during update . Where the app offers it, an Erase device during update switch appears above the update button. It is a per-update opt-in and is never remembered. | Method | What erasing does | . | BLE / Wi-Fi OTA | Factory-resets the device once the update is verified. All settings and Bluetooth pairing are removed. | . | USB | Wipes the device’s flash completely, then installs the selected firmware from scratch. | . It is not offered for a local firmware file, during a recovery update, or over USB in the desktop app — the USB erase runs the Android-only maintenance sequence below. Over USB it is offered for nRF52 and RP2040 nodes only, and when the app can’t erase one safely, the switch is shown disabled with the reason. Afterwards the device needs setting up — and pairing — again. OTA via Wi-Fi (network-connected ESP32) . When an ESP32 node is connected over the network rather than Bluetooth, the app offers Wi-Fi OTA, which pushes the same update over TCP: . | Connect to the node over the network (see Connections). | Open the Firmware Update screen and pick a version. | Tap Update via Wi-Fi OTA. Keep the node and phone on the same network for the whole transfer. | . Wi-Fi OTA installs the ESP32 app image, a .bin file, rather than the .uf2 a USB update uses. The app selects the right file from the release for you. In-App USB Update . When your nRF52 or RP2040 node is connected over USB/serial (rather than Bluetooth), the Firmware Update screen offers USB File Transfer. The app reboots the device into DFU mode, then prompts you to save the .uf2 file to the device’s DFU drive using the system file picker. This option appears only on a USB/serial connection. It is not available over Bluetooth, and ESP32 nodes have no USB update path in the app. A vendor nRF bootloader supplied as a .zip (e.g. RAK WisBlock RAK4631) has to be flashed with a serial DFU tool such as adafruit-nrfutil — copying that .zip to the drive won’t work. A bootloader supplied as an update-....uf2 can be installed by copying it to the drive; that is how the app’s own bootloader upgrade works. The app surfaces a hint when the serial-only route applies. Factory Erase and Bootloader Upgrade . On a USB/serial connection, nRF52 and RP2040 devices can be wiped as part of an update — that is the Erase device during update opt-in described earlier on this page. nRF52 devices additionally offer Upgrade bootloader where an upgraded bootloader is published for the board; RP2040 devices run no Adafruit bootloader, so they never see it. The upgrade installs the Meshtastic nRF52 Bootloader release named on the card. Both are Android-only. They depend on Android’s update-drive checks, so the desktop app does not show them — use the Web Flasher there instead. Select a firmware version before either one: the app hides both until a release is chosen, because the firmware is reinstalled after the device is wiped or the new bootloader is written. Both a USB erase and a bootloader upgrade write two files in turn, so you are asked to select the device’s update drive twice: once for the erase or bootloader image, then again for the firmware. The app reads INFO_UF2.TXT from the drive you select to confirm it really is the device’s update drive and to identify the board before writing anything. For a bootloader upgrade, the app also reads the installed bootloader version from INFO_UF2.TXT and shows it next to the latest release before writing anything. The running firmware doesn’t report its bootloader, so the installed version appears only once the device has restarted into update mode, never on the firmware screen while connected. If the two match, the bootloader is left as it is and the app moves straight on to reinstalling the firmware. Otherwise choose Upgrade bootloader to write it, or Skip to reinstall the firmware without changing it. On nRF52 the app must already know which Bluetooth stack your device uses before it starts, because it can’t read the bootloader until the device has rebooted. If it can’t confirm the stack, it refuses to erase and points you at the Web Flasher instead. In the Web Flasher, choosing the wrong Bluetooth stack can leave the node recoverable only with a hardware programmer. Once the drive is readable, how an nRF52 device is erased depends on its bootloader: . | Newer bootloaders erase themselves. A bootloader that advertises factory-erase support in INFO_UF2.TXT (OTAFIX 2.4 and later) takes a single, board-agnostic erase file. The bootloader wipes your settings, channels, keys and the stored node list itself, leaves the installed firmware in place, and comes back as an update drive a second or two later for the firmware file. There is no Bluetooth-stack choice to get wrong on this path. | Older bootloaders need a Bluetooth-stack-specific erase. On these the app writes a small erase program matched to your device’s Bluetooth stack, then starts it over the serial port. If the drive reports a different stack than expected, the app refuses rather than guessing. | . The app picks the path from what the drive reports; you don’t choose it. What the nRF52 bootloader does . Version 2.6.0 and later of the Meshtastic nRF52 Bootloader does the following while the update drive is up. | Backup. CURRENT.UF2 on the drive is a copy of the installed firmware. Copy it off to back up, or back onto the drive to reinstall. | Screen. On a node with a screen, the title reads BOOTLOADER, ERASE, WRONG FILE or NO FIRMWARE, and a progress bar shows the copy. | Wrong file. A firmware file the board cannot take is refused as WRONG FILE. | Interrupted copy. If the cable is pulled mid-copy, the node has no firmware. Plug it in again and copy the firmware once more. | Idle. After 6 minutes with no update activity, a node with firmware boots it. A node with no firmware keeps waiting. | Single-button boards. The T1000-E and the MeshTracker X1 have no reset button. Hold the button for about 3 seconds while the node powers on to enter update mode. Eject the drive from the computer to leave without copying a file. The app’s USB update needs no button. | . Other Flashing Options . For recovery or when neither OTA nor in-app USB is available: . | Use the Meshtastic Web Flasher | Or the Meshtastic CLI tool on desktop | .

Where the table has no method, the screen says firmware updates are not supported over this connection. Connect another way, or use the Web Flasher. OTA (Over-The-Air) via Bluetooth . The most common update method for Android users: . ⚠️ Warning: Interrupting a firmware update can leave the node unable to boot. Keep the phone nearby and both devices powered until the update completes. | Ensure your node is connected via Bluetooth. | Navigate to the Firmware Update screen. | Select the desired firmware version. | Tap Update via BLE OTA. An Update Warning dialog lists the pre-flight checks — read it, then tap I know what I’m doing. to start. This dialog appears for every update method, including Wi-Fi OTA, USB, and a local firmware file. | Wait for the update to complete. Do not disconnect during the update. | . While the update downloads, uploads or verifies, you can tap Play Chirpy Hop to play a short runner game: tap to jump, swipe down to crouch. The update’s progress stays visible above the game, and back returns to the update screen. When the update finishes or fails, the game stops and offers Back to update. Your best score is kept on this device. Some boards ship with a bootloader that cannot take a Bluetooth update. For these, the screen shows a warning card before you start, with a hint for the board where one exists. Don’t show again for this device hides it for that node. When a stock nRF bootloader limits how fast the upload can run, the screen says so during the upload, and again on the success screen, with a link to the Meshtastic nRF52 Bootloader, which makes Bluetooth updates much faster. Erase device during update . Where the app offers it, an Erase device during update switch appears above the update button. It is a per-update opt-in and is never remembered. | Method | What erasing does | . | BLE / Wi-Fi OTA | Factory-resets the device once the update is verified. All settings and Bluetooth pairing are removed. | . | USB | Wipes the device’s flash completely, then installs the selected firmware from scratch. | . It is not offered for a local firmware file, during a recovery update, or over USB in the desktop app — the USB erase runs the Android-only maintenance sequence below. Over USB it is offered for nRF52 and RP2040 nodes only, and when the app can’t erase one safely, the switch is shown disabled with the reason. Afterwards the device needs setting up — and pairing — again. OTA via Wi-Fi (network-connected ESP32) . When an ESP32 node is connected over the network rather than Bluetooth, the app offers Wi-Fi OTA, which pushes the same update over TCP: . | Connect to the node over the network (see Connections). | Open the Firmware Update screen and pick a version. | Tap Update via Wi-Fi OTA. Keep the node and phone on the same network for the whole transfer. | . Wi-Fi OTA installs the ESP32 app image, a .bin file, rather than the .uf2 a USB update uses. The app selects the right file from the release for you. In-App USB Update . When your nRF52 or RP2040 node is connected over USB/serial (rather than Bluetooth), the Firmware Update screen offers USB File Transfer. The app reboots the device into DFU mode, then prompts you to save the .uf2 file to the device’s DFU drive using the system file picker. This option appears only on a USB/serial connection. It is not available over Bluetooth, and ESP32 nodes have no USB update path in the app. A vendor nRF bootloader supplied as a .zip (e.g. RAK WisBlock RAK4631) has to be flashed with a serial DFU tool such as adafruit-nrfutil — copying that .zip to the drive won’t work. A bootloader supplied as an update-....uf2 can be installed by copying it to the drive; that is how the app’s own bootloader upgrade works. The app surfaces a hint when the serial-only route applies. Factory Erase and Bootloader Upgrade . On a USB/serial connection, nRF52 and RP2040 devices can be wiped as part of an update — that is the Erase device during update opt-in described earlier on this page. nRF52 devices additionally offer Upgrade bootloader where an upgraded bootloader is published for the board; RP2040 devices run no Adafruit bootloader, so they never see it. The upgrade installs the Meshtastic nRF52 Bootloader release named on the card. Both are Android-only. They depend on Android’s update-drive checks, so the desktop app does not show them — use the Web Flasher there instead. Select a firmware version before either one: the app hides both until a release is chosen, because the firmware is reinstalled after the device is wiped or the new bootloader is written. Both a USB erase and a bootloader upgrade write two files in turn, so you are asked to select the device’s update drive twice: once for the erase or bootloader image, then again for the firmware. The app reads INFO_UF2.TXT from the drive you select to confirm it really is the device’s update drive and to identify the board before writing anything. For a bootloader upgrade, the app also reads the installed bootloader version from INFO_UF2.TXT and shows it next to the latest release before writing anything. The running firmware doesn’t report its bootloader, so the installed version appears only once the device has restarted into update mode, never on the firmware screen while connected. If the two match, the bootloader is left as it is and the app moves straight on to reinstalling the firmware. Otherwise choose Upgrade bootloader to write it, or Skip to reinstall the firmware without changing it. On nRF52 the app must already know which Bluetooth stack your device uses before it starts, because it can’t read the bootloader until the device has rebooted. If it can’t confirm the stack, it refuses to erase and points you at the Web Flasher instead. In the Web Flasher, choosing the wrong Bluetooth stack can leave the node recoverable only with a hardware programmer. Once the drive is readable, how an nRF52 device is erased depends on its bootloader: . | Newer bootloaders erase themselves. A bootloader that advertises factory-erase support in INFO_UF2.TXT (OTAFIX 2.4 and later) takes a single, board-agnostic erase file. The bootloader wipes your settings, channels, keys and the stored node list itself, leaves the installed firmware in place, and comes back as an update drive a second or two later for the firmware file. There is no Bluetooth-stack choice to get wrong on this path. | Older bootloaders need a Bluetooth-stack-specific erase. On these the app writes a small erase program matched to your device’s Bluetooth stack, then starts it over the serial port. If the drive reports a different stack than expected, the app refuses rather than guessing. | . The app picks the path from what the drive reports; you don’t choose it. What the nRF52 bootloader does . Version 2.6.0 and later of the Meshtastic nRF52 Bootloader does the following while the update drive is up. | Backup. CURRENT.UF2 on the drive is a copy of the installed firmware. Copy it off to back up, or back onto the drive to reinstall. | Screen. On a node with a screen, the title reads BOOTLOADER, ERASE, WRONG FILE or NO FIRMWARE, and a progress bar shows the copy. | Wrong file. A firmware file the board cannot take is refused as WRONG FILE. | Interrupted copy. If the cable is pulled mid-copy, the node has no firmware. Plug it in again and copy the firmware once more. | Idle. After 6 minutes with no update activity, a node with firmware boots it. A node with no firmware keeps waiting. | Single-button boards. The T1000-E and the MeshTracker X1 have no reset button. Hold the button for about 3 seconds while the node powers on to enter update mode. Eject the drive from the computer to leave without copying a file. The app’s USB update needs no button. | . Other Flashing Options . For recovery or when neither OTA nor in-app USB is available: . | Use the Meshtastic Web Flasher | Or the Meshtastic CLI tool on desktop | .

1753.title: Pre-Update Checklist
1753.content: Before updating: . | Battery above 50%, recommended. The app itself refuses to start an update only when the node reports 10% or less | A stable connection over the method you’re updating with: Bluetooth, Wi-Fi, or USB | Note your current settings (they may reset on major version changes) | Check the release notes for breaking changes | Update the Meshtastic app itself, before or alongside firmware updates, to ensure compatibility | .

1754.title: Post-Update
1754.content: After the firmware is written, the app verifies the update and waits for the device to come back online: . Once the update succeeds: . | The node reboots automatically | The Bluetooth connection re-establishes | Verify your settings are intact | Confirm the new version under Currently Installed on the Firmware Update screen — it’s also shown on the node’s detail page and the Connections screen | .

1755.title: Troubleshooting
1755.content: Update Stuck . If the update appears frozen: . | Give it a minute. After writing the image the app waits up to 60 seconds for the node to come back and report its new version, so a pause at the verify step is expected. | If it is still stuck after that, power-cycle the node. | Attempt the update again. | . The message Verification timed out. Device did not reconnect in time. means the image was written but the node did not come back within that window. Power-cycle it and check the version under Currently Installed before re-running the update. Radio Won’t Boot After Update . A Bluetooth update that stops partway can leave the node waiting in bootloader mode. While the app is disconnected, the Connect tab then shows a Finish updating card naming the node. Tap Resume firmware update and keep the node nearby so the app can re-flash it, or dismiss the card if the update can’t be finished from the phone. If the app told you the Bluetooth update could not be finished, follow the instruction it gave: connect the node to a computer over USB and re-flash it with the vendor’s serial DFU tool, such as adafruit-nrfutil. A stock nRF bootloader cannot reliably complete an interrupted over-the-air update. On the Meshtastic nRF52 Bootloader 2.6.0 and later, a dropped Bluetooth update can start over, and where the node waits depends on its power: . | On battery, it waits for the Bluetooth update, so Resume firmware update can reach it. | Plugged into a computer, it shows NO FIRMWARE and comes up as its update drive, not over Bluetooth. Copy your board’s firmware .uf2 onto the drive, or use the Web Flasher. Unplug it to resume over Bluetooth. The app’s USB update cannot start here. | . Otherwise, if your node fails to boot: . | Try connecting via USB to a computer | Use the web flasher in recovery/DFU mode | Flash a known-good firmware version | Check the Meshtastic Discord for device-specific recovery steps | . Compatibility Warnings . On connecting, the app compares the node’s firmware against two thresholds and reacts differently to each: . | Firmware version | What you see | What happens | . | Below 2.3.15 | Firmware update required. | The app disconnects from the node. It does not operate against firmware this old. | . | 2.3.15 up to, but not including, 2.5.14 | Firmware update required | The node stays connected, but the dialog blocks the rest of the app until the firmware is updated. It names the installed, minimum, and latest stable versions. Update firmware opens the Firmware Update screen; Disconnect drops the node. | . | 2.5.14 or newer | Nothing | — | . A version string the app cannot parse is ignored rather than treated as too old, so a transient read never disconnects a working node.

On these the app writes a small erase program matched to your device’s Bluetooth stack, then starts it over the serial port. If the drive reports a different stack than expected, the app refuses rather than guessing. | . The app picks the path from what the drive reports; you don’t choose it.
