On a node with a screen, the title reads BOOTLOADER, ERASE, WRONG FILE or NO FIRMWARE, and a progress bar shows the copy. | Wrong file. A firmware file the board cannot take is refused as WRONG FILE. | Interrupted copy. If the cable is pulled mid-copy, the node has no firmware. Plug it in again and copy the firmware once more. | Idle. After 6 minutes with no update activity, a node with firmware boots it. A node with no firmware keeps waiting. | Single-button boards. The T1000-E and the MeshTracker X1 have no reset button. Hold the button for about 3 seconds while the node powers on to enter update mode. Eject the drive from the computer to leave without copying a file. The app’s USB update needs no button. | . Other Flashing Options . 1770.title: Post-Update
1770.content: After the firmware is written, the app verifies the update and waits for the device to come back online: . Once the update succeeds: . | The node reboots automatically | The Bluetooth connection re-establishes | Verify your settings are intact | Confirm the new version under Currently Installed on the Firmware Update screen — it’s also shown on the node’s detail page and the Connections screen | .

1771.title: Troubleshooting
1771.content: Update Stuck . If the update appears frozen: . | Give it a minute. After writing the image the app waits up to 60 seconds for the node to come back and report its new version, so a pause at the verify step is expected. | If it is still stuck after that, power-cycle the node. | Attempt the update again. | . Copy your board’s firmware .uf2 onto the drive, or use the Web Flasher. Unplug it to resume over Bluetooth. The app’s USB update cannot start here. | . It does not operate against firmware this old. | . | 2.3.15 up to, but not including, 2.5.14 | Firmware update required | The node stays connected, but the dialog blocks the rest of the app until the firmware is updated. 1791.title: Update Methods
1791.content: The Firmware Update screen picks the method from how the node is connected, and its update button names it: Update via BLE OTA, Update via Wi-Fi OTA, or Update via USB File Transfer. | Connection | nRF52 | ESP32 | RP2040 | . | Bluetooth | BLE OTA | BLE OTA | — | . | Сетка | — | Wi-Fi OTA | — | . | USB | USB File Transfer | — | USB File Transfer | . Where the table has no method, the screen says firmware updates are not supported over this connection. Connect another way, or use the Web Flasher. OTA (Over-The-Air) via Bluetooth . The most common update method for Android users: . ⚠️ Warning: Interrupting a firmware update can leave the node unable to boot. Keep the phone nearby and both devices powered until the update completes. | Ensure your node is connected via Bluetooth. | Navigate to the Firmware Update screen. | Select the desired firmware version. | Tap Update via BLE OTA. An Update Warning dialog lists the pre-flight checks — read it, then tap I know what I’m doing. to start. This dialog appears for every update method, including Wi-Fi OTA, USB, and a local firmware file. | Wait for the update to complete. Do not disconnect during the update. | . While the update downloads, uploads or verifies, you can tap Play Chirpy Hop to play a short runner game: tap to jump, swipe down to crouch. The update’s progress stays visible above the game, and back returns to the update screen. When the update finishes or fails, the game stops and offers Back to update. Your best score is kept on this device. Some boards ship with a bootloader that cannot take a Bluetooth update. For these, the screen shows a warning card before you start, with a hint for the board where one exists. Don’t show again for this device hides it for that node. When a stock nRF bootloader limits how fast the upload can run, the screen says so during the upload, and again on the success screen, with a link to the Meshtastic nRF52 Bootloader, which makes Bluetooth updates much faster. Erase device during update . Where the app offers it, an Erase device during update switch appears above the update button. It is a per-update opt-in and is never remembered. | Method | What erasing does | . | BLE / Wi-Fi OTA | Factory-resets the device once the update is verified. All settings and Bluetooth pairing are removed. | . | USB | Wipes the device’s flash completely, then installs the selected firmware from scratch. | . It is not offered for a local firmware file, during a recovery update, or over USB in the desktop app — the USB erase runs the Android-only maintenance sequence below. Over USB it is offered for nRF52 and RP2040 nodes only, and when the app can’t erase one safely, the switch is shown disabled with the reason. Afterwards the device needs setting up — and pairing — again. OTA via Wi-Fi (network-connected ESP32) . When an ESP32 node is connected over the network rather than Bluetooth, the app offers Wi-Fi OTA, which pushes the same update over TCP: . | Connect to the node over the network (see Connections). | Open the Firmware Update screen and pick a version. | Tap Update via Wi-Fi OTA. Keep the node and phone on the same network for the whole transfer. | . Wi-Fi OTA installs the ESP32 app image, a .bin file, rather than the .uf2 a USB update uses. The app selects the right file from the release for you. In-App USB Update . When your nRF52 or RP2040 node is connected over USB/serial (rather than Bluetooth), the Firmware Update screen offers USB File Transfer. The app reboots the device into DFU mode, then prompts you to save the .uf2 file to the device’s DFU drive using the system file picker. This option appears only on a USB/serial connection. It is not available over Bluetooth, and ESP32 nodes have no USB update path in the app. A vendor nRF bootloader supplied as a .zip (e.g. RAK WisBlock RAK4631) has to be flashed with a serial DFU tool such as adafruit-nrfutil — copying that .zip to the drive won’t work. A bootloader supplied as an update-....uf2 can be installed by copying it to the drive; that is how the app’s own bootloader upgrade works. The app surfaces a hint when the serial-only route applies. Factory Erase and Bootloader Upgrade . On a USB/serial connection, nRF52 and RP2040 devices can be wiped as part of an update — that is the Erase device during update opt-in described earlier on this page. nRF52 devices additionally offer Upgrade bootloader where an upgraded bootloader is published for the board; RP2040 devices run no Adafruit bootloader, so they never see it. The upgrade installs the Meshtastic nRF52 Bootloader release named on the card. Both are Android-only. They depend on Android’s update-drive checks, so the desktop app does not show them — use the Web Flasher there instead. Select a firmware version before either one: the app hides both until a release is chosen, because the firmware is reinstalled after the device is wiped or the new bootloader is written. Both a USB erase and a bootloader upgrade write two files in turn, so you are asked to select the device’s update drive twice: once for the erase or bootloader image, then again for the firmware. The app reads INFO_UF2.TXT from the drive you select to confirm it really is the device’s update drive and to identify the board before writing anything. For a bootloader upgrade, the app also reads the installed bootloader version from INFO_UF2.TXT and shows it next to the latest release before writing anything. The running firmware doesn’t report its bootloader, so the installed version appears only once the device has restarted into update mode, never on the firmware screen while connected. If the two match, the bootloader is left as it is and the app moves straight on to reinstalling the firmware. Otherwise choose Upgrade bootloader to write it, or Skip to reinstall the firmware without changing it. On nRF52 the app must already know which Bluetooth stack your device uses before it starts, because it can’t read the bootloader until the device has rebooted. If it can’t confirm the stack, it refuses to erase and points you at the Web Flasher instead. In the Web Flasher, choosing the wrong Bluetooth stack can leave the node recoverable only with a hardware programmer. Once the drive is readable, how an nRF52 device is erased depends on its bootloader: . | Newer bootloaders erase themselves. A bootloader that advertises factory-erase support in INFO_UF2.TXT (OTAFIX 2.4 and later) takes a single, board-agnostic erase file. The bootloader wipes your settings, channels, keys and the stored node list itself, leaves the installed firmware in place, and comes back as an update drive a second or two later for the firmware file. There is no Bluetooth-stack choice to get wrong on this path. | Older bootloaders need a Bluetooth-stack-specific erase. On these the app writes a small erase program matched to your device’s Bluetooth stack, then starts it over the serial port. If the drive reports a different stack than expected, the app refuses rather than guessing. | . The app picks the path from what the drive reports; you don’t choose it. What the nRF52 bootloader does . Version 2.6.0 and later of the Meshtastic nRF52 Bootloader does the following while the update drive is up. | Backup. CURRENT.UF2 on the drive is a copy of the installed firmware. Copy it off to back up, or back onto the drive to reinstall. | Screen. On a node with a screen, the title reads BOOTLOADER, ERASE, WRONG FILE or NO FIRMWARE, and a progress bar shows the copy. | Wrong file. A firmware file the board cannot take is refused as WRONG FILE. | Interrupted copy. If the cable is pulled mid-copy, the node has no firmware. Plug it in again and copy the firmware once more. | Idle. After 6 minutes with no update activity, a node with firmware boots it. A node with no firmware keeps waiting. | Single-button boards. The T1000-E and the MeshTracker X1 have no reset button. Hold the button for about 3 seconds while the node powers on to enter update mode. Eject the drive from the computer to leave without copying a file. The app’s USB update needs no button. | . Other Flashing Options . For recovery or when neither OTA nor in-app USB is available: . | Use the Meshtastic Web Flasher | Or the Meshtastic CLI tool on desktop | .

1810.title: Post-Update
1810.content: After the firmware is written, the app verifies the update and waits for the device to come back online: . Once the update succeeds: . | The node reboots automatically | The Bluetooth connection re-establishes | Verify your settings are intact | Confirm the new version under Currently Installed on the Firmware Update screen — it’s also shown on the node’s detail page and the Connections screen | .

1811.title: Troubleshooting
1811.content: Update Stuck . If the update appears frozen: . | Give it a minute. After writing the image the app waits up to 60 seconds for the node to come back and report its new version, so a pause at the verify step is expected. | If it is still stuck after that, power-cycle the node. | Attempt the update again. | . The message Verification timed out. Device did not reconnect in time. means the image was written but the node did not come back within that window. Power-cycle it and check the version under Currently Installed before re-running the update. Radio Won’t Boot After Update . A Bluetooth update that stops partway can leave the node waiting in bootloader mode. While the app is disconnected, the Connect tab then shows a Finish updating card naming the node. Tap Resume firmware update and keep the node nearby so the app can re-flash it, or dismiss the card if the update can’t be finished from the phone. A stock nRF bootloader cannot reliably complete an interrupted over-the-air update. On the Meshtastic nRF52 Bootloader 2.6.0 and later, a dropped Bluetooth update can start over, and where the node waits depends on its power: . | On battery, it waits for the Bluetooth update, so Resume firmware update can reach it. | Plugged into a computer, it shows NO FIRMWARE and comes up as its update drive, not over Bluetooth. Copy your board’s firmware .uf2 onto the drive, or use the Web Flasher. Unplug it to resume over Bluetooth. The app’s USB update cannot start here. | . Otherwise, if your node fails to boot: . | Try connecting via USB to a computer | Use the web flasher in recovery/DFU mode | Flash a known-good firmware version | Check the Meshtastic Discord for device-specific recovery steps | . Compatibility Warnings . On connecting, the app compares the node’s firmware against two thresholds and reacts differently to each: . | Firmware version | What you see | What happens | . | Below 2.3.15 | Firmware update required. | The app disconnects from the node. It does not operate against firmware this old. | . | 2.3.15 up to, but not including, 2.5.14 | Firmware update required | The node stays connected, but the dialog blocks the rest of the app until the firmware is updated. It names the installed, minimum, and latest stable versions. Update firmware opens the Firmware Update screen; Disconnect drops the node. | . | 2.5.14 or newer | Nothing | — | . 1826.title: Post-Update
1826.content: After the firmware is written, the app verifies the update and waits for the device to come back online: . Once the update succeeds: . | The node reboots automatically | The Bluetooth connection re-establishes | Verify your settings are intact | Confirm the new version under Currently Installed on the Firmware Update screen — it’s also shown on the node’s detail page and the Connections screen | .

1827.title: Felsökning
1827.content: Update Stuck . If the update appears frozen: . | Give it a minute. After writing the image the app waits up to 60 seconds for the node to come back and report its new version, so a pause at the verify step is expected. | If it is still stuck after that, power-cycle the node. | Attempt the update again. | . The message Verification timed out. Device did not reconnect in time. means the image was written but the node did not come back within that window. Power-cycle it and check the version under Currently Installed before re-running the update. Radio Won’t Boot After Update . Tap Resume firmware update and keep the node nearby so the app can re-flash it, or dismiss the card if the update can’t be finished from the phone. On the Meshtastic nRF52 Bootloader 2.6.0 and later, a dropped Bluetooth update can start over, and where the node waits depends on its power: . | On battery, it waits for the Bluetooth update, so Resume firmware update can reach it. | Plugged into a computer, it shows NO FIRMWARE and comes up as its update drive, not over Bluetooth. Copy your board’s firmware .uf2 onto the drive, or use the Web Flasher. Unplug it to resume over Bluetooth. The app’s USB update cannot start here. | . Otherwise, if your node fails to boot: . | Try connecting via USB to a computer | Use the web flasher in recovery/DFU mode | Flash a known-good firmware version | Check the Meshtastic Discord for device-specific recovery steps | . Compatibility Warnings . On connecting, the app compares the node’s firmware against two thresholds and reacts differently to each: . | Firmwareversion | What you see | What happens | . | Below 2.3.15 | Firmware update required. | The app disconnects from the node. It does not operate against firmware this old. | . | 2.3.15 up to, but not including, 2.5.14 | Firmware update required | The node stays connected, but the dialog blocks the rest of the app until the firmware is updated. It names the installed, minimum, and latest stable versions. Update firmware opens the Firmware Update screen; Disconnect drops the node. | . | 2.5.14 or newer | Nothing | — | . A version string the app cannot parse is ignored rather than treated as too old, so a transient read never disconnects a working node.

1846.content: The docs browser lists every user-guide page. Tap a page to read it; images and cross-links work as they do here. Search . 2171.title: Map & Waypoints
2171.content: The Map screen shows the geographic positions of nodes on your mesh, along with shared waypoints.

2172.title: Map View
2172.content: The map displays: . | Node positions — colored markers for each node reporting location | Waypoints — shared points of interest | Your position — your current GPS location | . Node Markers . Each node that reports a position is shown as a node chip marker displaying the node’s short name. The chip is colored by the node’s own identity color (a stable color derived from its node number) — the same chip used in the node list, so a node looks the same everywhere. Marker color does not encode online/offline status. When a node’s position updates live, its marker briefly pulses. Tapping a chip opens that node’s details. Nodes within 5 m of each other, which is common when they share a reduced position precision or sit at one site, are drawn as one chip with a count on its corner, showing a favorite or your own node when one is there. Tapping it lists every node at that spot, favorites first. Nearby markers are clustered as you zoom out. Tapping a cluster zooms in to fit its nodes, and a cluster whose nodes all share one spot lists them instead. With Show Precision Circles on, each spot’s circle stays visible inside a cluster too. Map Controls . | Zoom — pinch or use +/- buttons | Pan — drag to explore | Center — tap the location button to follow your position | Node tap — tap a node marker to view details | . The floating toolbar provides quick access to the compass, the map type and layers pickers, node filters, Site Planner, and location tracking. Tap the compass to reorient north-up, or tap the location button to follow your current position. While the map follows you, the compass instead turns heading lock on and off, so the map rotates with the phone. On Google Play builds a refresh button joins them while a network layer is showing; on F-Droid and Desktop, refresh a network layer from its own row in the layers sheet instead. Filtering the Map . Tap the filter button in the floating toolbar to open Filter map. Display controls what is drawn: Only Favorites, Show Waypoints, Show Precision Circles, and a slider that hides nodes not heard from recently. Node roles is a chip per device role, plus All to show every role; a selected chip means that role is shown. Nodes narrows the set further with Hide offline nodes, Only show direct nodes, Signed only, Encrypted only, Exclude MQTT, Show ignored nodes, and Include unknown — the same rules as the node list’s filter toggles. A dot on the filter button means at least one filter is hiding nodes — check it before concluding the mesh is quiet. Turning Show Waypoints off hides every waypoint, including your own. Show ignored nodes adds them to the map rather than showing only them — unlike the node list’s Only show ignored Nodes.

2173.title: AR mesh view
2173.content: The mesh view draws nodes and waypoints over the phone’s camera, each in the direction and at the height where it stands, with its distance and the age of its position. It needs a back camera and an orientation sensor, so it appears only on Android phones that have both, on Google Play and F-Droid builds alike. It isn’t available on Desktop. On opening, it asks for camera access and then location. Tap the mesh view button (Open mesh view) in the map’s top bar to see the whole mesh, filtered by the same Filter map settings as the map. The node list’s touch & hold menu, a node’s detail page, its compass sheet, its position log, and a traceroute map open the view too. Opened from a node, it shows only that node, plus the track or route you came from. | Tap a node to open its detail page, or a waypoint to open its info. | Touch & hold a node or waypoint to find it. The view says how far to turn and tilt, the phone ticks as you turn closer, and it pulses once you are on target. | A node whose position uncertainty covers your own spot has no meaningful direction, so it goes on the radar at the bottom instead. Point the phone down to enlarge the radar. | Waypoint geofences are outlined, and the view says when you are inside one. | . When your phone’s position has no altitude, targets sit level with you and the view says elevation is approximate. Without camera access, or while the phone is too hot, the view carries on as a compass.

2174.title: Waypoints
2174.content: Waypoints are shared points of interest, visible to everyone on your mesh. Creating a Waypoint . Your node must be connected — the map ignores a touch & hold while it is not, because saving a waypoint means broadcasting it. | Touch & hold the map at the desired location. | Enter a name and optional description. | Choose an icon/emoji for the waypoint. | Tap Send to share with the mesh. | . Waypoints always broadcast to the whole mesh on the primary channel. Unlike a message, a waypoint cannot be addressed to one channel or sent as a direct message. Waypoint Properties . | Property | Popis | . | Jméno | Short identifier (max 29 characters) | . | Popis | Optional longer description | . | Icon | Visual marker emoji on the map | . | Uzamknout | If locked, only the creator can edit or delete | . | Expiration | Optional auto-remove date and time | . | Geofence | Optional enter/exit alert area — see Waypoint Geofences | . Waypoint Expiration . A waypoint stays until it is deleted unless you turn on Expires in the waypoint editor. The switch starts the expiry eight hours out; change it with the Date and Time pickers. Once that time passes, the waypoint is removed, which suits temporary markers such as rally points, hazards, or meeting locations. Expired waypoints are automatically hidden from the map so they don’t clutter the display. The expiration countdown is based on the absolute time you picked, not a duration from when the waypoint was created or received. Waypoint Geofences . Any waypoint can also define a geofence — an alert area — so you or others get notified when a node enters or leaves it: . | Set a geofence radius from the preset chips (or Off to disable), or tap Set area on map to draw a custom rectangular area instead. | Once a region is set, toggle Notify on enter and/or Notify on exit. | Optionally enable Favorites only to limit alerts to your favorited nodes. | . Since waypoints (and their geofences) are broadcast to the whole mesh, only the creator is alerted by default. If someone else shares a geofenced waypoint with you, its detail view offers a Notify me of crossings opt-in so you can also receive enter/exit alerts for it. Managing Waypoints . | Tap a waypoint to see its name, description, and geofence radius. On Google Play builds the first tap opens the marker’s info bubble — tap the bubble to open the waypoint itself | Locked waypoints can only be changed on the mesh by the node that locked them | Unlocked waypoints can be edited by any mesh member while connected to a node — saving re-broadcasts the waypoint | Confirming a delete removes your own copy. To remove it from everyone else’s map too, select Delete for everyone in the delete dialog; that box appears only for a waypoint you may change (unlocked, or locked by you) and only while you are connected | .

2175.title: Mapové vrstvy
2175.content: Tap the layers icon on the map to open Manage Map Layers. It imports your own overlays in .kml, .kmz, or GeoJSON format, including KMZ ground overlays (georeferenced images, such as exported topo or aerial tiles), which drape at their stated bounds. Add one by picking a file with Add Layer, opening a file with Meshtastic, or sharing it into the app from another app. A file opened or shared this way is refused if it is over 50 MB. Add Network Layer instead takes a name and an https:// URL pointing at a KML or GeoJSON file (http:// also works on Desktop, but on Android only for localhost); that layer then carries its own refresh button in the sheet. On Google Play builds the toolbar’s refresh button re-fetches every visible network layer at once. Imported layers are listed with a toggle to show/hide each one and an option to remove it. Each layer — imported or built-in overlay — carries its own opacity slider while it is switched on, so an overlay can be faded back rather than only switched off. This works on the Google Play build, the F-Droid build, and Desktop, which shares the same layer store and file picker. Site Planner . Site Planner estimates RF coverage for a transmitter and draws it on the map as a color-coded overlay. Open it from the Site Planner button in the map toolbar, or from a node’s detail page with Estimate coverage (shown only for nodes with a known position). The form has four sections: . | Site / Transmitter: name, latitude and longitude, TX power (W), Frequency (MHz), Antenna height (m), and Antenna gain (dBi). Chips such as Use current node location and Use map center fill in the coordinates. | Receiver: Receiver sensitivity (dBm) and Receiver height (m). | Simulation Options: Max range (km), from 1 to 150. | Display: Color palette. | . Tap Estimate coverage to run it. The app computes the estimate itself, using the ITU-R P.1812 propagation model over Mapterhorn terrain, on Google Play, F-Droid, and Desktop alike. The terrain downloads the first time an area is estimated, so that step needs a network connection; if it fails, the form comes back with a note to check your connection. The finished estimate is added under Manage Map Layers as a coverage estimate layer, and the map moves to it.

2176.title: Position Sharing
2176.content: Enabling Position Sharing . Your node shares its GPS position based on: . | Broadcast Interval — share the position on a fixed timer | Smart Position — share only once you have moved far enough; Minimum Interval sets the shortest gap between broadcasts and Minimum Distance how far you must move | Fixed Position — publish a latitude, longitude, and altitude you enter by hand instead of the GPS reading | GPS Mode — Enabled, Disabled, or Not Present on this hardware; offered only while Fixed Position is off | . Configure position behavior in Settings → Device configuration → Position, and saving it reboots the node. Without a connection the screen opens read-only, with a prompt to connect before changing anything. For the full field list, see Settings — Radio & User. Privacy Considerations . 🔒 Privacy: Position data is broadcast to all nodes on your channel. If you don’t want your location shared, set GPS Mode to Disabled, or use a Fixed Position somewhere else. To keep sharing a position without pinpointing yourself, edit the channel in Settings → Channels, turn Precise location off, and set the slider beneath it — the channel then publishes an approximate area, shown as ± a distance, instead of an exact point.

2177.title: Map Sources
2177.content: Every build offers a base map picker from the map toolbar. Google Play builds open on Google’s own map types; F-Droid and Desktop builds open on MapLibre’s vector styles. Further down the base map picker, all three offer the same raster base maps: . | Base map | Poznámka | . | Normal / Satellite / Terrain / Hybrid | Google Play only — Google’s own map types | . | Liberty | Default on F-Droid and Desktop. Vector street map | . | Positron | F-Droid and Desktop only. Low-contrast vector map; keeps node markers legible over it | . | Tmavý | F-Droid and Desktop only. Vector map suited to dark themes | . | OpenStreetMap | Classic raster street tiles | . | OpenTopoMap | Raster topographic | . | USGS Topo / USGS Imagery | US coverage only | . | Esri Topo / Esri Imagery | Topographic and satellite imagery | . Overlays can be toggled on top of any base map, from the layers sheet: . | Weather radar — NOAA NEXRAD reflectivity (US coverage) | Hillshade — terrain relief from an online tile source, on F-Droid and Desktop only; Google Play draws hillshade from downloaded offline terrain instead. Useful for understanding why a link fails, since LoRa range is limited by terrain | . Adding your own tile source . Any XYZ tile endpoint can be added as a base map, on every flavor and on desktop. Open Manage Custom Tile Sources at the foot of the base map picker and paste a URL template using {z}, {x} and {y} — plus {s} if the provider uses rotating subdomains. A national mapping service, for example: . https://wmts.geo.admin.ch/1.0.0/ch.swisstopo.pixelkarte-farbe/default/current/3857/{z}/{x}/{y}.jpeg . On Android the template must use https://; plain http:// works only for localhost. Tiles are cached on disk, so panning does not re-download what you were just looking at. On Android, the same screen also imports a local .mbtiles archive for fully offline use. On F-Droid, select a vector base map first — Liberty, Positron, or Dark — since a download is defined against a vector style and Start Download stays disabled over a raster one. Frame the area you want on screen, then tap Start Download in the layers sheet’s Cache Manager section: that creates a paused pack covering the current zoom plus two levels deeper. Press play on the pack’s row to download it. While the offline database opens, the section shows a progress bar. If it cannot be opened, the section reads Offline maps are unavailable on this device and Start Download stays disabled. If the area cannot be saved, the section reads Couldn’t save this area for offline use. On Google Play, the layers sheet’s Offline Manager section downloads its own offline regions instead — water, roads and administrative boundaries extracted from the public Protomaps basemap dataset, drawn directly as map shapes rather than raster tiles. Frame the area you want, tap Start Download, and once it finishes turn on Show on map to draw it. The switch is off by default, so a download never covers up the live map unasked. Desktop has no offline base map downloads, though the offline terrain described next does work there. Offline terrain . Hillshade and elevation contours can be downloaded for offline use as well, so a downloaded area still shows why a link fails when there is no network. The terrain data comes from Mapterhorn and is credited on the map. On Google Play, each downloaded region in the Offline Manager list has a Download Terrain button. Terrain attaches to that region and shares its storage limit, and an area too large for terrain asks you to zoom in or pick a smaller region. Once the terrain is downloaded, the button gives way to Hillshade and Contours switches, both off until you turn them on. On F-Droid and Desktop, the layers sheet has an Offline Terrain section of its own: frame the area, tap Start Download, and the hillshade and contours draw automatically from then on, whenever the downloaded area is in view. Going offline . A pill reading Offline — showing cached map data appears over the map whenever the device has no network connection. On Google Play builds, if you’ve imported a local .mbtiles archive, the map switches to it automatically the moment the network drops — no toggle to remember — and switches back once you’re reconnected, as long as you haven’t picked a different base map yourself in between. On F-Droid, a downloaded offline area keeps rendering on its own; the pill is purely informational there. Desktop downloads offline terrain but no base-map packs, so the pill is informational there too.

Open Manage Custom Tile Sources at the foot of the base map picker and paste a URL template using {z}, {x} and {y} — plus {s} if the provider uses rotating subdomains. A national mapping service, for example: . https://wmts.geo.admin.ch/1.0.0/ch.swisstopo.pixelkarte-farbe/default/current/3857/{z}/{x}/{y}.jpeg . On Android the template must use https://; plain http:// works only for localhost. Tiles are cached on disk, so panning does not re-download what you were just looking at. On Android, the same screen also imports a local .mbtiles archive for fully offline use. On F-Droid, select a vector base map first — Liberty, Positron, or Dark — since a download is defined against a vector style and Start Download stays disabled over a raster one. Frame the area you want on screen, then tap Start Download in the layers sheet’s Cache Manager section: that creates a paused pack covering the current zoom plus two levels deeper. Press play on the pack’s row to download it. While the offline database opens, the section shows a progress bar. If it cannot be opened, the section reads Offline maps are unavailable on this device and Start Download stays disabled. If the area cannot be saved, the section reads Couldn’t save this area for offline use. On Google Play, the layers sheet’s Offline Manager section downloads its own offline regions instead — water, roads and administrative boundaries extracted from the public Protomaps basemap dataset, drawn directly as map shapes rather than raster tiles. Frame the area you want, tap Start Download, and once it finishes turn on Show on map to draw it. The switch is off by default, so a download never covers up the live map unasked. Desktop has no offline base map downloads, though the offline terrain described next does work there. Offline terrain . Hillshade and elevation contours can be downloaded for offline use as well, so a downloaded area still shows why a link fails when there is no network. The terrain data comes from Mapterhorn and is credited on the map. On Google Play, each downloaded region in the Offline Manager list has a Download Terrain button. Terrain attaches to that region and shares its storage limit, and an area too large for terrain asks you to zoom in or pick a smaller region. Once the terrain is downloaded, the button gives way to Hillshade and Contours switches, both off until you turn them on. On F-Droid and Desktop, the layers sheet has an Offline Terrain section of its own: frame the area, tap Start Download, and the hillshade and contours draw automatically from then on, whenever the downloaded area is in view. Going offline . A pill reading Offline — showing cached map data appears over the map whenever the device has no network connection. On Google Play builds, if you’ve imported a local .mbtiles archive, the map switches to it automatically the moment the network drops — no toggle to remember — and switches back once you’re reconnected, as long as you haven’t picked a different base map yourself in between. On F-Droid, a downloaded offline area keeps rendering on its own; the pill is purely informational there. Desktop downloads offline terrain but no base-map packs, so the pill is informational there too.

2189.title: Map & Waypoints
2189.content: The Map screen shows the geographic positions of nodes on your mesh, along with shared waypoints.

2190.title: Map View
2190.content: The map displays: . | Node positions — colored markers for each node reporting location | Waypoints — shared points of interest | Your position — your current GPS location | . Node Markers . Each node that reports a position is shown as a node chip marker displaying the node’s short name. The chip is colored by the node’s own identity color (a stable color derived from its node number) — the same chip used in the node list, so a node looks the same everywhere. Marker color does not encode online/offline status. When a node’s position updates live, its marker briefly pulses. Tapping a chip opens that node’s details. Nodes within 5 m of each other, which is common when they share a reduced position precision or sit at one site, are drawn as one chip with a count on its corner, showing a favorite or your own node when one is there. Tapping it lists every node at that spot, favorites first. Nearby markers are clustered as you zoom out. Tapping a cluster zooms in to fit its nodes, and a cluster whose nodes all share one spot lists them instead. With Show Precision Circles on, each spot’s circle stays visible inside a cluster too. Map Controls . | Zoom — pinch or use +/- buttons | Pan — drag to explore | Center — tap the location button to follow your position | Node tap — tap a node marker to view details | . The floating toolbar provides quick access to the compass, the map type and layers pickers, node filters, Site Planner, and location tracking. Tap the compass to reorient north-up, or tap the location button to follow your current position. While the map follows you, the compass instead turns heading lock on and off, so the map rotates with the phone. On Google Play builds a refresh button joins them while a network layer is showing; on F-Droid and Desktop, refresh a network layer from its own row in the layers sheet instead. Filtering the Map . Tap the filter button in the floating toolbar to open Filter map. Display controls what is drawn: Only Favorites, Show Waypoints, Show Precision Circles, and a slider that hides nodes not heard from recently. Node roles is a chip per device role, plus All to show every role; a selected chip means that role is shown. Nodes narrows the set further with Hide offline nodes, Only show direct nodes, Signed only, Encrypted only, Exclude MQTT, Show ignored nodes, and Include unknown — the same rules as the node list’s filter toggles. A dot on the filter button means at least one filter is hiding nodes — check it before concluding the mesh is quiet. Turning Show Waypoints off hides every waypoint, including your own. Show ignored nodes adds them to the map rather than showing only them — unlike the node list’s Only show ignored Nodes.

2191.title: AR mesh view
2191.content: The mesh view draws nodes and waypoints over the phone’s camera, each in the direction and at the height where it stands, with its distance and the age of its position. It needs a back camera and an orientation sensor, so it appears only on Android phones that have both, on Google Play and F-Droid builds alike. It isn’t available on Desktop. On opening, it asks for camera access and then location. Tap the mesh view button (Open mesh view) in the map’s top bar to see the whole mesh, filtered by the same Filter map settings as the map. The node list’s touch & hold menu, a node’s detail page, its compass sheet, its position log, and a traceroute map open the view too. Opened from a node, it shows only that node, plus the track or route you came from. | Tap a node to open its detail page, or a waypoint to open its info. | Touch & hold a node or waypoint to find it. The view says how far to turn and tilt, the phone ticks as you turn closer, and it pulses once you are on target. | A node whose position uncertainty covers your own spot has no meaningful direction, so it goes on the radar at the bottom instead. Point the phone down to enlarge the radar. | Waypoint geofences are outlined, and the view says when you are inside one. | . When your phone’s position has no altitude, targets sit level with you and the view says elevation is approximate. Without camera access, or while the phone is too hot, the view carries on as a compass.

2192.title: Waypoints
2192.content: Waypoints are shared points of interest, visible to everyone on your mesh. Creating a Waypoint . Your node must be connected — the map ignores a touch & hold while it is not, because saving a waypoint means broadcasting it. | Touch & hold the map at the desired location. | Enter a name and optional description. | Choose an icon/emoji for the waypoint. | Tap Send to share with the mesh. | . Waypoints always broadcast to the whole mesh on the primary channel. Unlike a message, a waypoint cannot be addressed to one channel or sent as a direct message. Waypoint Properties . | Property | Descripció | . | Nom | Short identifier (max 29 characters) | . | Descripció | Optional longer description | . | Icon | Visual marker emoji on the map | . | Bloquejat | If locked, only the creator can edit or delete | . | Expiration | Optional auto-remove date and time | . | Geofence | Optional enter/exit alert area — see Waypoint Geofences | . Waypoint Expiration . A waypoint stays until it is deleted unless you turn on Expires in the waypoint editor. The switch starts the expiry eight hours out; change it with the Date and Time pickers. Once that time passes, the waypoint is removed, which suits temporary markers such as rally points, hazards, or meeting locations. Expired waypoints are automatically hidden from the map so they don’t clutter the display. The expiration countdown is based on the absolute time you picked, not a duration from when the waypoint was created or received. Waypoint Geofences . Any waypoint can also define a geofence — an alert area — so you or others get notified when a node enters or leaves it: . | Set a geofence radius from the preset chips (or Off to disable), or tap Set area on map to draw a custom rectangular area instead. | Once a region is set, toggle Notify on enter and/or Notify on exit. | Optionally enable Favorites only to limit alerts to your favorited nodes. | . Since waypoints (and their geofences) are broadcast to the whole mesh, only the creator is alerted by default. If someone else shares a geofenced waypoint with you, its detail view offers a Notify me of crossings opt-in so you can also receive enter/exit alerts for it. Managing Waypoints . | Tap a waypoint to see its name, description, and geofence radius. On Google Play builds the first tap opens the marker’s info bubble — tap the bubble to open the waypoint itself | Locked waypoints can only be changed on the mesh by the node that locked them | Unlocked waypoints can be edited by any mesh member while connected to a node — saving re-broadcasts the waypoint | Confirming a delete removes your own copy. To remove it from everyone else’s map too, select Delete for everyone in the delete dialog; that box appears only for a waypoint you may change (unlocked, or locked by you) and only while you are connected | .

2193.title: Map Layers
2193.content: Tap the layers icon on the map to open Manage Map Layers. It imports your own overlays in .kml, .kmz, or GeoJSON format, including KMZ ground overlays (georeferenced images, such as exported topo or aerial tiles), which drape at their stated bounds. Add one by picking a file with Add Layer, opening a file with Meshtastic, or sharing it into the app from another app. A file opened or shared this way is refused if it is over 50 MB. Add Network Layer instead takes a name and an https:// URL pointing at a KML or GeoJSON file (http:// also works on Desktop, but on Android only for localhost); that layer then carries its own refresh button in the sheet. On Google Play builds the toolbar’s refresh button re-fetches every visible network layer at once. Imported layers are listed with a toggle to show/hide each one and an option to remove it. Each layer — imported or built-in overlay — carries its own opacity slider while it is switched on, so an overlay can be faded back rather than only switched off. This works on the Google Play build, the F-Droid build, and Desktop, which shares the same layer store and file picker. Site Planner . Site Planner estimates RF coverage for a transmitter and draws it on the map as a color-coded overlay. Open it from the Site Planner button in the map toolbar, or from a node’s detail page with Estimate coverage (shown only for nodes with a known position). The form has four sections: . | Site / Transmitter: name, latitude and longitude, TX power (W), Frequency (MHz), Antenna height (m), and Antenna gain (dBi). Chips such as Use current node location and Use map center fill in the coordinates. | Receiver: Receiver sensitivity (dBm) and Receiver height (m). | Simulation Options: Max range (km), from 1 to 150. | Display: Color palette. | . Tap Estimate coverage to run it. The app computes the estimate itself, using the ITU-R P.1812 propagation model over Mapterhorn terrain, on Google Play, F-Droid, and Desktop alike. The terrain downloads the first time an area is estimated, so that step needs a network connection; if it fails, the form comes back with a note to check your connection. The finished estimate is added under Manage Map Layers as a coverage estimate layer, and the map moves to it.

2194.title: Position Sharing
2194.content: Enabling Position Sharing . Your node shares its GPS position based on: . | Broadcast Interval — share the position on a fixed timer | Smart Position — share only once you have moved far enough; Minimum Interval sets the shortest gap between broadcasts and Minimum Distance how far you must move | Fixed Position — publish a latitude, longitude, and altitude you enter by hand instead of the GPS reading | GPS Mode — Enabled, Disabled, or Not Present on this hardware; offered only while Fixed Position is off | . Configure position behavior in Settings → Device configuration → Position, and saving it reboots the node. Without a connection the screen opens read-only, with a prompt to connect before changing anything. For the full field list, see Settings — Radio & User. Privacy Considerations . 🔒 Privacy: Position data is broadcast to all nodes on your channel. If you don’t want your location shared, set GPS Mode to Disabled, or use a Fixed Position somewhere else. To keep sharing a position without pinpointing yourself, edit the channel in Settings → Channels, turn Precise location off, and set the slider beneath it — the channel then publishes an approximate area, shown as ± a distance, instead of an exact point.

2207.title: Map & Waypoints
2207.content: The Map screen shows the geographic positions of nodes on your mesh, along with shared waypoints.

2208.title: Map View
2208.content: The map displays: . | Node positions — colored markers for each node reporting location | Waypoints — shared points of interest | Your position — your current GPS location | . Node Markers . Each node that reports a position is shown as a node chip marker displaying the node’s short name. The chip is colored by the node’s own identity color (a stable color derived from its node number) — the same chip used in the node list, so a node looks the same everywhere. Marker color does not encode online/offline status. When a node’s position updates live, its marker briefly pulses. Tapping a chip opens that node’s details. Nodes within 5 m of each other, which is common when they share a reduced position precision or sit at one site, are drawn as one chip with a count on its corner, showing a favorite or your own node when one is there. Tapping it lists every node at that spot, favorites first. Nearby markers are clustered as you zoom out. Tapping a cluster zooms in to fit its nodes, and a cluster whose nodes all share one spot lists them instead. With Show Precision Circles on, each spot’s circle stays visible inside a cluster too. Map Controls . | Zoom — pinch or use +/- buttons | Pan — drag to explore | Center — tap the location button to follow your position | Node tap — tap a node marker to view details | . The floating toolbar provides quick access to the compass, the map type and layers pickers, node filters, Site Planner, and location tracking. Tap the compass to reorient north-up, or tap the location button to follow your current position. While the map follows you, the compass instead turns heading lock on and off, so the map rotates with the phone. On Google Play builds a refresh button joins them while a network layer is showing; on F-Droid and Desktop, refresh a network layer from its own row in the layers sheet instead. Filtering the Map . Tap the filter button in the floating toolbar to open Filter map. Display controls what is drawn: Only Favorites, Show Waypoints, Show Precision Circles, and a slider that hides nodes not heard from recently. Node roles is a chip per device role, plus All to show every role; a selected chip means that role is shown. Nodes narrows the set further with Hide offline nodes, Only show direct nodes, Signed only, Encrypted only, Exclude MQTT, Show ignored nodes, and Include unknown — the same rules as the node list’s filter toggles. A dot on the filter button means at least one filter is hiding nodes — check it before concluding the mesh is quiet. Turning Show Waypoints off hides every waypoint, including your own. Show ignored nodes adds them to the map rather than showing only them — unlike the node list’s Only show ignored Nodes.

2209.title: AR mesh view
2209.content: The mesh view draws nodes and waypoints over the phone’s camera, each in the direction and at the height where it stands, with its distance and the age of its position. It needs a back camera and an orientation sensor, so it appears only on Android phones that have both, on Google Play and F-Droid builds alike. It isn’t available on Desktop. On opening, it asks for camera access and then location. Tap the mesh view button (Open mesh view) in the map’s top bar to see the whole mesh, filtered by the same Filter map settings as the map. The node list’s touch & hold menu, a node’s detail page, its compass sheet, its position log, and a traceroute map open the view too. Opened from a node, it shows only that node, plus the track or route you came from. | Tap a node to open its detail page, or a waypoint to open its info. | Touch & hold a node or waypoint to find it. The view says how far to turn and tilt, the phone ticks as you turn closer, and it pulses once you are on target. | A node whose position uncertainty covers your own spot has no meaningful direction, so it goes on the radar at the bottom instead. Point the phone down to enlarge the radar. | Waypoint geofences are outlined, and the view says when you are inside one. | . When your phone’s position has no altitude, targets sit level with you and the view says elevation is approximate. Without camera access, or while the phone is too hot, the view carries on as a compass.

2210.title: Waypoints
2210.content: Waypoints are shared points of interest, visible to everyone on your mesh. Creating a Waypoint . Your node must be connected — the map ignores a touch & hold while it is not, because saving a waypoint means broadcasting it. | Touch & hold the map at the desired location. | Enter a name and optional description. | Choose an icon/emoji for the waypoint. | Tap Send to share with the mesh. | . Waypoints always broadcast to the whole mesh on the primary channel. Unlike a message, a waypoint cannot be addressed to one channel or sent as a direct message. Waypoint Properties . | Property | Lýsing | . | Heiti | Short identifier (max 29 characters) | . | Lýsing | Optional longer description | . | Icon | Visual marker emoji on the map | . | Læst | If locked, only the creator can edit or delete | . | Expiration | Optional auto-remove date and time | . | Geofence | Optional enter/exit alert area — see Waypoint Geofences | . Waypoint Expiration . A waypoint stays until it is deleted unless you turn on Expires in the waypoint editor. The switch starts the expiry eight hours out; change it with the Date and Time pickers. Once that time passes, the waypoint is removed, which suits temporary markers such as rally points, hazards, or meeting locations. Expired waypoints are automatically hidden from the map so they don’t clutter the display. The expiration countdown is based on the absolute time you picked, not a duration from when the waypoint was created or received. Waypoint Geofences . Any waypoint can also define a geofence — an alert area — so you or others get notified when a node enters or leaves it: . | Set a geofence radius from the preset chips (or Off to disable), or tap Set area on map to draw a custom rectangular area instead. | Once a region is set, toggle Notify on enter and/or Notify on exit. | Optionally enable Favorites only to limit alerts to your favorited nodes. | . Since waypoints (and their geofences) are broadcast to the whole mesh, only the creator is alerted by default. If someone else shares a geofenced waypoint with you, its detail view offers a Notify me of crossings opt-in so you can also receive enter/exit alerts for it. Managing Waypoints . | Tap a waypoint to see its name, description, and geofence radius. On Google Play builds the first tap opens the marker’s info bubble — tap the bubble to open the waypoint itself | Locked waypoints can only be changed on the mesh by the node that locked them | Unlocked waypoints can be edited by any mesh member while connected to a node — saving re-broadcasts the waypoint | Confirming a delete removes your own copy. To remove it from everyone else’s map too, select Delete for everyone in the delete dialog; that box appears only for a waypoint you may change (unlocked, or locked by you) and only while you are connected | .

2211.title: Map Layers
2211.content: Tap the layers icon on the map to open Manage Map Layers. It imports your own overlays in .kml, .kmz, or GeoJSON format, including KMZ ground overlays (georeferenced images, such as exported topo or aerial tiles), which drape at their stated bounds. Add one by picking a file with Add Layer, opening a file with Meshtastic, or sharing it into the app from another app. A file opened or shared this way is refused if it is over 50 MB. Add Network Layer instead takes a name and an https:// URL pointing at a KML or GeoJSON file (http:// also works on Desktop, but on Android only for localhost); that layer then carries its own refresh button in the sheet. On Google Play builds the toolbar’s refresh button re-fetches every visible network layer at once. Imported layers are listed with a toggle to show/hide each one and an option to remove it. Each layer — imported or built-in overlay — carries its own opacity slider while it is switched on, so an overlay can be faded back rather than only switched off. This works on the Google Play build, the F-Droid build, and Desktop, which shares the same layer store and file picker. Site Planner . Site Planner estimates RF coverage for a transmitter and draws it on the map as a color-coded overlay. Open it from the Site Planner button in the map toolbar, or from a node’s detail page with Estimate coverage (shown only for nodes with a known position). The form has four sections: . | Site / Transmitter: name, latitude and longitude, TX power (W), Frequency (MHz), Antenna height (m), and Antenna gain (dBi). Chips such as Use current node location and Use map center fill in the coordinates. | Receiver: Receiver sensitivity (dBm) and Receiver height (m). | Simulation Options: Max range (km), from 1 to 150. | Display: Color palette. | . Tap Estimate coverage to run it. The app computes the estimate itself, using the ITU-R P.1812 propagation model over Mapterhorn terrain, on Google Play, F-Droid, and Desktop alike. The terrain downloads the first time an area is estimated, so that step needs a network connection; if it fails, the form comes back with a note to check your connection. The finished estimate is added under Manage Map Layers as a coverage estimate layer, and the map moves to it.

2212.title: Position Sharing
2212.content: Enabling Position Sharing . Your node shares its GPS position based on: . | Broadcast Interval — share the position on a fixed timer | Smart Position — share only once you have moved far enough; Minimum Interval sets the shortest gap between broadcasts and Minimum Distance how far you must move | Fixed Position — publish a latitude, longitude, and altitude you enter by hand instead of the GPS reading | GPS Mode — Enabled, Disabled, or Not Present on this hardware; offered only while Fixed Position is off | . Configure position behavior in Settings → Device configuration → Position, and saving it reboots the node. Without a connection the screen opens read-only, with a prompt to connect before changing anything. For the full field list, see Settings — Radio & User. Privacy Considerations . 🔒 Privacy: Position data is broadcast to all nodes on your channel. If you don’t want your location shared, set GPS Mode to Disabled, or use a Fixed Position somewhere else. To keep sharing a position without pinpointing yourself, edit the channel in Settings → Channels, turn Precise location off, and set the slider beneath it — the channel then publishes an approximate area, shown as ± a distance, instead of an exact point.

The chip is colored by the node’s own identity color (a stable color derived from its node number) — the same chip used in the node list, so a node looks the same everywhere. Marker color does not encode online/offline status. When a node’s position updates live, its marker briefly pulses. Tapping a chip opens that node’s details. Nodes within 5 m of each other, which is common when they share a reduced position precision or sit at one site, are drawn as one chip with a count on its corner, showing a favorite or your own node when one is there. Tapping it lists every node at that spot, favorites first. Nearby markers are clustered as you zoom out. Tapping a cluster zooms in to fit its nodes, and a cluster whose nodes all share one spot lists them instead. With Show Precision Circles on, each spot’s circle stays visible inside a cluster too. Map Controls . | Zoom — pinch or use +/- buttons | Pan — drag to explore | Center — tap the location button to follow your position | Node tap — tap a node marker to view details | . The floating toolbar provides quick access to the compass, the map type and layers pickers, node filters, Site Planner, and location tracking. Tap the compass to reorient north-up, or tap the location button to follow your current position. While the map follows you, the compass instead turns heading lock on and off, so the map rotates with the phone. On Google Play builds a refresh button joins them while a network layer is showing; on F-Droid and Desktop, refresh a network layer from its own row in the layers sheet instead. Filtering the Map . Tap the filter button in the floating toolbar to open Filter map. Display controls what is drawn: Only Favorites, Show Waypoints, Show Precision Circles, and a slider that hides nodes not heard from recently. Node roles is a chip per device role, plus All to show every role; a selected chip means that role is shown. Nodes narrows the set further with Hide offline nodes, Only show direct nodes, Signed only, Encrypted only, Exclude MQTT, Show ignored nodes, and Include unknown — the same rules as the node list’s filter toggles. A dot on the filter button means at least one filter is hiding nodes — check it before concluding the mesh is quiet. Turning Show Waypoints off hides every waypoint, including your own. Show ignored nodes adds them to the map rather than showing only them — unlike the node list’s Only show ignored Nodes.

2227.title: AR mesh view
2227.content: The mesh view draws nodes and waypoints over the phone’s camera, each in the direction and at the height where it stands, with its distance and the age of its position. It needs a back camera and an orientation sensor, so it appears only on Android phones that have both, on Google Play and F-Droid builds alike. It isn’t available on Desktop. On opening, it asks for camera access and then location. Tap the mesh view button (Open mesh view) in the map’s top bar to see the whole mesh, filtered by the same Filter map settings as the map. The node list’s touch & hold menu, a node’s detail page, its compass sheet, its position log, and a traceroute map open the view too. Opened from a node, it shows only that node, plus the track or route you came from. | Tap a node to open its detail page, or a waypoint to open its info. | Touch & hold a node or waypoint to find it. The view says how far to turn and tilt, the phone ticks as you turn closer, and it pulses once you are on target. | A node whose position uncertainty covers your own spot has no meaningful direction, so it goes on the radar at the bottom instead. Point the phone down to enlarge the radar. | Waypoint geofences are outlined, and the view says when you are inside one. | . When your phone’s position has no altitude, targets sit level with you and the view says elevation is approximate. Without camera access, or while the phone is too hot, the view carries on as a compass.

2228.title: Waypoints
2228.content: Waypoints are shared points of interest, visible to everyone on your mesh. Creating a Waypoint . Your node must be connected — the map ignores a touch & hold while it is not, because saving a waypoint means broadcasting it. | Touch & hold the map at the desired location. | Enter a name and optional description. | Choose an icon/emoji for the waypoint. | Tap Send to share with the mesh. | . Waypoints always broadcast to the whole mesh on the primary channel. Unlike a message, a waypoint cannot be addressed to one channel or sent as a direct message. Waypoint Properties . | Property | Açıklaması | . | İsmi | Short identifier (max 29 characters) | . | Açıklaması | Optional longer description | . | Icon | Visual marker emoji on the map | . | Kilitli | If locked, only the creator can edit or delete | . | Expiration | Optional auto-remove date and time | . | Geofence | Optional enter/exit alert area — see Waypoint Geofences | . Waypoint Expiration . A waypoint stays until it is deleted unless you turn on Expires in the waypoint editor. The switch starts the expiry eight hours out; change it with the Date and Time pickers. Once that time passes, the waypoint is removed, which suits temporary markers such as rally points, hazards, or meeting locations. Expired waypoints are automatically hidden from the map so they don’t clutter the display. The expiration countdown is based on the absolute time you picked, not a duration from when the waypoint was created or received. Waypoint Geofences . Any waypoint can also define a geofence — an alert area — so you or others get notified when a node enters or leaves it: . | Set a geofence radius from the preset chips (or Off to disable), or tap Set area on map to draw a custom rectangular area instead. | Once a region is set, toggle Notify on enter and/or Notify on exit. | Optionally enable Favorites only to limit alerts to your favorited nodes. | . Since waypoints (and their geofences) are broadcast to the whole mesh, only the creator is alerted by default. If someone else shares a geofenced waypoint with you, its detail view offers a Notify me of crossings opt-in so you can also receive enter/exit alerts for it. Managing Waypoints . | Tap a waypoint to see its name, description, and geofence radius. On Google Play builds the first tap opens the marker’s info bubble — tap the bubble to open the waypoint itself | Locked waypoints can only be changed on the mesh by the node that locked them | Unlocked waypoints can be edited by any mesh member while connected to a node — saving re-broadcasts the waypoint | Confirming a delete removes your own copy. To remove it from everyone else’s map too, select Delete for everyone in the delete dialog; that box appears only for a waypoint you may change (unlocked, or locked by you) and only while you are connected | .

2229.title: Map Layers
2229.content: Tap the layers icon on the map to open Manage Map Layers. It imports your own overlays in .kml, .kmz, or GeoJSON format, including KMZ ground overlays (georeferenced images, such as exported topo or aerial tiles), which drape at their stated bounds. Add one by picking a file with Add Layer, opening a file with Meshtastic, or sharing it into the app from another app. A file opened or shared this way is refused if it is over 50 MB. Add Network Layer instead takes a name and an https:// URL pointing at a KML or GeoJSON file (http:// also works on Desktop, but on Android only for localhost); that layer then carries its own refresh button in the sheet. On Google Play builds the toolbar’s refresh button re-fetches every visible network layer at once. Imported layers are listed with a toggle to show/hide each one and an option to remove it. Each layer — imported or built-in overlay — carries its own opacity slider while it is switched on, so an overlay can be faded back rather than only switched off. This works on the Google Play build, the F-Droid build, and Desktop, which shares the same layer store and file picker. Site Planner . Site Planner estimates RF coverage for a transmitter and draws it on the map as a color-coded overlay. Open it from the Site Planner button in the map toolbar, or from a node’s detail page with Estimate coverage (shown only for nodes with a known position). The form has four sections: . | Site / Transmitter: name, latitude and longitude, TX power (W), Frequency (MHz), Antenna height (m), and Antenna gain (dBi). Chips such as Use current node location and Use map center fill in the coordinates. | Receiver: Receiver sensitivity (dBm) and Receiver height (m). | Simulation Options: Max range (km), from 1 to 150. | Display: Color palette. | . Tap Estimate coverage to run it. The app computes the estimate itself, using the ITU-R P.1812 propagation model over Mapterhorn terrain, on Google Play, F-Droid, and Desktop alike. The terrain downloads the first time an area is estimated, so that step needs a network connection; if it fails, the form comes back with a note to check your connection. The finished estimate is added under Manage Map Layers as a coverage estimate layer, and the map moves to it.

2230.title: Position Sharing
2230.content: Enabling Position Sharing . Your node shares its GPS position based on: . | Broadcast Interval — share the position on a fixed timer | Smart Position — share only once you have moved far enough; Minimum Interval sets the shortest gap between broadcasts and Minimum Distance how far you must move | Fixed Position — publish a latitude, longitude, and altitude you enter by hand instead of the GPS reading | GPS Mode — Enabled, Disabled, or Not Present on this hardware; offered only while Fixed Position is off | . Configure position behavior in Settings → Device configuration → Position, and saving it reboots the node. Without a connection the screen opens read-only, with a prompt to connect before changing anything. For the full field list, see Settings — Radio & User. Privacy Considerations . 🔒 Privacy: Position data is broadcast to all nodes on your channel. If you don’t want your location shared, set GPS Mode to Disabled, or use a Fixed Position somewhere else. To keep sharing a position without pinpointing yourself, edit the channel in Settings → Channels, turn Precise location off, and set the slider beneath it — the channel then publishes an approximate area, shown as ± a distance, instead of an exact point.

2231.title: Map Sources
2231.content: Every build offers a base map picker from the map toolbar. Google Play builds open on Google’s own map types; F-Droid and Desktop builds open on MapLibre’s vector styles. Further down the base map picker, all three offer the same raster base maps: . | Base map | Notes | . | Normal / Satellite / Terrain / Hybrid | Google Play only — Google’s own map types | . | Liberty | Default on F-Droid and Desktop. Vector street map | . | Positron | F-Droid and Desktop only. Low-contrast vector map; keeps node markers legible over it | . | Koyu | F-Droid and Desktop only. Vector map suited to dark themes | . | OpenStreetMap | Classic raster street tiles | . | OpenTopoMap | Raster topographic | . | USGS Topo / USGS Imagery | US coverage only | . | Esri Topo / Esri Imagery | Topographic and satellite imagery | . Overlays can be toggled on top of any base map, from the layers sheet: . | Weather radar — NOAA NEXRAD reflectivity (US coverage) | Hillshade — terrain relief from an online tile source, on F-Droid and Desktop only; Google Play draws hillshade from downloaded offline terrain instead. Useful for understanding why a link fails, since LoRa range is limited by terrain | . Adding your own tile source . Any XYZ tile endpoint can be added as a base map, on every flavor and on desktop. Open Manage Custom Tile Sources at the foot of the base map picker and paste a URL template using {z}, {x} and {y} — plus {s} if the provider uses rotating subdomains. A national mapping service, for example: . https://wmts.geo.admin.ch/1.0.0/ch.swisstopo.pixelkarte-farbe/default/current/3857/{z}/{x}/{y}.jpeg . On Android the template must use https://; plain http:// works only for localhost. Tiles are cached on disk, so panning does not re-download what you were just looking at. On Android, the same screen also imports a local .mbtiles archive for fully offline use. On F-Droid, select a vector base map first — Liberty, Positron, or Dark — since a download is defined against a vector style and Start Download stays disabled over a raster one. Frame the area you want on screen, then tap Start Download in the layers sheet’s Cache Manager section: that creates a paused pack covering the current zoom plus two levels deeper. Press play on the pack’s row to download it. While the offline database opens, the section shows a progress bar. If it cannot be opened, the section reads Offline maps are unavailable on this device and Start Download stays disabled. If the area cannot be saved, the section reads Couldn’t save this area for offline use. On Google Play, the layers sheet’s Offline Manager section downloads its own offline regions instead — water, roads and administrative boundaries extracted from the public Protomaps basemap dataset, drawn directly as map shapes rather than raster tiles. Frame the area you want, tap Start Download, and once it finishes turn on Show on map to draw it. The switch is off by default, so a download never covers up the live map unasked. Desktop has no offline base map downloads, though the offline terrain described next does work there. Offline terrain . Hillshade and elevation contours can be downloaded for offline use as well, so a downloaded area still shows why a link fails when there is no network. The terrain data comes from Mapterhorn and is credited on the map. On Google Play, each downloaded region in the Offline Manager list has a Download Terrain button. Terrain attaches to that region and shares its storage limit, and an area too large for terrain asks you to zoom in or pick a smaller region. Once the terrain is downloaded, the button gives way to Hillshade and Contours switches, both off until you turn them on. On F-Droid and Desktop, the layers sheet has an Offline Terrain section of its own: frame the area, tap Start Download, and the hillshade and contours draw automatically from then on, whenever the downloaded area is in view. Going offline . A pill reading Offline — showing cached map data appears over the map whenever the device has no network connection. On Google Play builds, if you’ve imported a local .mbtiles archive, the map switches to it automatically the moment the network drops — no toggle to remember — and switches back once you’re reconnected, as long as you haven’t picked a different base map yourself in between. On F-Droid, a downloaded offline area keeps rendering on its own; the pill is purely informational there. Desktop downloads offline terrain but no base-map packs, so the pill is informational there too.
