2445.title: Map & Waypoints
2445.content: The Map screen shows the geographic positions of nodes on your mesh, along with shared waypoints.

2446.title: Map View
2446.content: The map displays: . | Node positions — colored markers for each node reporting location | Waypoints — shared points of interest | Your position — your current GPS location | . Node Markers . Each node that reports a position is shown as a node chip marker displaying the node’s short name. The chip is colored by the node’s own identity color (a stable color derived from its node number) — the same chip used in the node list, so a node looks the same everywhere. Marker color does not encode online/offline status. When a node’s position updates live, its marker briefly pulses. Tapping a chip opens that node’s details. Nodes within 5 m of each other, which is common when they share a reduced position precision or sit at one site, are drawn as one chip with a count on its corner, showing a favorite or your own node when one is there. Tapping it lists every node at that spot, favorites first. Nearby markers are clustered as you zoom out. Tapping a cluster zooms in to fit its nodes, and a cluster whose nodes all share one spot lists them instead. With Show Precision Circles on, each spot’s circle stays visible inside a cluster too. Map Controls . | Zoom — pinch or use +/- buttons | Pan — drag to explore | Center — tap the location button to follow your position | Node tap — tap a node marker to view details | . The floating toolbar provides quick access to the compass, the map type and layers pickers, node filters, Site Planner, and location tracking. Tap the compass to reorient north-up, or tap the location button to follow your current position. While the map follows you, the compass instead turns heading lock on and off, so the map rotates with the phone. On Google Play builds a refresh button joins them while a network layer is showing; on F-Droid and Desktop, refresh a network layer from its own row in the layers sheet instead. Filtering the Map . Tap the filter button in the floating toolbar to open Filter map. Display controls what is drawn: Only Favorites, Show Waypoints, Show Precision Circles, and a slider that hides nodes not heard from recently. Node roles is a chip per device role, plus All to show every role; a selected chip means that role is shown. Nodes narrows the set further with Hide offline nodes, Only show direct nodes, Signed only, Encrypted only, Exclude MQTT, Show ignored nodes, and Include unknown — the same rules as the node list’s filter toggles. A dot on the filter button means at least one filter is hiding nodes — check it before concluding the mesh is quiet. Turning Show Waypoints off hides every waypoint, including your own. Show ignored nodes adds them to the map rather than showing only them — unlike the node list’s Only show ignored Nodes.

2447.title: AR mesh view
2447.content: The mesh view draws nodes and waypoints over the phone’s camera, each in the direction and at the height where it stands, with its distance and the age of its position. It needs a back camera and an orientation sensor, so it appears only on Android phones that have both, on Google Play and F-Droid builds alike. It isn’t available on Desktop. On opening, it asks for camera access and then location. Tap the mesh view button (Open mesh view) in the map’s top bar to see the whole mesh, filtered by the same Filter map settings as the map. The node list’s touch & hold menu, a node’s detail page, its compass sheet, its position log, and a traceroute map open the view too. Opened from a node, it shows only that node, plus the track or route you came from. | Tap a node to open its detail page, or a waypoint to open its info. | Touch & hold a node or waypoint to find it. The view says how far to turn and tilt, the phone ticks as you turn closer, and it pulses once you are on target. | A node whose position uncertainty covers your own spot has no meaningful direction, so it goes on the radar at the bottom instead. Point the phone down to enlarge the radar. | Waypoint geofences are outlined, and the view says when you are inside one. | . When your phone’s position has no altitude, targets sit level with you and the view says elevation is approximate. Without camera access, or while the phone is too hot, the view carries on as a compass.

2448.title: Waypoints
2448.content: Waypoints are shared points of interest, visible to everyone on your mesh. Creating a Waypoint . Your node must be connected — the map ignores a touch & hold while it is not, because saving a waypoint means broadcasting it. | Touch & hold the map at the desired location. | Enter a name and optional description. | Choose an icon/emoji for the waypoint. | Tap Send to share with the mesh. | . Waypoints always broadcast to the whole mesh on the primary channel. Unlike a message, a waypoint cannot be addressed to one channel or sent as a direct message. Waypoint Properties . | Property | Descrição | . | Nome | Short identifier (max 29 characters) | . | Descrição | Optional longer description | . | Icon | Visual marker emoji on the map | . | Bloqueado | If locked, only the creator can edit or delete | . | Expiration | Optional auto-remove date and time | . | Geofence | Optional enter/exit alert area — see Waypoint Geofences | . Waypoint Expiration . A waypoint stays until it is deleted unless you turn on Expires in the waypoint editor. The switch starts the expiry eight hours out; change it with the Date and Time pickers. Once that time passes, the waypoint is removed, which suits temporary markers such as rally points, hazards, or meeting locations. Expired waypoints are automatically hidden from the map so they don’t clutter the display. The expiration countdown is based on the absolute time you picked, not a duration from when the waypoint was created or received. Waypoint Geofences . Any waypoint can also define a geofence — an alert area — so you or others get notified when a node enters or leaves it: . | Set a geofence radius from the preset chips (or Off to disable), or tap Set area on map to draw a custom rectangular area instead. | Once a region is set, toggle Notify on enter and/or Notify on exit. | Optionally enable Favorites only to limit alerts to your favorited nodes. | . Since waypoints (and their geofences) are broadcast to the whole mesh, only the creator is alerted by default. If someone else shares a geofenced waypoint with you, its detail view offers a Notify me of crossings opt-in so you can also receive enter/exit alerts for it. Managing Waypoints . | Tap a waypoint to see its name, description, and geofence radius. On Google Play builds the first tap opens the marker’s info bubble — tap the bubble to open the waypoint itself | Locked waypoints can only be changed on the mesh by the node that locked them | Unlocked waypoints can be edited by any mesh member while connected to a node — saving re-broadcasts the waypoint | Confirming a delete removes your own copy. To remove it from everyone else’s map too, select Delete for everyone in the delete dialog; that box appears only for a waypoint you may change (unlocked, or locked by you) and only while you are connected | .

2449.title: Camadas do Mapa
2449.content: Tap the layers icon on the map to open Manage Map Layers. It imports your own overlays in .kml, .kmz, or GeoJSON format, including KMZ ground overlays (georeferenced images, such as exported topo or aerial tiles), which drape at their stated bounds. Add one by picking a file with Add Layer, opening a file with Meshtastic, or sharing it into the app from another app. A file opened or shared this way is refused if it is over 50 MB. Add Network Layer instead takes a name and an https:// URL pointing at a KML or GeoJSON file (http:// also works on Desktop, but on Android only for localhost); that layer then carries its own refresh button in the sheet. On Google Play builds the toolbar’s refresh button re-fetches every visible network layer at once. Imported layers are listed with a toggle to show/hide each one and an option to remove it. Each layer — imported or built-in overlay — carries its own opacity slider while it is switched on, so an overlay can be faded back rather than only switched off. This works on the Google Play build, the F-Droid build, and Desktop, which shares the same layer store and file picker. Site Planner . Site Planner estimates RF coverage for a transmitter and draws it on the map as a color-coded overlay. Open it from the Site Planner button in the map toolbar, or from a node’s detail page with Estimate coverage (shown only for nodes with a known position). The form has four sections: . | Site / Transmitter: name, latitude and longitude, TX power (W), Frequency (MHz), Antenna height (m), and Antenna gain (dBi). Chips such as Use current node location and Use map center fill in the coordinates. | Receiver: Receiver sensitivity (dBm) and Receiver height (m). | Simulation Options: Max range (km), from 1 to 150. | Display: Color palette. | . Tap Estimate coverage to run it. The app computes the estimate itself, using the ITU-R P.1812 propagation model over Mapterhorn terrain, on Google Play, F-Droid, and Desktop alike. The terrain downloads the first time an area is estimated, so that step needs a network connection; if it fails, the form comes back with a note to check your connection. The finished estimate is added under Manage Map Layers as a coverage estimate layer, and the map moves to it.

2450.title: Position Sharing
2450.content: Enabling Position Sharing . Your node shares its GPS position based on: . | Broadcast Interval — share the position on a fixed timer | Smart Position — share only once you have moved far enough; Minimum Interval sets the shortest gap between broadcasts and Minimum Distance how far you must move | Fixed Position — publish a latitude, longitude, and altitude you enter by hand instead of the GPS reading | GPS Mode — Enabled, Disabled, or Not Present on this hardware; offered only while Fixed Position is off | . Configure position behavior in Settings → Device configuration → Position, and saving it reboots the node. Without a connection the screen opens read-only, with a prompt to connect before changing anything. For the full field list, see Settings — Radio & User. Privacy Considerations . 🔒 Privacy: Position data is broadcast to all nodes on your channel. If you don’t want your location shared, set GPS Mode to Disabled, or use a Fixed Position somewhere else. To keep sharing a position without pinpointing yourself, edit the channel in Settings → Channels, turn Precise location off, and set the slider beneath it — the channel then publishes an approximate area, shown as ± a distance, instead of an exact point.

2463.title: Map & Waypoints
2463.content: The Map screen shows the geographic positions of nodes on your mesh, along with shared waypoints.

2464.title: Map View
2464.content: The map displays: . | Node positions — colored markers for each node reporting location | Waypoints — shared points of interest | Your position — your current GPS location | . Node Markers . Each node that reports a position is shown as a node chip marker displaying the node’s short name. The chip is colored by the node’s own identity color (a stable color derived from its node number) — the same chip used in the node list, so a node looks the same everywhere. Marker color does not encode online/offline status. When a node’s position updates live, its marker briefly pulses. Tapping a chip opens that node’s details. Nodes within 5 m of each other, which is common when they share a reduced position precision or sit at one site, are drawn as one chip with a count on its corner, showing a favorite or your own node when one is there. Tapping it lists every node at that spot, favorites first. Nearby markers are clustered as you zoom out. Tapping a cluster zooms in to fit its nodes, and a cluster whose nodes all share one spot lists them instead. With Show Precision Circles on, each spot’s circle stays visible inside a cluster too. Map Controls . | Zoom — pinch or use +/- buttons | Pan — drag to explore | Center — tap the location button to follow your position | Node tap — tap a node marker to view details | . The floating toolbar provides quick access to the compass, the map type and layers pickers, node filters, Site Planner, and location tracking. Tap the compass to reorient north-up, or tap the location button to follow your current position. While the map follows you, the compass instead turns heading lock on and off, so the map rotates with the phone. On Google Play builds a refresh button joins them while a network layer is showing; on F-Droid and Desktop, refresh a network layer from its own row in the layers sheet instead. Filtering the Map . Tap the filter button in the floating toolbar to open Filter map. Display controls what is drawn: Only Favorites, Show Waypoints, Show Precision Circles, and a slider that hides nodes not heard from recently. Node roles is a chip per device role, plus All to show every role; a selected chip means that role is shown. Nodes narrows the set further with Hide offline nodes, Only show direct nodes, Signed only, Encrypted only, Exclude MQTT, Show ignored nodes, and Include unknown — the same rules as the node list’s filter toggles. A dot on the filter button means at least one filter is hiding nodes — check it before concluding the mesh is quiet. Turning Show Waypoints off hides every waypoint, including your own. Show ignored nodes adds them to the map rather than showing only them — unlike the node list’s Only show ignored Nodes.

2465.title: AR mesh view
2465.content: The mesh view draws nodes and waypoints over the phone’s camera, each in the direction and at the height where it stands, with its distance and the age of its position. It needs a back camera and an orientation sensor, so it appears only on Android phones that have both, on Google Play and F-Droid builds alike. It isn’t available on Desktop. On opening, it asks for camera access and then location. Tap the mesh view button (Open mesh view) in the map’s top bar to see the whole mesh, filtered by the same Filter map settings as the map. The node list’s touch & hold menu, a node’s detail page, its compass sheet, its position log, and a traceroute map open the view too. Opened from a node, it shows only that node, plus the track or route you came from. | Tap a node to open its detail page, or a waypoint to open its info. | Touch & hold a node or waypoint to find it. The view says how far to turn and tilt, the phone ticks as you turn closer, and it pulses once you are on target. | A node whose position uncertainty covers your own spot has no meaningful direction, so it goes on the radar at the bottom instead. Point the phone down to enlarge the radar. | Waypoint geofences are outlined, and the view says when you are inside one. | . When your phone’s position has no altitude, targets sit level with you and the view says elevation is approximate. Without camera access, or while the phone is too hot, the view carries on as a compass.

2466.title: Waypoints
2466.content: Waypoints are shared points of interest, visible to everyone on your mesh. Creating a Waypoint . Your node must be connected — the map ignores a touch & hold while it is not, because saving a waypoint means broadcasting it. | Touch & hold the map at the desired location. | Enter a name and optional description. | Choose an icon/emoji for the waypoint. | Tap Send to share with the mesh. | . Waypoints always broadcast to the whole mesh on the primary channel. Unlike a message, a waypoint cannot be addressed to one channel or sent as a direct message. Waypoint Properties . | Property | Përshkrimi | . | Emri | Short identifier (max 29 characters) | . | Përshkrimi | Optional longer description | . | Icon | Visual marker emoji on the map | . | I bllokuar | If locked, only the creator can edit or delete | . | Expiration | Optional auto-remove date and time | . | Geofence | Optional enter/exit alert area — see Waypoint Geofences | . Waypoint Expiration . A waypoint stays until it is deleted unless you turn on Expires in the waypoint editor. The switch starts the expiry eight hours out; change it with the Date and Time pickers. Once that time passes, the waypoint is removed, which suits temporary markers such as rally points, hazards, or meeting locations. Expired waypoints are automatically hidden from the map so they don’t clutter the display. The expiration countdown is based on the absolute time you picked, not a duration from when the waypoint was created or received. Waypoint Geofences . Any waypoint can also define a geofence — an alert area — so you or others get notified when a node enters or leaves it: . | Set a geofence radius from the preset chips (or Off to disable), or tap Set area on map to draw a custom rectangular area instead. | Once a region is set, toggle Notify on enter and/or Notify on exit. | Optionally enable Favorites only to limit alerts to your favorited nodes. | . Since waypoints (and their geofences) are broadcast to the whole mesh, only the creator is alerted by default. If someone else shares a geofenced waypoint with you, its detail view offers a Notify me of crossings opt-in so you can also receive enter/exit alerts for it. Managing Waypoints . | Tap a waypoint to see its name, description, and geofence radius. On Google Play builds the first tap opens the marker’s info bubble — tap the bubble to open the waypoint itself | Locked waypoints can only be changed on the mesh by the node that locked them | Unlocked waypoints can be edited by any mesh member while connected to a node — saving re-broadcasts the waypoint | Confirming a delete removes your own copy. To remove it from everyone else’s map too, select Delete for everyone in the delete dialog; that box appears only for a waypoint you may change (unlocked, or locked by you) and only while you are connected | .

2467.title: Map Layers
2467.content: Tap the layers icon on the map to open Manage Map Layers. It imports your own overlays in .kml, .kmz, or GeoJSON format, including KMZ ground overlays (georeferenced images, such as exported topo or aerial tiles), which drape at their stated bounds. Add one by picking a file with Add Layer, opening a file with Meshtastic, or sharing it into the app from another app. A file opened or shared this way is refused if it is over 50 MB. Add Network Layer instead takes a name and an https:// URL pointing at a KML or GeoJSON file (http:// also works on Desktop, but on Android only for localhost); that layer then carries its own refresh button in the sheet. On Google Play builds the toolbar’s refresh button re-fetches every visible network layer at once. Imported layers are listed with a toggle to show/hide each one and an option to remove it. Each layer — imported or built-in overlay — carries its own opacity slider while it is switched on, so an overlay can be faded back rather than only switched off. This works on the Google Play build, the F-Droid build, and Desktop, which shares the same layer store and file picker. Site Planner . Site Planner estimates RF coverage for a transmitter and draws it on the map as a color-coded overlay. Open it from the Site Planner button in the map toolbar, or from a node’s detail page with Estimate coverage (shown only for nodes with a known position). The form has four sections: . | Site / Transmitter: name, latitude and longitude, TX power (W), Frequency (MHz), Antenna height (m), and Antenna gain (dBi). Chips such as Use current node location and Use map center fill in the coordinates. | Receiver: Receiver sensitivity (dBm) and Receiver height (m). | Simulation Options: Max range (km), from 1 to 150. | Display: Color palette. | . Tap Estimate coverage to run it. The app computes the estimate itself, using the ITU-R P.1812 propagation model over Mapterhorn terrain, on Google Play, F-Droid, and Desktop alike. The terrain downloads the first time an area is estimated, so that step needs a network connection; if it fails, the form comes back with a note to check your connection. The finished estimate is added under Manage Map Layers as a coverage estimate layer, and the map moves to it.

2468.title: Position Sharing
2468.content: Enabling Position Sharing . Your node shares its GPS position based on: . | Broadcast Interval — share the position on a fixed timer | Smart Position — share only once you have moved far enough; Minimum Interval sets the shortest gap between broadcasts and Minimum Distance how far you must move | Fixed Position — publish a latitude, longitude, and altitude you enter by hand instead of the GPS reading | GPS Mode — Enabled, Disabled, or Not Present on this hardware; offered only while Fixed Position is off | . Configure position behavior in Settings → Device configuration → Position, and saving it reboots the node. Without a connection the screen opens read-only, with a prompt to connect before changing anything. For the full field list, see Settings — Radio & User. Privacy Considerations . 🔒 Privacy: Position data is broadcast to all nodes on your channel. If you don’t want your location shared, set GPS Mode to Disabled, or use a Fixed Position somewhere else. To keep sharing a position without pinpointing yourself, edit the channel in Settings → Channels, turn Precise location off, and set the slider beneath it — the channel then publishes an approximate area, shown as ± a distance, instead of an exact point.

2481.title: Map & Waypoints
2481.content: The Map screen shows the geographic positions of nodes on your mesh, along with shared waypoints.

2482.title: Map View
2482.content: The map displays: . | Node positions — colored markers for each node reporting location | Waypoints — shared points of interest | Your position — your current GPS location | . Node Markers . Each node that reports a position is shown as a node chip marker displaying the node’s short name. The chip is colored by the node’s own identity color (a stable color derived from its node number) — the same chip used in the node list, so a node looks the same everywhere. Marker color does not encode online/offline status. When a node’s position updates live, its marker briefly pulses. Tapping a chip opens that node’s details. Nodes within 5 m of each other, which is common when they share a reduced position precision or sit at one site, are drawn as one chip with a count on its corner, showing a favorite or your own node when one is there. Tapping it lists every node at that spot, favorites first. Nearby markers are clustered as you zoom out. Tapping a cluster zooms in to fit its nodes, and a cluster whose nodes all share one spot lists them instead. With Show Precision Circles on, each spot’s circle stays visible inside a cluster too. Map Controls . | Zoom — pinch or use +/- buttons | Pan — drag to explore | Center — tap the location button to follow your position | Node tap — tap a node marker to view details | . The floating toolbar provides quick access to the compass, the map type and layers pickers, node filters, Site Planner, and location tracking. Tap the compass to reorient north-up, or tap the location button to follow your current position. While the map follows you, the compass instead turns heading lock on and off, so the map rotates with the phone. On Google Play builds a refresh button joins them while a network layer is showing; on F-Droid and Desktop, refresh a network layer from its own row in the layers sheet instead. Filtering the Map . Tap the filter button in the floating toolbar to open Filter map. Display controls what is drawn: Only Favorites, Show Waypoints, Show Precision Circles, and a slider that hides nodes not heard from recently. Node roles is a chip per device role, plus All to show every role; a selected chip means that role is shown. Nodes narrows the set further with Hide offline nodes, Only show direct nodes, Signed only, Encrypted only, Exclude MQTT, Show ignored nodes, and Include unknown — the same rules as the node list’s filter toggles. A dot on the filter button means at least one filter is hiding nodes — check it before concluding the mesh is quiet. Turning Show Waypoints off hides every waypoint, including your own. Show ignored nodes adds them to the map rather than showing only them — unlike the node list’s Only show ignored Nodes.

2483.title: AR mesh view
2483.content: The mesh view draws nodes and waypoints over the phone’s camera, each in the direction and at the height where it stands, with its distance and the age of its position. It needs a back camera and an orientation sensor, so it appears only on Android phones that have both, on Google Play and F-Droid builds alike. It isn’t available on Desktop. On opening, it asks for camera access and then location. Tap the mesh view button (Open mesh view) in the map’s top bar to see the whole mesh, filtered by the same Filter map settings as the map. The node list’s touch & hold menu, a node’s detail page, its compass sheet, its position log, and a traceroute map open the view too. Opened from a node, it shows only that node, plus the track or route you came from. | Tap a node to open its detail page, or a waypoint to open its info. | Touch & hold a node or waypoint to find it. The view says how far to turn and tilt, the phone ticks as you turn closer, and it pulses once you are on target. | A node whose position uncertainty covers your own spot has no meaningful direction, so it goes on the radar at the bottom instead. Point the phone down to enlarge the radar. | Waypoint geofences are outlined, and the view says when you are inside one. | . When your phone’s position has no altitude, targets sit level with you and the view says elevation is approximate. Without camera access, or while the phone is too hot, the view carries on as a compass.

2484.title: Waypoints
2484.content: Waypoints are shared points of interest, visible to everyone on your mesh. Creating a Waypoint . Your node must be connected — the map ignores a touch & hold while it is not, because saving a waypoint means broadcasting it. | Touch & hold the map at the desired location. | Enter a name and optional description. | Choose an icon/emoji for the waypoint. | Tap Send to share with the mesh. | . Waypoints always broadcast to the whole mesh on the primary channel. Unlike a message, a waypoint cannot be addressed to one channel or sent as a direct message. Waypoint Properties . | Property | Opis | . | Ime | Short identifier (max 29 characters) | . | Opis | Optional longer description | . | Icon | Visual marker emoji on the map | . | Zaključano | If locked, only the creator can edit or delete | . | Expiration | Optional auto-remove date and time | . | Geofence | Optional enter/exit alert area — see Waypoint Geofences | . Waypoint Expiration . A waypoint stays until it is deleted unless you turn on Expires in the waypoint editor. The switch starts the expiry eight hours out; change it with the Date and Time pickers. Once that time passes, the waypoint is removed, which suits temporary markers such as rally points, hazards, or meeting locations. Expired waypoints are automatically hidden from the map so they don’t clutter the display. The expiration countdown is based on the absolute time you picked, not a duration from when the waypoint was created or received. Waypoint Geofences . Any waypoint can also define a geofence — an alert area — so you or others get notified when a node enters or leaves it: . | Set a geofence radius from the preset chips (or Off to disable), or tap Set area on map to draw a custom rectangular area instead. | Once a region is set, toggle Notify on enter and/or Notify on exit. | Optionally enable Favorites only to limit alerts to your favorited nodes. | . Since waypoints (and their geofences) are broadcast to the whole mesh, only the creator is alerted by default. If someone else shares a geofenced waypoint with you, its detail view offers a Notify me of crossings opt-in so you can also receive enter/exit alerts for it. Managing Waypoints . | Tap a waypoint to see its name, description, and geofence radius. On Google Play builds the first tap opens the marker’s info bubble — tap the bubble to open the waypoint itself | Locked waypoints can only be changed on the mesh by the node that locked them | Unlocked waypoints can be edited by any mesh member while connected to a node — saving re-broadcasts the waypoint | Confirming a delete removes your own copy. To remove it from everyone else’s map too, select Delete for everyone in the delete dialog; that box appears only for a waypoint you may change (unlocked, or locked by you) and only while you are connected | .

2485.title: Map Layers
2485.content: Tap the layers icon on the map to open Manage Map Layers. It imports your own overlays in .kml, .kmz, or GeoJSON format, including KMZ ground overlays (georeferenced images, such as exported topo or aerial tiles), which drape at their stated bounds. Add one by picking a file with Add Layer, opening a file with Meshtastic, or sharing it into the app from another app. A file opened or shared this way is refused if it is over 50 MB. Add Network Layer instead takes a name and an https:// URL pointing at a KML or GeoJSON file (http:// also works on Desktop, but on Android only for localhost); that layer then carries its own refresh button in the sheet. On Google Play builds the toolbar’s refresh button re-fetches every visible network layer at once. Imported layers are listed with a toggle to show/hide each one and an option to remove it. Each layer — imported or built-in overlay — carries its own opacity slider while it is switched on, so an overlay can be faded back rather than only switched off. This works on the Google Play build, the F-Droid build, and Desktop, which shares the same layer store and file picker. Site Planner . Site Planner estimates RF coverage for a transmitter and draws it on the map as a color-coded overlay. Open it from the Site Planner button in the map toolbar, or from a node’s detail page with Estimate coverage (shown only for nodes with a known position). The form has four sections: . | Site / Transmitter: name, latitude and longitude, TX power (W), Frequency (MHz), Antenna height (m), and Antenna gain (dBi). Chips such as Use current node location and Use map center fill in the coordinates. | Receiver: Receiver sensitivity (dBm) and Receiver height (m). | Simulation Options: Max range (km), from 1 to 150. | Display: Color palette. | . Tap Estimate coverage to run it. The app computes the estimate itself, using the ITU-R P.1812 propagation model over Mapterhorn terrain, on Google Play, F-Droid, and Desktop alike. The terrain downloads the first time an area is estimated, so that step needs a network connection; if it fails, the form comes back with a note to check your connection. The finished estimate is added under Manage Map Layers as a coverage estimate layer, and the map moves to it.

2486.title: Position Sharing
2486.content: Enabling Position Sharing . Your node shares its GPS position based on: . | Broadcast Interval — share the position on a fixed timer | Smart Position — share only once you have moved far enough; Minimum Interval sets the shortest gap between broadcasts and Minimum Distance how far you must move | Fixed Position — publish a latitude, longitude, and altitude you enter by hand instead of the GPS reading | GPS Mode — Enabled, Disabled, or Not Present on this hardware; offered only while Fixed Position is off | . Configure position behavior in Settings → Device configuration → Position, and saving it reboots the node. Without a connection the screen opens read-only, with a prompt to connect before changing anything. For the full field list, see Settings — Radio & User. Privacy Considerations . 🔒 Privacy: Position data is broadcast to all nodes on your channel. If you don’t want your location shared, set GPS Mode to Disabled, or use a Fixed Position somewhere else. To keep sharing a position without pinpointing yourself, edit the channel in Settings → Channels, turn Precise location off, and set the slider beneath it — the channel then publishes an approximate area, shown as ± a distance, instead of an exact point.

2487.title: Map Sources
2487.content: Every build offers a base map picker from the map toolbar. Google Play builds open on Google’s own map types; F-Droid and Desktop builds open on MapLibre’s vector styles. Further down the base map picker, all three offer the same raster base maps: . | Base map | Notes | . | Normal / Satellite / Terrain / Hybrid | Google Play only — Google’s own map types | . | Liberty | Default on F-Droid and Desktop. Vector street map | . | Positron | F-Droid and Desktop only. Low-contrast vector map; keeps node markers legible over it | . | Tamna | F-Droid and Desktop only. Vector map suited to dark themes | . | OpenStreetMap | Classic raster street tiles | . | OpenTopoMap | Raster topographic | . | USGS Topo / USGS Imagery | US coverage only | . | Esri Topo / Esri Imagery | Topographic and satellite imagery | . Overlays can be toggled on top of any base map, from the layers sheet: . | Weather radar — NOAA NEXRAD reflectivity (US coverage) | Hillshade — terrain relief from an online tile source, on F-Droid and Desktop only; Google Play draws hillshade from downloaded offline terrain instead. Useful for understanding why a link fails, since LoRa range is limited by terrain | . Adding your own tile source . Any XYZ tile endpoint can be added as a base map, on every flavor and on desktop. Open Manage Custom Tile Sources at the foot of the base map picker and paste a URL template using {z}, {x} and {y} — plus {s} if the provider uses rotating subdomains. A national mapping service, for example: . https://wmts.geo.admin.ch/1.0.0/ch.swisstopo.pixelkarte-farbe/default/current/3857/{z}/{x}/{y}.jpeg . On Android the template must use https://; plain http:// works only for localhost. Tiles are cached on disk, so panning does not re-download what you were just looking at. On Android, the same screen also imports a local .mbtiles archive for fully offline use. On F-Droid, select a vector base map first — Liberty, Positron, or Dark — since a download is defined against a vector style and Start Download stays disabled over a raster one. Frame the area you want on screen, then tap Start Download in the layers sheet’s Cache Manager section: that creates a paused pack covering the current zoom plus two levels deeper. Press play on the pack’s row to download it. While the offline database opens, the section shows a progress bar. If it cannot be opened, the section reads Offline maps are unavailable on this device and Start Download stays disabled. If the area cannot be saved, the section reads Couldn’t save this area for offline use. On Google Play, the layers sheet’s Offline Manager section downloads its own offline regions instead — water, roads and administrative boundaries extracted from the public Protomaps basemap dataset, drawn directly as map shapes rather than raster tiles. Frame the area you want, tap Start Download, and once it finishes turn on Show on map to draw it. The switch is off by default, so a download never covers up the live map unasked. Desktop has no offline base map downloads, though the offline terrain described next does work there. Offline terrain . Hillshade and elevation contours can be downloaded for offline use as well, so a downloaded area still shows why a link fails when there is no network. The terrain data comes from Mapterhorn and is credited on the map. On Google Play, each downloaded region in the Offline Manager list has a Download Terrain button. Terrain attaches to that region and shares its storage limit, and an area too large for terrain asks you to zoom in or pick a smaller region. Once the terrain is downloaded, the button gives way to Hillshade and Contours switches, both off until you turn them on. On F-Droid and Desktop, the layers sheet has an Offline Terrain section of its own: frame the area, tap Start Download, and the hillshade and contours draw automatically from then on, whenever the downloaded area is in view. Going offline . A pill reading Offline — showing cached map data appears over the map whenever the device has no network connection. On Google Play builds, if you’ve imported a local .mbtiles archive, the map switches to it automatically the moment the network drops — no toggle to remember — and switches back once you’re reconnected, as long as you haven’t picked a different base map yourself in between. On F-Droid, a downloaded offline area keeps rendering on its own; the pill is purely informational there. Desktop downloads offline terrain but no base-map packs, so the pill is informational there too.

Tap the filter button in the floating toolbar to open Filter map. Nodes narrows the set further with Hide offline nodes, Only show direct nodes, Signed only, Encrypted only, Exclude MQTT, Show ignored nodes, and Include unknown — the same rules as the node list’s filter toggles. A dot on the filter button means at least one filter is hiding nodes — check it before concluding the mesh is quiet. Turning Show Waypoints off hides every waypoint, including your own. Show ignored nodes adds them to the map rather than showing only them — unlike the node list’s Only show ignored Nodes.

2501.title: AR mesh view
2501.content: The mesh view draws nodes and waypoints over the phone’s camera, each in the direction and at the height where it stands, with its distance and the age of its position. It needs a back camera and an orientation sensor, so it appears only on Android phones that have both, on Google Play and F-Droid builds alike. It isn’t available on Desktop. On opening, it asks for camera access and then location. Tap the mesh view button (Open mesh view) in the map’s top bar to see the whole mesh, filtered by the same Filter map settings as the map. The node list’s touch & hold menu, a node’s detail page, its compass sheet, its position log, and a traceroute map open the view too. Opened from a node, it shows only that node, plus the track or route you came from. | Tap a node to open its detail page, or a waypoint to open its info. | Touch & hold a node or waypoint to find it. The view says how far to turn and tilt, the phone ticks as you turn closer, and it pulses once you are on target. | A node whose position uncertainty covers your own spot has no meaningful direction, so it goes on the radar at the bottom instead. Point the phone down to enlarge the radar. | Waypoint geofences are outlined, and the view says when you are inside one. | . When your phone’s position has no altitude, targets sit level with you and the view says elevation is approximate. Without camera access, or while the phone is too hot, the view carries on as a compass.

2502.title: Waypoints
2502.content: Waypoints are shared points of interest, visible to everyone on your mesh. Creating a Waypoint . Your node must be connected — the map ignores a touch & hold while it is not, because saving a waypoint means broadcasting it. | Touch & hold the map at the desired location. | Enter a name and optional description. | Choose an icon/emoji for the waypoint. | Tap Send to share with the mesh. | . Waypoints always broadcast to the whole mesh on the primary channel. Unlike a message, a waypoint cannot be addressed to one channel or sent as a direct message. Waypoint Properties . | Property | الوصف | . | الاسم | Short identifier (max 29 characters) | . | الوصف | Optional longer description | . | Icon | Visual marker emoji on the map | . | مقفل | If locked, only the creator can edit or delete | . | Expiration | Optional auto-remove date and time | . | Geofence | Optional enter/exit alert area — see Waypoint Geofences | . Waypoint Expiration . A waypoint stays until it is deleted unless you turn on Expires in the waypoint editor. The switch starts the expiry eight hours out; change it with the Date and Time pickers. Once that time passes, the waypoint is removed, which suits temporary markers such as rally points, hazards, or meeting locations. Expired waypoints are automatically hidden from the map so they don’t clutter the display. The expiration countdown is based on the absolute time you picked, not a duration from when the waypoint was created or received. Waypoint Geofences . Any waypoint can also define a geofence — an alert area — so you or others get notified when a node enters or leaves it: . | Set a geofence radius from the preset chips (or Off to disable), or tap Set area on map to draw a custom rectangular area instead. | Once a region is set, toggle Notify on enter and/or Notify on exit. | Optionally enable Favorites only to limit alerts to your favorited nodes. | . Since waypoints (and their geofences) are broadcast to the whole mesh, only the creator is alerted by default. If someone else shares a geofenced waypoint with you, its detail view offers a Notify me of crossings opt-in so you can also receive enter/exit alerts for it. Managing Waypoints . | Tap a waypoint to see its name, description, and geofence radius. On Google Play builds the first tap opens the marker’s info bubble — tap the bubble to open the waypoint itself | Locked waypoints can only be changed on the mesh by the node that locked them | Unlocked waypoints can be edited by any mesh member while connected to a node — saving re-broadcasts the waypoint | Confirming a delete removes your own copy. To remove it from everyone else’s map too, select Delete for everyone in the delete dialog; that box appears only for a waypoint you may change (unlocked, or locked by you) and only while you are connected | .

2503.title: Map Layers
2503.content: Tap the layers icon on the map to open Manage Map Layers. It imports your own overlays in .kml, .kmz, or GeoJSON format, including KMZ ground overlays (georeferenced images, such as exported topo or aerial tiles), which drape at their stated bounds. Add one by picking a file with Add Layer, opening a file with Meshtastic, or sharing it into the app from another app. A file opened or shared this way is refused if it is over 50 MB. Add Network Layer instead takes a name and an https:// URL pointing at a KML or GeoJSON file (http:// also works on Desktop, but on Android only for localhost); that layer then carries its own refresh button in the sheet. On Google Play builds the toolbar’s refresh button re-fetches every visible network layer at once. Imported layers are listed with a toggle to show/hide each one and an option to remove it. Each layer — imported or built-in overlay — carries its own opacity slider while it is switched on, so an overlay can be faded back rather than only switched off. This works on the Google Play build, the F-Droid build, and Desktop, which shares the same layer store and file picker. Site Planner . Site Planner estimates RF coverage for a transmitter and draws it on the map as a color-coded overlay. Open it from the Site Planner button in the map toolbar, or from a node’s detail page with Estimate coverage (shown only for nodes with a known position). The form has four sections: . | Site / Transmitter: name, latitude and longitude, TX power (W), Frequency (MHz), Antenna height (m), and Antenna gain (dBi). Chips such as Use current node location and Use map center fill in the coordinates. | Receiver: Receiver sensitivity (dBm) and Receiver height (m). | Simulation Options: Max range (km), from 1 to 150. | Display: Color palette. | . Tap Estimate coverage to run it. The app computes the estimate itself, using the ITU-R P.1812 propagation model over Mapterhorn terrain, on Google Play, F-Droid, and Desktop alike. The terrain downloads the first time an area is estimated, so that step needs a network connection; if it fails, the form comes back with a note to check your connection. The finished estimate is added under Manage Map Layers as a coverage estimate layer, and the map moves to it.

2504.title: Position Sharing
2504.content: Enabling Position Sharing . Your node shares its GPS position based on: . | Broadcast Interval — share the position on a fixed timer | Smart Position — share only once you have moved far enough; Minimum Interval sets the shortest gap between broadcasts and Minimum Distance how far you must move | Fixed Position — publish a latitude, longitude, and altitude you enter by hand instead of the GPS reading | GPS Mode — Enabled, Disabled, or Not Present on this hardware; offered only while Fixed Position is off | . Configure position behavior in Settings → Device configuration → Position, and saving it reboots the node. Without a connection the screen opens read-only, with a prompt to connect before changing anything. For the full field list, see Settings — Radio & User. Privacy Considerations . 🔒 Privacy: Position data is broadcast to all nodes on your channel. If you don’t want your location shared, set GPS Mode to Disabled, or use a Fixed Position somewhere else. To keep sharing a position without pinpointing yourself, edit the channel in Settings → Channels, turn Precise location off, and set the slider beneath it — the channel then publishes an approximate area, shown as ± a distance, instead of an exact point.

2505.title: Map Sources
2505.content: Every build offers a base map picker from the map toolbar. Google Play builds open on Google’s own map types; F-Droid and Desktop builds open on MapLibre’s vector styles. Further down the base map picker, all three offer the same raster base maps: . | Base map | Notes | . | Normal / Satellite / Terrain / Hybrid | Google Play only — Google’s own map types | . | Liberty | Default on F-Droid and Desktop. Vector street map | . | Positron | F-Droid and Desktop only. Low-contrast vector map; keeps node markers legible over it | . | Dark | F-Droid and Desktop only. Vector map suited to dark themes | . | OpenStreetMap | Classic raster street tiles | . | OpenTopoMap | Raster topographic | . | USGS Topo / USGS Imagery | US coverage only | . | Esri Topo / Esri Imagery | Topographic and satellite imagery | . Overlays can be toggled on top of any base map, from the layers sheet: . | Weather radar — NOAA NEXRAD reflectivity (US coverage) | Hillshade — terrain relief from an online tile source, on F-Droid and Desktop only; Google Play draws hillshade from downloaded offline terrain instead. Useful for understanding why a link fails, since LoRa range is limited by terrain | . Adding your own tile source . Any XYZ tile endpoint can be added as a base map, on every flavor and on desktop. Open Manage Custom Tile Sources at the foot of the base map picker and paste a URL template using {z}, {x} and {y} — plus {s} if the provider uses rotating subdomains. A national mapping service, for example: . https://wmts.geo.admin.ch/1.0.0/ch.swisstopo.pixelkarte-farbe/default/current/3857/{z}/{x}/{y}.jpeg . On Android the template must use https://; plain http:// works only for localhost. Tiles are cached on disk, so panning does not re-download what you were just looking at. On Android, the same screen also imports a local .mbtiles archive for fully offline use. On F-Droid, select a vector base map first — Liberty, Positron, or Dark — since a download is defined against a vector style and Start Download stays disabled over a raster one. Frame the area you want on screen, then tap Start Download in the layers sheet’s Cache Manager section: that creates a paused pack covering the current zoom plus two levels deeper. Press play on the pack’s row to download it. While the offline database opens, the section shows a progress bar. If it cannot be opened, the section reads Offline maps are unavailable on this device and Start Download stays disabled. If the area cannot be saved, the section reads Couldn’t save this area for offline use. On Google Play, the layers sheet’s Offline Manager section downloads its own offline regions instead — water, roads and administrative boundaries extracted from the public Protomaps basemap dataset, drawn directly as map shapes rather than raster tiles. Frame the area you want, tap Start Download, and once it finishes turn on Show on map to draw it. The switch is off by default, so a download never covers up the live map unasked. Desktop has no offline base map downloads, though the offline terrain described next does work there. Offline terrain . Hillshade and elevation contours can be downloaded for offline use as well, so a downloaded area still shows why a link fails when there is no network. The terrain data comes from Mapterhorn and is credited on the map. On Google Play, each downloaded region in the Offline Manager list has a Download Terrain button. Terrain attaches to that region and shares its storage limit, and an area too large for terrain asks you to zoom in or pick a smaller region. Once the terrain is downloaded, the button gives way to Hillshade and Contours switches, both off until you turn them on. On F-Droid and Desktop, the layers sheet has an Offline Terrain section of its own: frame the area, tap Start Download, and the hillshade and contours draw automatically from then on, whenever the downloaded area is in view. Going offline . A pill reading Offline — showing cached map data appears over the map whenever the device has no network connection. On Google Play builds, if you’ve imported a local .mbtiles archive, the map switches to it automatically the moment the network drops — no toggle to remember — and switches back once you’re reconnected, as long as you haven’t picked a different base map yourself in between. On F-Droid, a downloaded offline area keeps rendering on its own; the pill is purely informational there. Desktop downloads offline terrain but no base-map packs, so the pill is informational there too.

2521.title: Kaardikihid
2521.content: Tap the layers icon on the map to open Manage Map Layers. It imports your own overlays in .kml, .kmz, or GeoJSON format, including KMZ ground overlays (georeferenced images, such as exported topo or aerial tiles), which drape at their stated bounds. Add one by picking a file with Add Layer, opening a file with Meshtastic, or sharing it into the app from another app. A file opened or shared this way is refused if it is over 50 MB. Add Network Layer instead takes a name and an https:// URL pointing at a KML or GeoJSON file (http:// also works on Desktop, but on Android only for localhost); that layer then carries its own refresh button in the sheet. On Google Play builds the toolbar’s refresh button re-fetches every visible network layer at once. Imporditud kihid on loetletud koos lülitiga iga kihi kuvamiseks/peitmiseks ja valikuga selle eemaldamiseks. Each layer — imported or built-in overlay — carries its own opacity slider while it is switched on, so an overlay can be faded back rather than only switched off. This works on the Google Play build, the F-Droid build, and Desktop, which shares the same layer store and file picker. Saidi planeerija . Asukoha planeerija hindab saatja raadiosageduslikku leviala ja joonistab selle kaardile värvikoodiga kihina. Open it from the Site Planner button in the map toolbar, or from a node’s detail page with Estimate coverage (shown only for nodes with a known position). The form has four sections: . | Site / Transmitter: name, latitude and longitude, TX power (W), Frequency (MHz), Antenna height (m), and Antenna gain (dBi). Chips such as Use current node location and Use map center fill in the coordinates. | Receiver: Receiver sensitivity (dBm) and Receiver height (m). | Simulation Options: Max range (km), from 1 to 150. | Display: Color palette. | . 2522.title: Position Sharing
2522.content: Enabling Position Sharing . Sõlm jagab oma GPS asukohta järgmise alusel: . | Broadcast Interval — share the position on a fixed timer | Smart Position — share only once you have moved far enough; Minimum Interval sets the shortest gap between broadcasts and Minimum Distance how far you must move | Fixed Position — publish a latitude, longitude, and altitude you enter by hand instead of the GPS reading | GPS Mode — Enabled, Disabled, or Not Present on this hardware; offered only while Fixed Position is off | . Configure position behavior in Settings → Device configuration → Position, and saving it reboots the node. Without a connection the screen opens read-only, with a prompt to connect before changing anything. For the full field list, see Settings — Radio & User. Privacy Considerations . 🔒 Privaatsus: asukoha andmed levitatakse kõigile sinu kanali sõlmedele. If you don’t want your location shared, set GPS Mode to Disabled, or use a Fixed Position somewhere else. 2523.title: Kaardi allikad
2523.content: Every build offers a base map picker from the map toolbar. Google Play builds open on Google’s own map types; F-Droid and Desktop builds open on MapLibre’s vector styles. Further down the base map picker, all three offer the same raster base maps: . | Base map | Sõnumid | . | Normal / Satellite / Terrain / Hybrid | Google Play only — Google’s own map types | . | Liberty | Default on F-Droid and Desktop. Vector street map | . | Positron | F-Droid and Desktop only. Low-contrast vector map; keeps node markers legible over it | . | Tume | F-Droid and Desktop only. Vector map suited to dark themes | . | OpenStreetMap | Classic raster street tiles | . | OpenTopoMap | Raster topographic | . | USGS Topo / USGS Imagery | US coverage only | . | Esri Topo / Esri Imagery | Topographic and satellite imagery | . Overlays can be toggled on top of any base map, from the layers sheet: . | Weather radar — NOAA NEXRAD reflectivity (US coverage) | Hillshade — terrain relief from an online tile source, on F-Droid and Desktop only; Google Play draws hillshade from downloaded offline terrain instead. Useful for understanding why a link fails, since LoRa range is limited by terrain | . Adding your own tile source . Any XYZ tile endpoint can be added as a base map, on every flavor and on desktop. Open Manage Custom Tile Sources at the foot of the base map picker and paste a URL template using {z}, {x} and {y} — plus {s} if the provider uses rotating subdomains. A national mapping service, for example: . https://wmts.geo.admin.ch/1.0.0/ch.swisstopo.pixelkarte-farbe/default/current/3857/{z}/{x}/{y}.jpeg . On Android the template must use https://; plain http:// works only for localhost. Tiles are cached on disk, so panning does not re-download what you were just looking at. On Android, the same screen also imports a local .mbtiles archive for fully offline use. On F-Droid, select a vector base map first — Liberty, Positron, or Dark — since a download is defined against a vector style and Start Download stays disabled over a raster one. Frame the area you want on screen, then tap Start Download in the layers sheet’s Cache Manager section: that creates a paused pack covering the current zoom plus two levels deeper. Press play on the pack’s row to download it. While the offline database opens, the section shows a progress bar. If it cannot be opened, the section reads Offline maps are unavailable on this device and Start Download stays disabled. If the area cannot be saved, the section reads Couldn’t save this area for offline use. On Google Play, the layers sheet’s Offline Manager section downloads its own offline regions instead — water, roads and administrative boundaries extracted from the public Protomaps basemap dataset, drawn directly as map shapes rather than raster tiles. Frame the area you want, tap Start Download, and once it finishes turn on Show on map to draw it. The switch is off by default, so a download never covers up the live map unasked. Desktop has no offline base map downloads, though the offline terrain described next does work there. Offline terrain . Hillshade and elevation contours can be downloaded for offline use as well, so a downloaded area still shows why a link fails when there is no network. The terrain data comes from Mapterhorn and is credited on the map. On Google Play, each downloaded region in the Offline Manager list has a Download Terrain button. Terrain attaches to that region and shares its storage limit, and an area too large for terrain asks you to zoom in or pick a smaller region. Once the terrain is downloaded, the button gives way to Hillshade and Contours switches, both off until you turn them on. On F-Droid and Desktop, the layers sheet has an Offline Terrain section of its own: frame the area, tap Start Download, and the hillshade and contours draw automatically from then on, whenever the downloaded area is in view. Going offline . A pill reading Offline — showing cached map data appears over the map whenever the device has no network connection. On Google Play builds, if you’ve imported a local .mbtiles archive, the map switches to it automatically the moment the network drops — no toggle to remember — and switches back once you’re reconnected, as long as you haven’t picked a different base map yourself in between. On F-Droid, a downloaded offline area keeps rendering on its own; the pill is purely informational there. Desktop downloads offline terrain but no base-map packs, so the pill is informational there too.

2534.title: Measurement & Formatting
2534.content: How the Meshtastic Android/KMP app formats numbers, units, and locale-sensitive values.

2535.title: Overview
2535.content: All measurement data transmitted by Meshtastic nodes uses metric units (meters, °C, hPa, m/s, etc.). The app converts and formats these values for display with these utilities: . | Utility | Location | Purpose | . | MetricFormatter | core/common/.../util/MetricFormatter.kt | Converts and formats physical measurements (temperature, pressure, speed, etc.) | . | NumberFormatter | core/common/.../util/NumberFormatter.kt | Decimal formatting: format follows the OS locale, formatInvariant keeps a fixed dot separator | . | formatMeasure | core/common/.../util/MeasureFormatting.kt | Pairs a fixed English unit symbol (MeasureUnitKind) with a locale-formatted number, for the units that convert | . | toDistanceString and siblings | core/model/.../util/DistanceExtensions.kt | Distance, elevation, speed and small-distance strings, rendered through CLDR where the platform can and by hand where it can’t | . The core/common utilities live in org.meshtastic.core.common.util and compile for every KMP target (Android, Desktop, iOS). iOS is a compile-only target: its locale formatting falls back to the invariant form.

2536.title: MetricFormatter API
2536.content: MetricFormatter is a Kotlin object with pure functions for each measurement type: . object MetricFormatter { fun degreeSymbol(isFahrenheit: Boolean): String fun temperature(celsius: Float, isFahrenheit: Boolean): String fun voltage(volts: Float, decimalPlaces: Int = 2): String fun current(milliAmps: Float, decimalPlaces: Int = 1): String fun percent(value: Float, decimalPlaces: Int = 1): String fun percent(value: Int): String fun humidity(value: Float): String fun pressure(hPa: Float, decimalPlaces: Int = 1): String fun snr(value: Float?, decimalPlaces: Int = 1): String fun rssi(value: Int?): String fun windSpeed(metersPerSecond: Float, isImperial: Boolean, decimalPlaces: Int = 1): String fun rainfall(millimeters: Float, isImperial: Boolean, decimalPlaces: Int = 1): String fun weight(kilograms: Float, isImperial: Boolean, decimalPlaces: Int = 2): String } . snr and rssi take a nullable reading and render the — placeholder when it is absent. 0 dB and 0 dBm are real readings, so they never stand in for a missing one. Usage . Output shown for an en-US locale: . // Temperature — Fahrenheit conversion is handled automatically MetricFormatter.temperature(22.5f, isFahrenheit = true) // "72.5°F" MetricFormatter.temperature(22.5f, isFahrenheit = false) // "22.5°C" // Signal metrics MetricFormatter.snr(-5.2f) // "-5.2 dB" MetricFormatter.rssi(-97) // "-97 dBm" // Environment MetricFormatter.pressure(1013.25f) // "1,013.3 hPa" MetricFormatter.humidity(65.0f) // "65%" MetricFormatter.windSpeed(3.7f, isImperial = false) // "13.3 km/h" MetricFormatter.windSpeed(3.7f, isImperial = true) // "8.3 mph" MetricFormatter.rainfall(12.3f, isImperial = false) // "12.3 mm" MetricFormatter.rainfall(12.3f, isImperial = true) // "0.5 in" // Power MetricFormatter.voltage(3.95f) // "3.95 V" MetricFormatter.current(125.0f) // "125.0 mA" .

2537.title: NumberFormatter
2537.content: NumberFormatter has two halves, and picking the wrong one is the mistake to avoid: . object NumberFormatter { fun format(value: Double, decimalPlaces: Int): String // follows the OS locale fun format(value: Float, decimalPlaces: Int): String // follows the OS locale fun formatInvariant(value: Double, decimalPlaces: Int): String // fixed dot separator fun formatInvariant(value: Float, decimalPlaces: Int): String // fixed dot separator fun parseDecimalOrNull(text: String): Double? // reads a comma or dot decimal } . Use format for anything a person reads. It delegates to the platform’s own number formatter through an expect/actual (java.text.NumberFormat on JVM and Android), with the locale’s decimal and grouping separators, so a number reads the way that user writes numbers. NaN and infinity render as —. Use formatInvariant for anything a machine parses — a CoT payload another client reads, or a value written out and read back. Localizing those turns 1.5 into 1,5 and breaks the reader. It rounds half away from zero to match the locale path, which matters because firmware reports SNR in quarter-dB steps and ties are routine. parseDecimalOrNull is the input-side counterpart: it accepts a number typed with the keyboard locale’s decimal separator, such as 48,21, which String.toDoubleOrNull rejects.

2538.title: Unit conversion
2538.content: Four MetricFormatter measurements convert away from metric for display, each gated by a boolean flag that callers take from LocaleUnitsProvider: . | Measurement | Flag | Source | Conversion | . | temperature | isFahrenheit | LocaleUnitsProvider.temperatureUnit | °F = °C × 1.8 + 32 | . | windSpeed | isImperial | LocaleUnitsProvider.measurementSystem | m/s × 3.6 → km/h, or × 2.23694 → mph | . | rainfall | isImperial | LocaleUnitsProvider.measurementSystem | mm ÷ 25.4 → in | . | weight | isImperial | LocaleUnitsProvider.measurementSystem | kg × 2.20462 → lb | . The OS resolution behind those flags is two separate functions in core/common/.../util/MeasurementSystem.kt, getSystemMeasurementSystem() and getSystemTemperatureUnit(). They are deliberately separate: some locales mix systems (the UK uses miles for distance but Celsius for temperature), so temperature must never be derived from the distance unit. On Android, getSystemTemperatureUnit() delegates to androidx.core.text.util.LocalePreferences, which resolves CLDR locale data and honors the Android 14+ Regional preferences temperature override. The in-app Units choice (UnitsOverride, stored in UiPrefs) is folded in by LocaleUnitsProvider, which is the only place display code takes units from. A Konsist rule (MeasurementSystemSourceTest) keeps direct reads of the OS resolution out of the rest of the codebase, because a direct read follows the locale but ignores the setting. A forced system carries its temperature with it (metric → °C, imperial → °F), overriding even an explicit OS regional temperature preference. getSystemMeasurementSystem() resolves the locale in this order (temperature is separate: as described earlier, getSystemTemperatureUnit() reads the regional temperature preference via LocalePreferences, shares only the region backfill, and falls back to Celsius): . | The ms Unicode extension (the Android 16+ Measurement system preference) wins outright. | A locale with no region — the in-app language picker offers bare tags like en — takes its region from the system configuration rather than letting ICU guess one from the language. | Anything still unclassified falls back to metric, never imperial. | . The Android and Desktop implementations share the region table and the override reader in commonMain, so the two clients can’t disagree about the same locale. Everything else MetricFormatter formats (voltage, current, pressure, SNR, RSSI, humidity, percent) displays in its native metric units. The user-facing Units & Locale page explains what end users see.

2539.title: Distance, elevation, and speed
2539.content: Lengths and speeds go through the extension functions in core/model/.../util/DistanceExtensions.kt, which take the MeasurementSystem from LocaleUnitsProvider: . | Function | Renders | . | Int.toDistanceString | A distance in meters, as m or km, or ft or mi, by magnitude | . | Int.toElevationString | An altitude in whole meters or feet at any magnitude | . | Float.toSpeedString | A speed in m/s, as km/h or mph | . | Float.toSmallDistanceString | Millimeters, as mm or inches | . | Float.toStormDistanceString | Whole kilometers, or miles to one decimal | . Each first asks the expect functions in LocalizedUnitFormatting.kt (formatLengthLocalized, formatElevationLocalized, formatSpeedLocalized, formatRainfallLocalized), which render through the platform’s ICU data with CLDR’s digits, symbol, and spacing. They return null where the platform can’t answer: on Desktop and iOS, on Android versions without the ICU API they need, and for a non-finite value. The caller then renders its own fallback through formatMeasure. None of them uses CLDR’s road usage, whose rounding would show a node 87 m away as 90 m.

2540.title: Adding a new measurement type
2540.content: To add a new measurement formatter: . | Add a function to MetricFormatter in core/common/src/commonMain/kotlin/org/meshtastic/core/common/util/MetricFormatter.kt. Take the value in the unit the node sends; the protobuf EnvironmentMetrics.radiation field, for example, is µR/h: . fun radiation(microRoentgensPerHour: Float, decimalPlaces: Int = 2): String = "${NumberFormatter.format(microRoentgensPerHour, decimalPlaces)} µR/h" . | Add tests in core/common/src/commonTest/: . @Test fun radiationFormatting() { assertEquals("0.15 µR/h", MetricFormatter.radiation(0.15f)) assertEquals("1.23 µR/h", MetricFormatter.radiation(1.234f)) } . | Use in UI — call from any commonMain composable or ViewModel: . envMetrics.radiation?.let { Text(text = MetricFormatter.radiation(it)) } . | Run verification: ./gradlew :core:common:allTests . | .

2541.title: DateFormatter
2541.content: Date and time formatting uses the DateFormatter expect object with platform-specific actual implementations. The Android formats, all in the device locale: . | Function | Format | . | formatRelativeTime() | Abbreviated relative time to the minute, from DateUtils.getRelativeTimeSpanString | . | formatDateTime() | Date and time with abbreviated month, from DateUtils.formatDateTime | . | formatShortDate() | Short time within the last 24 hours, short date otherwise | . | formatTime() | Short time | . | formatTimeWithSeconds() | Medium time, with seconds | . | formatDate() | Short date | . | formatDateTimeShort() | Short date and medium time | . Unlike MetricFormatter, DateFormatter is declared with expect/actual (an expect object in commonMain, an actual object per platform) because date formatting inherently depends on platform locale APIs. Desktop uses java.time formatters; the iOS stub returns empty strings.

2542.title: Design decisions
2542.content: | Decision | Rationale | . | Display formatting follows the OS locale | A number shown to a user should read the way that user writes numbers | . | formatInvariant keeps a fixed . for machine-read values | Interop payloads and re-parsed values break if localized | . | MetricFormatter converts only temperature, wind speed, rainfall and weight; lengths and speeds convert in DistanceExtensions.kt | The remaining metric units are universally understood in their native form | . | object singleton pattern | Stateless utility — no instance management needed | .
