2839.content: The MQTT module connects your node to an MQTT broker, allowing: . | Messages to reach nodes on different physical meshes via the internet | Integration with home automation and monitoring systems | Publishing node positions to the public Meshtastic map | Custom data pipelines for logging and alerting | .

2860.title: MQTT
2860.content: MQTT bridges your Meshtastic mesh network to the internet, enabling long-range communication beyond radio range.

2861.title: Overview
2861.content: The MQTT module connects your node to an MQTT broker, allowing: . | Messages to reach nodes on different physical meshes via the internet | Integration with home automation and monitoring systems | Publishing node positions to the public Meshtastic map | Custom data pipelines for logging and alerting | .

2862.title: How It Works
2862.content: [Your Node] → Radio → [Gateway Node with Wi-Fi] → MQTT Broker → [Remote Gateway] → Radio → [Remote Node] . A gateway node with internet access (Wi-Fi or Ethernet) publishes mesh messages to an MQTT topic. Remote gateways subscribed to the same topic inject those messages into their local mesh.

2863.title: Configuration
2863.content: Enabling MQTT . | Navigate to Settings → Module configuration → MQTT. | Turn on MQTT Enabled. | Configure the broker connection: | . | Setting | Opis | Default | . | Address | MQTT broker hostname. Empty means the public broker | mqtt.meshtastic.org | . | Username | Broker authentication | meshdev | . | Password | Broker authentication | large4cats | . | Encryption Enabled | Publish packets still encrypted with the channel key | Enabled | . | JSON output enabled | Shown only for a node on firmware older than 2.8, or while the setting is still on. See Message Formats | Disabled | . | TLS Enabled | Secure connection to broker | Disabled | . | Root Topic | Base topic for messages | msh, which the node rewrites to msh/<REGION> when you set a region while it uses the public broker | . | MQTT Client Proxy | Relay MQTT through the connected app | Disabled | . | Map Reporting | Report position to public map | Disabled | . Connection Status and Test Connection . The top of the MQTT settings screen shows the status of the relay this app runs: Connected, Connecting…, Reconnecting…, Disconnected, or Inactive. It reads Inactive whenever the app is not relaying, which includes the normal case of a node reaching the broker over its own Wi-Fi or Ethernet. The node’s own connection to the broker is not reported here. When the broker accepts the connection but refuses a subscription, the status names the refused topics and the broker’s reason: Connected, but the broker refused every topic when nothing was granted, or Connected, but the broker refused followed by the topics when only some were. A broker’s access-control list is the usual cause. Test connection probes the broker before you commit the settings to the node, and distinguishes the failure modes: the hostname not resolving, the TCP connection being refused, TLS failing, the attempt timing out, or the broker rejecting your credentials with a reason. Find Topics Near You . The region topic (msh/US) carries every gateway in the region. Find topics near you, under the root topic field, listens to the broker for one minute and lists the narrower roots in use around you, with the number of nodes heard on each. | Near you lists the region, then the country when the broker shows it in use (msh/EU_868/DE), then your state or province and city, named from the node’s position or, failing that, the phone’s location. The phone’s geocoder turns the location into place names; the location itself never reaches the broker. Community roots whose names don’t say where they are (msh/US/DMV) follow when they serve your area, from a directory the app refreshes from the Meshtastic API. | Active topics lists every other root heard. Roots under your state or city come first, then roots in neighboring states, then the rest. | Custom topic takes any root the node accepts: up to 31 ASCII characters, no leading or trailing slash, no + or #. | . The finder only subscribes and publishes nothing. Picking a topic fills in the root topic field, and nothing reaches the node until you save. It needs the LoRa region to be set. Without a location, or on desktop, it still lists the region and every root it hears. MQTT Proxy in This App . If your node has no internet access of its own, it can use the app as its MQTT gateway. Turn on MQTT Enabled and MQTT Client Proxy in the module config. The app then relays MQTT traffic between the node and the broker over your phone’s or computer’s internet connection. The MQTT proxy in this app toggle at the top of the MQTT settings screen shows whether this relay is running and lets you cut it off (or restart it) immediately, without editing and re-saving the node’s MQTT configuration. Default Meshtastic Broker . The community maintains a public broker at mqtt.meshtastic.org. This is intended for general use and testing. When this app relays MQTT for the node, connections to that broker always use TLS on port 8883 even if TLS Enabled is off. That upgrade is the app’s own, and the switch says so. A node that reaches the broker over its own Wi-Fi or Ethernet forces nothing: it uses TLS Enabled as stored, so turn it on yourself or the node connects in the clear on port 1883. For any other broker the toggle decides in both cases. A port written in the address, as in broker.example.com:8884, is kept; without one, TLS uses port 8883 and plain connections use 1883. 🔒 Privacy: Messages on the public broker are readable by anyone subscribed. Always use channel encryption for private communications. Private Broker . For better privacy and control, you can run your own MQTT broker: . | Mosquitto (lightweight, open-source) | HiveMQ | EMQX | . Configure your node to point to your private broker with appropriate credentials.

2864.title: Map Reporting
2864.content: When Map Reporting is on, your node periodically publishes a map report to the broker. The report goes out unencrypted, whatever keys your channels use, and carries your node id, long and short name, approximate location, hardware model, role, firmware version, LoRa region, modem preset, and primary channel name. Turning it on opens a consent card. Turn on I agree. and choose a Map Publish Interval of one hour or more — the screen will not save until you do. A slider sets the position precision, and the app shows the resulting accuracy as a ± distance, so you can publish an approximate location rather than an exact one. Reports appear at meshmap.net and similar community map services. 🔒 Privacy: A map report is readable by anyone subscribed to the broker. Leave Map Reporting off if you do not want your approximate location published.

2865.title: Uplink vs Downlink
2865.content: | Direction | Opis | . | Uplink | Messages from mesh → MQTT broker | . | Downlink | Messages from MQTT broker → mesh | . Uplink and downlink are per-channel settings, not MQTT module settings. Open Settings → Channels, tap the channel, and use MQTT Uplink Enabled and MQTT Downlink Enabled. Every channel you want bridged out needs uplink on, and every channel you want MQTT traffic injected into needs downlink on.

2866.title: Message Formats
2866.content: Gateways publish packets as binary Meshtastic protobufs on the /2/e/ topic, which is what node-to-node mesh bridging uses. Firmware 2.7 and older can also publish human-readable JSON on the /2/json/ topic for consumers outside the mesh, such as dashboards and home automation, when json_enabled is on. Firmware 2.8 removed JSON support and ignores the field. The app shows JSON output enabled only for a node on older firmware, or while the setting is still on, and while it is on the app’s own MQTT proxy also subscribes to the /2/json/ topic and decodes those payloads.

2867.title: Encryption & Privacy
2867.content: Understanding the layered encryption model: . | Channel encryption happens on the mesh before MQTT. If your channel has a PSK, the MQTT payload is already encrypted — the broker and any subscribers see only the ciphertext. | Encryption Enabled (the module setting) decides which copy of the packet the gateway publishes — it is not an extra layer. Leave it on and the broker receives the packet still encrypted with your channel key. Turn it off and the gateway publishes the decrypted packet, so anyone subscribed to the topic reads your messages in the clear. Turn it off only when you own the broker and want plain payloads for a dashboard. | TLS encrypts the TCP connection to the broker itself, preventing network-level eavesdropping. | . 🔒 Security: The default public channel has a well-known key. Messages on the default channel sent via MQTT are effectively unencrypted — anyone can decode them. Always use a custom PSK for private communications.

2868.title: Best Practices
2868.content: . | Use channel-level encryption (PSK) on channels that bridge to MQTT | Don’t enable MQTT on a node with no internet access of its own unless MQTT Client Proxy is on (the node queues messages it can’t send and wastes memory) | Use a private broker for sensitive deployments | Be mindful of airtime when downlinking messages from busy MQTT topics — every downlinked message consumes radio airtime on your local mesh | Consider enabling uplink-only if you only need to monitor your mesh remotely without injecting messages back | .

2869.title: Troubleshooting
2869.content: MQTT Not Connecting . | Check Wi-Fi — the gateway node must have an active internet connection (Wi-Fi or Ethernet). MQTT does not work over the LoRa radio link itself. | Verify credentials — with incorrect credentials, most brokers fail silently — double-check for trailing spaces. | Firewall — port 1883 (MQTT) or 8883 (MQTT over TLS) must be reachable. Some networks allow only web traffic (ports 80 and 443). | DNS resolution — if using a custom broker hostname, verify the node can resolve it. Try the broker’s IP address directly. | . Messages Not Bridging . | Check uplink/downlink settings — if only uplink is enabled, messages flow from mesh to MQTT but not back. Enable downlink on the receiving gateway. | Channel mismatch — both gateways must share the same channel with the same PSK. A mismatch means messages are encrypted with different keys and appear as garbage. | Topic mismatch — both gateways must use exactly the same root topic. On the public broker, setting a region rewrites a default root to msh/<REGION> (for example msh/US), so gateways in different regions do not meet until you give both the same explicit root. Firmware 2.8.0 and older also rewrite a root starting with msh on a private broker. | Ignore MQTT is on — in a region with a duty-cycle limit, the node turns on Ignore MQTT (LoRa config, Advanced) when you set the region, and then drops every packet that reached it via MQTT. Turn it off on the receiving nodes, not only on the gateway. | OK to MQTT is off — on a public broker a gateway uplinks other nodes’ packets only when the sending node has OK to MQTT (LoRa config, Advanced) on. Your own traffic bridges either way; your neighbors’ does not until they opt in. | .

2891.content: MQTT Not Connecting . | Check Wi-Fi — the gateway node must have an active internet connection (Wi-Fi or Ethernet). Some networks allow only web traffic (ports 80 and 443). | DNS resolution — if using a custom broker hostname, verify the node can resolve it. Try the broker’s IP address directly. | . Messages Not Bridging . | Check uplink/downlink settings — if only uplink is enabled, messages flow from mesh to MQTT but not back. Enable downlink on the receiving gateway. | Channel mismatch — both gateways must share the same channel with the same PSK. A mismatch means messages are encrypted with different keys and appear as garbage. | Topic mismatch — both gateways must use exactly the same root topic. On the public broker, setting a region rewrites a default root to msh/<REGION> (for example msh/US), so gateways in different regions do not meet until you give both the same explicit root. Firmware 2.8.0 and older also rewrite a root starting with msh on a private broker. | Ignore MQTT is on — in a region with a duty-cycle limit, the node turns on Ignore MQTT (LoRa config, Advanced) when you set the region, and then drops every packet that reached it via MQTT. Turn it off on the receiving nodes, not only on the gateway. | OK to MQTT is off — on a public broker a gateway uplinks other nodes’ packets only when the sending node has OK to MQTT (LoRa config, Advanced) on. Your own traffic bridges either way; your neighbors’ does not until they opt in. | .

2893.title: MQTT
2893.content: MQTT bridges your Meshtastic mesh network to the internet, enabling long-range communication beyond radio range.

2894.title: Genel Bakış
2894.content: The MQTT module connects your node to an MQTT broker, allowing: . | Messages to reach nodes on different physical meshes via the internet | Integration with home automation and monitoring systems | Publishing node positions to the public Meshtastic map | Custom data pipelines for logging and alerting | .

2895.title: How It Works
2895.content: [Your Node] → Radio → [Gateway Node with Wi-Fi] → MQTT Broker → [Remote Gateway] → Radio → [Remote Node] . A gateway node with internet access (Wi-Fi or Ethernet) publishes mesh messages to an MQTT topic. Remote gateways subscribed to the same topic inject those messages into their local mesh.

2896.title: Yapılandırma
2896.content: Enabling MQTT . | Navigate to Settings → Module configuration → MQTT. | Turn on MQTT Enabled. | Configure the broker connection: | . | Setting | Açıklaması | Varsayılan | . | Address | MQTT broker hostname. Empty means the public broker | mqtt.meshtastic.org | . | Username | Broker authentication | meshdev | . | Password | Broker authentication | large4cats | . | Encryption Enabled | Publish packets still encrypted with the channel key | Açık | . | JSON output enabled | Shown only for a node on firmware older than 2.8, or while the setting is still on. See Message Formats | Disabled | . | TLS Enabled | Secure connection to broker | Disabled | . | Root Topic | Base topic for messages | msh, which the node rewrites to msh/<REGION> when you set a region while it uses the public broker | . | MQTT Client Proxy | Relay MQTT through the connected app | Disabled | . | Map Reporting | Report position to public map | Disabled | . Connection Status and Test Connection . The top of the MQTT settings screen shows the status of the relay this app runs: Connected, Connecting…, Reconnecting…, Disconnected, or Inactive. It reads Inactive whenever the app is not relaying, which includes the normal case of a node reaching the broker over its own Wi-Fi or Ethernet. The node’s own connection to the broker is not reported here. When the broker accepts the connection but refuses a subscription, the status names the refused topics and the broker’s reason: Connected, but the broker refused every topic when nothing was granted, or Connected, but the broker refused followed by the topics when only some were. A broker’s access-control list is the usual cause. Test connection probes the broker before you commit the settings to the node, and distinguishes the failure modes: the hostname not resolving, the TCP connection being refused, TLS failing, the attempt timing out, or the broker rejecting your credentials with a reason. Find Topics Near You . The region topic (msh/US) carries every gateway in the region. Find topics near you, under the root topic field, listens to the broker for one minute and lists the narrower roots in use around you, with the number of nodes heard on each. | Near you lists the region, then the country when the broker shows it in use (msh/EU_868/DE), then your state or province and city, named from the node’s position or, failing that, the phone’s location. The phone’s geocoder turns the location into place names; the location itself never reaches the broker. Community roots whose names don’t say where they are (msh/US/DMV) follow when they serve your area, from a directory the app refreshes from the Meshtastic API. | Active topics lists every other root heard. Roots under your state or city come first, then roots in neighboring states, then the rest. | Custom topic takes any root the node accepts: up to 31 ASCII characters, no leading or trailing slash, no + or #. | . The finder only subscribes and publishes nothing. Picking a topic fills in the root topic field, and nothing reaches the node until you save. It needs the LoRa region to be set. Without a location, or on desktop, it still lists the region and every root it hears. MQTT Proxy in This App . If your node has no internet access of its own, it can use the app as its MQTT gateway. Turn on MQTT Enabled and MQTT Client Proxy in the module config. The app then relays MQTT traffic between the node and the broker over your phone’s or computer’s internet connection. The MQTT proxy in this app toggle at the top of the MQTT settings screen shows whether this relay is running and lets you cut it off (or restart it) immediately, without editing and re-saving the node’s MQTT configuration. Default Meshtastic Broker . The community maintains a public broker at mqtt.meshtastic.org. This is intended for general use and testing. When this app relays MQTT for the node, connections to that broker always use TLS on port 8883 even if TLS Enabled is off. That upgrade is the app’s own, and the switch says so. A node that reaches the broker over its own Wi-Fi or Ethernet forces nothing: it uses TLS Enabled as stored, so turn it on yourself or the node connects in the clear on port 1883. For any other broker the toggle decides in both cases. A port written in the address, as in broker.example.com:8884, is kept; without one, TLS uses port 8883 and plain connections use 1883. 🔒 Privacy: Messages on the public broker are readable by anyone subscribed. Always use channel encryption for private communications. Private Broker . For better privacy and control, you can run your own MQTT broker: . | Mosquitto (lightweight, open-source) | HiveMQ | EMQX | . Configure your node to point to your private broker with appropriate credentials.

2897.title: Map Reporting
2897.content: When Map Reporting is on, your node periodically publishes a map report to the broker. The report goes out unencrypted, whatever keys your channels use, and carries your node id, long and short name, approximate location, hardware model, role, firmware version, LoRa region, modem preset, and primary channel name. Turning it on opens a consent card. Turn on I agree. and choose a Map Publish Interval of one hour or more — the screen will not save until you do. A slider sets the position precision, and the app shows the resulting accuracy as a ± distance, so you can publish an approximate location rather than an exact one. Reports appear at meshmap.net and similar community map services. 🔒 Privacy: A map report is readable by anyone subscribed to the broker. Leave Map Reporting off if you do not want your approximate location published.

2898.title: Uplink vs Downlink
2898.content: | Direction | Açıklaması | . | Uplink | Messages from mesh → MQTT broker | . | Downlink | Messages from MQTT broker → mesh | . Uplink and downlink are per-channel settings, not MQTT module settings. Open Settings → Channels, tap the channel, and use MQTT Uplink Enabled and MQTT Downlink Enabled. Every channel you want bridged out needs uplink on, and every channel you want MQTT traffic injected into needs downlink on.

2899.title: Message Formats
2899.content: Gateways publish packets as binary Meshtastic protobufs on the /2/e/ topic, which is what node-to-node mesh bridging uses. Firmware 2.7 and older can also publish human-readable JSON on the /2/json/ topic for consumers outside the mesh, such as dashboards and home automation, when json_enabled is on. Firmware 2.8 removed JSON support and ignores the field. The app shows JSON output enabled only for a node on older firmware, or while the setting is still on, and while it is on the app’s own MQTT proxy also subscribes to the /2/json/ topic and decodes those payloads.

2900.title: Encryption & Privacy
2900.content: Understanding the layered encryption model: . | Channel encryption happens on the mesh before MQTT. If your channel has a PSK, the MQTT payload is already encrypted — the broker and any subscribers see only the ciphertext. | Encryption Enabled (the module setting) decides which copy of the packet the gateway publishes — it is not an extra layer. Leave it on and the broker receives the packet still encrypted with your channel key. Turn it off and the gateway publishes the decrypted packet, so anyone subscribed to the topic reads your messages in the clear. Turn it off only when you own the broker and want plain payloads for a dashboard. | TLS encrypts the TCP connection to the broker itself, preventing network-level eavesdropping. | . 🔒 Security: The default public channel has a well-known key. Messages on the default channel sent via MQTT are effectively unencrypted — anyone can decode them. Always use a custom PSK for private communications.

For any other broker the toggle decides in both cases. 2919.title: Map Reporting
2919.content: When Map Reporting is on, your node periodically publishes a map report to the broker. The report goes out unencrypted, whatever keys your channels use, and carries your node id, long and short name, approximate location, hardware model, role, firmware version, LoRa region, modem preset, and primary channel name. Turning it on opens a consent card. Turn on I agree. and choose a Map Publish Interval of one hour or more — the screen will not save until you do. A slider sets the position precision, and the app shows the resulting accuracy as a ± distance, so you can publish an approximate location rather than an exact one. Reports appear at meshmap.net and similar community map services. 🔒 Privacy: A map report is readable by anyone subscribed to the broker. 2920.title: Uplink vs Downlink

Uplink and downlink are per-channel settings, not MQTT module settings. Open Settings → Channels, tap the channel, and use MQTT Uplink Enabled and MQTT Downlink Enabled. Every channel you want bridged out needs uplink on, and every channel you want MQTT traffic injected into needs downlink on.

2921.title: Message Formats
2921.content: Gateways publish packets as binary Meshtastic protobufs on the /2/e/ topic, which is what node-to-node mesh bridging uses. Firmware 2.8 removed JSON support and ignores the field. The app shows JSON output enabled only for a node on older firmware, or while the setting is still on, and while it is on the app’s own MQTT proxy also subscribes to the /2/json/ topic and decodes those payloads.

2922.title: Encryption & Privacy
2922.content: Understanding the layered encryption model: . | Channel encryption happens on the mesh before MQTT. If your channel has a PSK, the MQTT payload is already encrypted — the broker and any subscribers see only the ciphertext. | Encryption Enabled (the module setting) decides which copy of the packet the gateway publishes — it is not an extra layer. Leave it on and the broker receives the packet still encrypted with your channel key. Turn it off and the gateway publishes the decrypted packet, so anyone subscribed to the topic reads your messages in the clear. Turn it off only when you own the broker and want plain payloads for a dashboard. | TLS encrypts the TCP connection to the broker itself, preventing network-level eavesdropping. | . 🔒 Security: The default public channel has a well-known key. 2923.title: Best Practices
2923.content: . | Use channel-level encryption (PSK) on channels that bridge to MQTT | Don’t enable MQTT on a node with no internet access of its own unless MQTT Client Proxy is on (the node queues messages it can’t send and wastes memory) | Use a private broker for sensitive deployments | Be mindful of airtime when downlinking messages from busy MQTT topics — every downlinked message consumes radio airtime on your local mesh | Consider enabling uplink-only if you only need to monitor your mesh remotely without injecting messages back | .

2924.title: Troubleshooting
2924.content: MQTT Not Connecting . | Check Wi-Fi — the gateway node must have an active internet connection (Wi-Fi or Ethernet). MQTT does not work over the LoRa radio link itself. | Verify credentials — with incorrect credentials, most brokers fail silently — double-check for trailing spaces. | Firewall — port 1883 (MQTT) or 8883 (MQTT over TLS) must be reachable. Some networks allow only web traffic (ports 80 and 443). | DNS resolution — if using a custom broker hostname, verify the node can resolve it. Try the broker’s IP address directly. | . Messages Not Bridging . | Check uplink/downlink settings — if only uplink is enabled, messages flow from mesh to MQTT but not back. Enable downlink on the receiving gateway. | Channel mismatch — both gateways must share the same channel with the same PSK. A mismatch means messages are encrypted with different keys and appear as garbage. | Topic mismatch — both gateways must use exactly the same root topic. On the public broker, setting a region rewrites a default root to msh/<REGION> (for example msh/US), so gateways in different regions do not meet until you give both the same explicit root. Firmware 2.8.0 and older also rewrite a root starting with msh on a private broker. | Ignore MQTT is on — in a region with a duty-cycle limit, the node turns on Ignore MQTT (LoRa config, Advanced) when you set the region, and then drops every packet that reached it via MQTT. Turn it off on the receiving nodes, not only on the gateway. | OK to MQTT is off — on a public broker a gateway uplinks other nodes’ packets only when the sending node has OK to MQTT (LoRa config, Advanced) on. Your own traffic bridges either way; your neighbors’ does not until they opt in. | .

See Message Formats | Disabled | . | TLS Enabled | Secure connection to broker | Disabled | . | Root Topic | Base topic for messages | msh, which the node rewrites to msh/<REGION> when you set a region while it uses the public broker | . | MQTT Client Proxy | Relay MQTT through the connected app | Disabled | . | Map Reporting | Report position to public map | Disabled | . Connection Status and Test Connection . The top of the MQTT settings screen shows the status of the relay this app runs: Connected, Connecting…, Reconnecting…, Disconnected, or Inactive. It reads Inactive whenever the app is not relaying, which includes the normal case of a node reaching the broker over its own Wi-Fi or Ethernet. The node’s own connection to the broker is not reported here. When the broker accepts the connection but refuses a subscription, the status names the refused topics and the broker’s reason: Connected, but the broker refused every topic when nothing was granted, or Connected, but the broker refused followed by the topics when only some were. A broker’s access-control list is the usual cause. Test connection probes the broker before you commit the settings to the node, and distinguishes the failure modes: the hostname not resolving, the TCP connection being refused, TLS failing, the attempt timing out, or the broker rejecting your credentials with a reason. Find Topics Near You . The region topic (msh/US) carries every gateway in the region. Find topics near you, under the root topic field, listens to the broker for one minute and lists the narrower roots in use around you, with the number of nodes heard on each. | Near you lists the region, then the country when the broker shows it in use (msh/EU_868/DE), then your state or province and city, named from the node’s position or, failing that, the phone’s location. The phone’s geocoder turns the location into place names; the location itself never reaches the broker. Community roots whose names don’t say where they are (msh/US/DMV) follow when they serve your area, from a directory the app refreshes from the Meshtastic API. | Active topics lists every other root heard. Roots under your state or city come first, then roots in neighboring states, then the rest. | Custom topic takes any root the node accepts: up to 31 ASCII characters, no leading or trailing slash, no + or #. | . The finder only subscribes and publishes nothing. Picking a topic fills in the root topic field, and nothing reaches the node until you save. It needs the LoRa region to be set. Without a location, or on desktop, it still lists the region and every root it hears. MQTT Proxy in This App . If your node has no internet access of its own, it can use the app as its MQTT gateway. Turn on MQTT Enabled and MQTT Client Proxy in the module config. The app then relays MQTT traffic between the node and the broker over your phone’s or computer’s internet connection. The MQTT proxy in this app toggle at the top of the MQTT settings screen shows whether this relay is running and lets you cut it off (or restart it) immediately, without editing and re-saving the node’s MQTT configuration. Default Meshtastic Broker . The community maintains a public broker at mqtt.meshtastic.org. This is intended for general use and testing. When this app relays MQTT for the node, connections to that broker always use TLS on port 8883 even if TLS Enabled is off. That upgrade is the app’s own, and the switch says so. A node that reaches the broker over its own Wi-Fi or Ethernet forces nothing: it uses TLS Enabled as stored, so turn it on yourself or the node connects in the clear on port 1883. For any other broker the toggle decides in both cases. A port written in the address, as in broker.example.com:8884, is kept; without one, TLS uses port 8883 and plain connections use 1883. 🔒 Privacy: Messages on the public broker are readable by anyone subscribed. Always use channel encryption for private communications. Private Broker . For better privacy and control, you can run your own MQTT broker: . | Mosquitto (lightweight, open-source) | HiveMQ | EMQX | . Configure your node to point to your private broker with appropriate credentials.

2952.title: Map Reporting
2952.content: When Map Reporting is on, your node periodically publishes a map report to the broker. The report goes out unencrypted, whatever keys your channels use, and carries your node id, long and short name, approximate location, hardware model, role, firmware version, LoRa region, modem preset, and primary channel name. Turning it on opens a consent card. Turn on I agree. and choose a Map Publish Interval of one hour or more — the screen will not save until you do. A slider sets the position precision, and the app shows the resulting accuracy as a ± distance, so you can publish an approximate location rather than an exact one. Reports appear at meshmap.net and similar community map services. 🔒 Privacy: A map report is readable by anyone subscribed to the broker. Leave Map Reporting off if you do not want your approximate location published.

2953.title: Uplink vs Downlink
2953.content: | Direction | Περιγραφή | . | Uplink | Messages from mesh → MQTT broker | . | Downlink | Messages from MQTT broker → mesh | . Uplink and downlink are per-channel settings, not MQTT module settings. Open Settings → Channels, tap the channel, and use MQTT Uplink Enabled and MQTT Downlink Enabled. Every channel you want bridged out needs uplink on, and every channel you want MQTT traffic injected into needs downlink on.

2954.title: Message Formats
2954.content: Gateways publish packets as binary Meshtastic protobufs on the /2/e/ topic, which is what node-to-node mesh bridging uses. Firmware 2.7 and older can also publish human-readable JSON on the /2/json/ topic for consumers outside the mesh, such as dashboards and home automation, when json_enabled is on. Firmware 2.8 removed JSON support and ignores the field. The app shows JSON output enabled only for a node on older firmware, or while the setting is still on, and while it is on the app’s own MQTT proxy also subscribes to the /2/json/ topic and decodes those payloads.

2955.title: Encryption & Privacy
2955.content: Understanding the layered encryption model: . | Channel encryption happens on the mesh before MQTT. If your channel has a PSK, the MQTT payload is already encrypted — the broker and any subscribers see only the ciphertext. | Encryption Enabled (the module setting) decides which copy of the packet the gateway publishes — it is not an extra layer. Leave it on and the broker receives the packet still encrypted with your channel key. Turn it off and the gateway publishes the decrypted packet, so anyone subscribed to the topic reads your messages in the clear. Turn it off only when you own the broker and want plain payloads for a dashboard. | TLS encrypts the TCP connection to the broker itself, preventing network-level eavesdropping. | . 🔒 Security: The default public channel has a well-known key. Messages on the default channel sent via MQTT are effectively unencrypted — anyone can decode them. Always use a custom PSK for private communications.

2956.title: Best Practices
2956.content: . | Use channel-level encryption (PSK) on channels that bridge to MQTT | Don’t enable MQTT on a node with no internet access of its own unless MQTT Client Proxy is on (the node queues messages it can’t send and wastes memory) | Use a private broker for sensitive deployments | Be mindful of airtime when downlinking messages from busy MQTT topics — every downlinked message consumes radio airtime on your local mesh | Consider enabling uplink-only if you only need to monitor your mesh remotely without injecting messages back | .

2957.title: Troubleshooting
2957.content: MQTT Not Connecting . | Check Wi-Fi — the gateway node must have an active internet connection (Wi-Fi or Ethernet). MQTT does not work over the LoRa radio link itself. | Verify credentials — with incorrect credentials, most brokers fail silently — double-check for trailing spaces. | Firewall — port 1883 (MQTT) or 8883 (MQTT over TLS) must be reachable. Some networks allow only web traffic (ports 80 and 443). | DNS resolution — if using a custom broker hostname, verify the node can resolve it. Try the broker’s IP address directly. | . Messages Not Bridging . | Check uplink/downlink settings — if only uplink is enabled, messages flow from mesh to MQTT but not back. Enable downlink on the receiving gateway. | Channel mismatch — both gateways must share the same channel with the same PSK. A mismatch means messages are encrypted with different keys and appear as garbage. | Topic mismatch — both gateways must use exactly the same root topic. On the public broker, setting a region rewrites a default root to msh/<REGION> (for example msh/US), so gateways in different regions do not meet until you give both the same explicit root. Firmware 2.8.0 and older also rewrite a root starting with msh on a private broker. | Ignore MQTT is on — in a region with a duty-cycle limit, the node turns on Ignore MQTT (LoRa config, Advanced) when you set the region, and then drops every packet that reached it via MQTT. Turn it off on the receiving nodes, not only on the gateway. | OK to MQTT is off — on a public broker a gateway uplinks other nodes’ packets only when the sending node has OK to MQTT (LoRa config, Advanced) on. Your own traffic bridges either way; your neighbors’ does not until they opt in. | .

2981.title: MQTT
2981.content: MQTT bridges your Meshtastic mesh network to the internet, enabling long-range communication beyond radio range.

2982.title: Overview
2982.content: The MQTT module connects your node to an MQTT broker, allowing: . | Messages to reach nodes on different physical meshes via the internet | Integration with home automation and monitoring systems | Publishing node positions to the public Meshtastic map | Custom data pipelines for logging and alerting | .

2983.title: How It Works
2983.content: [Your Node] → Radio → [Gateway Node with Wi-Fi] → MQTT Broker → [Remote Gateway] → Radio → [Remote Node] . A gateway node with internet access (Wi-Fi or Ethernet) publishes mesh messages to an MQTT topic. Remote gateways subscribed to the same topic inject those messages into their local mesh.

2984.title: Configuration
2984.content: Enabling MQTT . | Navigate to Settings → Module configuration → MQTT. | Turn on MQTT Enabled. | Configure the broker connection: | . | Setting | Descrición | Default | . | Address | MQTT broker hostname. Empty means the public broker | mqtt.meshtastic.org | . | Username | Broker authentication | meshdev | . | Password | Broker authentication | large4cats | . | Encryption Enabled | Publish packets still encrypted with the channel key | Enabled | . | JSON output enabled | Shown only for a node on firmware older than 2.8, or while the setting is still on. See Message Formats | Disabled | . | TLS Enabled | Secure connection to broker | Disabled | . | Root Topic | Base topic for messages | msh, which the node rewrites to msh/<REGION> when you set a region while it uses the public broker | . | MQTT Client Proxy | Relay MQTT through the connected app | Disabled | . | Map Reporting | Report position to public map | Disabled | . Connection Status and Test Connection . The top of the MQTT settings screen shows the status of the relay this app runs: Connected, Connecting…, Reconnecting…, Disconnected, or Inactive. It reads Inactive whenever the app is not relaying, which includes the normal case of a node reaching the broker over its own Wi-Fi or Ethernet. The node’s own connection to the broker is not reported here. When the broker accepts the connection but refuses a subscription, the status names the refused topics and the broker’s reason: Connected, but the broker refused every topic when nothing was granted, or Connected, but the broker refused followed by the topics when only some were. A broker’s access-control list is the usual cause. Test connection probes the broker before you commit the settings to the node, and distinguishes the failure modes: the hostname not resolving, the TCP connection being refused, TLS failing, the attempt timing out, or the broker rejecting your credentials with a reason. Find Topics Near You . The region topic (msh/US) carries every gateway in the region. Find topics near you, under the root topic field, listens to the broker for one minute and lists the narrower roots in use around you, with the number of nodes heard on each. | Near you lists the region, then the country when the broker shows it in use (msh/EU_868/DE), then your state or province and city, named from the node’s position or, failing that, the phone’s location. The phone’s geocoder turns the location into place names; the location itself never reaches the broker. Community roots whose names don’t say where they are (msh/US/DMV) follow when they serve your area, from a directory the app refreshes from the Meshtastic API. | Active topics lists every other root heard. Roots under your state or city come first, then roots in neighboring states, then the rest. | Custom topic takes any root the node accepts: up to 31 ASCII characters, no leading or trailing slash, no + or #. | . The finder only subscribes and publishes nothing. Picking a topic fills in the root topic field, and nothing reaches the node until you save. It needs the LoRa region to be set. Without a location, or on desktop, it still lists the region and every root it hears. MQTT Proxy in This App . If your node has no internet access of its own, it can use the app as its MQTT gateway. Turn on MQTT Enabled and MQTT Client Proxy in the module config. The app then relays MQTT traffic between the node and the broker over your phone’s or computer’s internet connection. The MQTT proxy in this app toggle at the top of the MQTT settings screen shows whether this relay is running and lets you cut it off (or restart it) immediately, without editing and re-saving the node’s MQTT configuration. Default Meshtastic Broker . The community maintains a public broker at mqtt.meshtastic.org. This is intended for general use and testing. When this app relays MQTT for the node, connections to that broker always use TLS on port 8883 even if TLS Enabled is off. That upgrade is the app’s own, and the switch says so. A node that reaches the broker over its own Wi-Fi or Ethernet forces nothing: it uses TLS Enabled as stored, so turn it on yourself or the node connects in the clear on port 1883. For any other broker the toggle decides in both cases. A port written in the address, as in broker.example.com:8884, is kept; without one, TLS uses port 8883 and plain connections use 1883. 🔒 Privacy: Messages on the public broker are readable by anyone subscribed. Always use channel encryption for private communications. Private Broker . For better privacy and control, you can run your own MQTT broker: . | Mosquitto (lightweight, open-source) | HiveMQ | EMQX | . Configure your node to point to your private broker with appropriate credentials.

2985.title: Map Reporting
2985.content: When Map Reporting is on, your node periodically publishes a map report to the broker. The report goes out unencrypted, whatever keys your channels use, and carries your node id, long and short name, approximate location, hardware model, role, firmware version, LoRa region, modem preset, and primary channel name. Turning it on opens a consent card. Turn on I agree. and choose a Map Publish Interval of one hour or more — the screen will not save until you do. A slider sets the position precision, and the app shows the resulting accuracy as a ± distance, so you can publish an approximate location rather than an exact one. Reports appear at meshmap.net and similar community map services. 🔒 Privacy: A map report is readable by anyone subscribed to the broker. Leave Map Reporting off if you do not want your approximate location published.

2986.title: Uplink vs Downlink
2986.content: | Direction | Descrición | . | Uplink | Messages from mesh → MQTT broker | . | Downlink | Messages from MQTT broker → mesh | . Uplink and downlink are per-channel settings, not MQTT module settings. Open Settings → Channels, tap the channel, and use MQTT Uplink Enabled and MQTT Downlink Enabled. Every channel you want bridged out needs uplink on, and every channel you want MQTT traffic injected into needs downlink on.

2987.title: Message Formats
2987.content: Gateways publish packets as binary Meshtastic protobufs on the /2/e/ topic, which is what node-to-node mesh bridging uses. Firmware 2.7 and older can also publish human-readable JSON on the /2/json/ topic for consumers outside the mesh, such as dashboards and home automation, when json_enabled is on. Firmware 2.8 removed JSON support and ignores the field. The app shows JSON output enabled only for a node on older firmware, or while the setting is still on, and while it is on the app’s own MQTT proxy also subscribes to the /2/json/ topic and decodes those payloads.

2988.title: Encryption & Privacy
2988.content: Understanding the layered encryption model: . | Channel encryption happens on the mesh before MQTT. If your channel has a PSK, the MQTT payload is already encrypted — the broker and any subscribers see only the ciphertext. | Encryption Enabled (the module setting) decides which copy of the packet the gateway publishes — it is not an extra layer. Leave it on and the broker receives the packet still encrypted with your channel key. Turn it off and the gateway publishes the decrypted packet, so anyone subscribed to the topic reads your messages in the clear. Turn it off only when you own the broker and want plain payloads for a dashboard. | TLS encrypts the TCP connection to the broker itself, preventing network-level eavesdropping. | . 🔒 Security: The default public channel has a well-known key. Messages on the default channel sent via MQTT are effectively unencrypted — anyone can decode them. Always use a custom PSK for private communications.

2989.title: Best Practices
2989.content: . | Use channel-level encryption (PSK) on channels that bridge to MQTT | Don’t enable MQTT on a node with no internet access of its own unless MQTT Client Proxy is on (the node queues messages it can’t send and wastes memory) | Use a private broker for sensitive deployments | Be mindful of airtime when downlinking messages from busy MQTT topics — every downlinked message consumes radio airtime on your local mesh | Consider enabling uplink-only if you only need to monitor your mesh remotely without injecting messages back | .

Enable downlink on the receiving gateway. | Channel mismatch — both gateways must share the same channel with the same PSK. A mismatch means messages are encrypted with different keys and appear as garbage. | Topic mismatch — both gateways must use exactly the same root topic. Turn it off on the receiving nodes, not only on the gateway. | OK to MQTT is off — on a public broker a gateway uplinks other nodes’ packets only when the sending node has OK to MQTT (LoRa config, Advanced) on. Your own traffic bridges either way; your neighbors’ does not until they opt in. | .

3014.title: MQTT
3014.content: MQTT соединяет твою mesh-сеть Meshtastic с интернетом, обеспечивая связь на больших расстояниях за пределами радиодиапазона.

3015.title: Обзор
3015.content: Модуль MQTT подключает вашу ноду к MQTT-брокеру, что позволяет: . | Сообщениям достигать нод в других физических mesh-сетях через интернет | Интегрироваться с системами домашней автоматизации и мониторинга | Публиковать местоположения нод на публичной карте Meshtastic | Создавать собственные каналы данных для журналирования и оповещений | .

3016.title: Как это работает
3016.content: [Your Node] → Radio → [Gateway Node with Wi-Fi] → MQTT Broker → [Remote Gateway] → Radio → [Remote Node] . A gateway node with internet access (Wi-Fi or Ethernet) publishes mesh messages to an MQTT topic. Удалённые шлюзы, подписанные на тот же топик, передают эти сообщения в свою локальную mesh-сеть.

3017.title: Настройки
3017.content: Включение MQTT . | Navigate to Settings → Module configuration → MQTT. | Turn on MQTT Enabled. | Настройте подключение к брокеру: | . | Настройка | Описание | По умолчанию | . | Address | MQTT broker hostname. Empty means the public broker | mqtt.meshtastic.org | . | Username | Аутентификация брокера | meshdev | . | Password | Аутентификация брокера | large4cats | . | Encryption Enabled | Publish packets still encrypted with the channel key | Включено | . | JSON output enabled | Shown only for a node on firmware older than 2.8, or while the setting is still on. See Message Formats | Отключено | . | TLS Enabled | Безопасное подключение к брокеру | Отключено | . | Root Topic | Базовый топик для сообщений | msh, which the node rewrites to msh/<REGION> when you set a region while it uses the public broker | . | MQTT Client Proxy | Relay MQTT through the connected app | Отключено | . | Map Reporting | Сообщать о местоположении на публичную карту | Включено | . Connection Status and Test Connection . The top of the MQTT settings screen shows the status of the relay this app runs: Connected, Connecting…, Reconnecting…, Disconnected, or Inactive. It reads Inactive whenever the app is not relaying, which includes the normal case of a node reaching the broker over its own Wi-Fi or Ethernet. The node’s own connection to the broker is not reported here. When the broker accepts the connection but refuses a subscription, the status names the refused topics and the broker’s reason: Connected, but the broker refused every topic when nothing was granted, or Connected, but the broker refused followed by the topics when only some were. A broker’s access-control list is the usual cause. Test connection probes the broker before you commit the settings to the node, and distinguishes the failure modes: the hostname not resolving, the TCP connection being refused, TLS failing, the attempt timing out, or the broker rejecting your credentials with a reason. Find Topics Near You . The region topic (msh/US) carries every gateway in the region. Find topics near you, under the root topic field, listens to the broker for one minute and lists the narrower roots in use around you, with the number of nodes heard on each. | Near you lists the region, then the country when the broker shows it in use (msh/EU_868/DE), then your state or province and city, named from the node’s position or, failing that, the phone’s location. The phone’s geocoder turns the location into place names; the location itself never reaches the broker. Community roots whose names don’t say where they are (msh/US/DMV) follow when they serve your area, from a directory the app refreshes from the Meshtastic API. | Active topics lists every other root heard. Roots under your state or city come first, then roots in neighboring states, then the rest. | Custom topic takes any root the node accepts: up to 31 ASCII characters, no leading or trailing slash, no + or #. | . The finder only subscribes and publishes nothing. Picking a topic fills in the root topic field, and nothing reaches the node until you save. It needs the LoRa region to be set. Without a location, or on desktop, it still lists the region and every root it hears. MQTT Proxy in This App . If your node has no internet access of its own, it can use the app as its MQTT gateway. Turn on MQTT Enabled and MQTT Client Proxy in the module config. The app then relays MQTT traffic between the node and the broker over your phone’s or computer’s internet connection. The MQTT proxy in this app toggle at the top of the MQTT settings screen shows whether this relay is running and lets you cut it off (or restart it) immediately, without editing and re-saving the node’s MQTT configuration. Стандартный брокер Meshtastic . Сообщество поддерживает публичный брокер по адресу mqtt.meshtastic.org. Он предназначен для общего использования и тестирования. When this app relays MQTT for the node, connections to that broker always use TLS on port 8883 even if TLS Enabled is off. That upgrade is the app’s own, and the switch says so. A node that reaches the broker over its own Wi-Fi or Ethernet forces nothing: it uses TLS Enabled as stored, so turn it on yourself or the node connects in the clear on port 1883. For any other broker the toggle decides in both cases. A port written in the address, as in broker.example.com:8884, is kept; without one, TLS uses port 8883 and plain connections use 1883. 🔒 Приватность: Сообщения на публичном брокере доступны для чтения всем, кто подписан. Всегда используйте шифрование каналов для конфиденциальной связи. Частный брокер . Для большей приватности и контроля ты можешь запустить собственный MQTT-брокер: . | Mosquitto (легковесный, с открытым исходным кодом) | HiveMQ | EMQX | . Настройте свою ноду на подключение к частному брокеру с соответствующими учётными данными.

3018.title: Публикация на карте
3018.content: When Map Reporting is on, your node periodically publishes a map report to the broker. The report goes out unencrypted, whatever keys your channels use, and carries your node id, long and short name, approximate location, hardware model, role, firmware version, LoRa region, modem preset, and primary channel name. Turning it on opens a consent card. Turn on I agree. and choose a Map Publish Interval of one hour or more — the screen will not save until you do. A slider sets the position precision, and the app shows the resulting accuracy as a ± distance, so you can publish an approximate location rather than an exact one. Reports appear at meshmap.net and similar community map services. 🔒 Privacy: A map report is readable by anyone subscribed to the broker. Leave Map Reporting off if you do not want your approximate location published.

3019.title: Uplink и Downlink
3019.content: | Направление | Описание | . | Uplink (восходящий) | Сообщения из mesh-сети → MQTT-брокер | . | Downlink (нисходящий) | Сообщения от MQTT-брокера → mesh-сеть | . Uplink and downlink are per-channel settings, not MQTT module settings. Open Settings → Channels, tap the channel, and use MQTT Uplink Enabled and MQTT Downlink Enabled. Every channel you want bridged out needs uplink on, and every channel you want MQTT traffic injected into needs downlink on.

3020.content: Gateways publish packets as binary Meshtastic protobufs on the /2/e/ topic, which is what node-to-node mesh bridging uses. Сообщения в канале по умолчанию, отправленные через MQTT, фактически не зашифрованы — кто угодно может их расшифровать. Всегда используйте собственный PSK для конфиденциальной связи.

The phone’s geocoder turns the location into place names; the location itself never reaches the broker. Community roots whose names don’t say where they are (msh/US/DMV) follow when they serve your area, from a directory the app refreshes from the Meshtastic API. | Active topics lists every other root heard. Roots under your state or city come first, then roots in neighboring states, then the rest. | Custom topic takes any root the node accepts: up to 31 ASCII characters, no leading or trailing slash, no + or #. | . The finder only subscribes and publishes nothing. Picking a topic fills in the root topic field, and nothing reaches the node until you save. It needs the LoRa region to be set. Without a location, or on desktop, it still lists the region and every root it hears. MQTT Proxy in This App . If your node has no internet access of its own, it can use the app as its MQTT gateway. Turn on MQTT Enabled and MQTT Client Proxy in the module config. The app then relays MQTT traffic between the node and the broker over your phone’s or computer’s internet connection. The MQTT proxy in this app toggle at the top of the MQTT settings screen shows whether this relay is running and lets you cut it off (or restart it) immediately, without editing and re-saving the node’s MQTT configuration. A node that reaches the broker over its own Wi-Fi or Ethernet forces nothing: it uses TLS Enabled as stored, so turn it on yourself or the node connects in the clear on port 1883. For any other broker the toggle decides in both cases. A port written in the address, as in broker.example.com:8884, is kept; without one, TLS uses port 8883 and plain connections use 1883. 🔒 Privacy: Messages on the public broker are readable by anyone subscribed. Always use channel encryption for private communications. Private Broker . For better privacy and control, you can run your own MQTT broker: . | Mosquitto (lightweight, open-source) | HiveMQ | EMQX | . Configure your node to point to your private broker with appropriate credentials.

3040.title: Map Reporting
3040.content: When Map Reporting is on, your node periodically publishes a map report to the broker. The report goes out unencrypted, whatever keys your channels use, and carries your node id, long and short name, approximate location, hardware model, role, firmware version, LoRa region, modem preset, and primary channel name. Turning it on opens a consent card. Turn on I agree. and choose a Map Publish Interval of one hour or more — the screen will not save until you do. A slider sets the position precision, and the app shows the resulting accuracy as a ± distance, so you can publish an approximate location rather than an exact one. Reports appear at meshmap.net and similar community map services. 🔒 Privacy: A map report is readable by anyone subscribed to the broker. Leave Map Reporting off if you do not want your approximate location published.

3041.title: Uplink vs Downlink
3041.content: | Direction | Deskripsyon | . | Uplink | Messages from mesh → MQTT broker | . | Downlink | Messages from MQTT broker → mesh | . 3043.title: Encryption & Privacy
3043.content: Understanding the layered encryption model: . | Channel encryption happens on the mesh before MQTT. If your channel has a PSK, the MQTT payload is already encrypted — the broker and any subscribers see only the ciphertext. | Encryption Enabled (the module setting) decides which copy of the packet the gateway publishes — it is not an extra layer. Leave it on and the broker receives the packet still encrypted with your channel key. Turn it off and the gateway publishes the decrypted packet, so anyone subscribed to the topic reads your messages in the clear. Turn it off only when you own the broker and want plain payloads for a dashboard. | TLS encrypts the TCP connection to the broker itself, preventing network-level eavesdropping. | . 🔒 Security: The default public channel has a well-known key. 3044.title: Best Practices
3044.content: . | Use channel-level encryption (PSK) on channels that bridge to MQTT | Don’t enable MQTT on a node with no internet access of its own unless MQTT Client Proxy is on (the node queues messages it can’t send and wastes memory) | Use a private broker for sensitive deployments | Be mindful of airtime when downlinking messages from busy MQTT topics — every downlinked message consumes radio airtime on your local mesh | Consider enabling uplink-only if you only need to monitor your mesh remotely without injecting messages back | .

3045.title: Troubleshooting
3045.content: MQTT Not Connecting . | Check Wi-Fi — the gateway node must have an active internet connection (Wi-Fi or Ethernet). MQTT does not work over the LoRa radio link itself. | Verify credentials — with incorrect credentials, most brokers fail silently — double-check for trailing spaces. | Firewall — port 1883 (MQTT) or 8883 (MQTT over TLS) must be reachable. Some networks allow only web traffic (ports 80 and 443). | DNS resolution — if using a custom broker hostname, verify the node can resolve it. Try the broker’s IP address directly. | . Messages Not Bridging . | Check uplink/downlink settings — if only uplink is enabled, messages flow from mesh to MQTT but not back. Enable downlink on the receiving gateway. | Channel mismatch — both gateways must share the same channel with the same PSK. A mismatch means messages are encrypted with different keys and appear as garbage. | Topic mismatch — both gateways must use exactly the same root topic. Firmware 2.8.0 and older also rewrite a root starting with msh on a private broker. | Ignore MQTT is on — in a region with a duty-cycle limit, the node turns on Ignore MQTT (LoRa config, Advanced) when you set the region, and then drops every packet that reached it via MQTT. Turn it off on the receiving nodes, not only on the gateway. | OK to MQTT is off — on a public broker a gateway uplinks other nodes’ packets only when the sending node has OK to MQTT (LoRa config, Advanced) on. Your own traffic bridges either way; your neighbors’ does not until they opt in. | .

A node that reaches the broker over its own Wi-Fi or Ethernet forces nothing: it uses TLS Enabled as stored, so turn it on yourself or the node connects in the clear on port 1883. For any other broker the toggle decides in both cases. A port written in the address, as in broker.example.com:8884, is kept; without one, TLS uses port 8883 and plain connections use 1883. 🔒 Privacy: Messages on the public broker are readable by anyone subscribed. Always use channel encryption for private communications. Private Broker . 3073.title: Map Reporting
3073.content: When Map Reporting is on, your node periodically publishes a map report to the broker. The report goes out unencrypted, whatever keys your channels use, and carries your node id, long and short name, approximate location, hardware model, role, firmware version, LoRa region, modem preset, and primary channel name. Turning it on opens a consent card. Turn on I agree. and choose a Map Publish Interval of one hour or more — the screen will not save until you do. A slider sets the position precision, and the app shows the resulting accuracy as a ± distance, so you can publish an approximate location rather than an exact one. Reports appear at meshmap.net and similar community map services. 🔒 Privacy: A map report is readable by anyone subscribed to the broker. Every channel you want bridged out needs uplink on, and every channel you want MQTT traffic injected into needs downlink on.

Firmware 2.8 removed JSON support and ignores the field. The app shows JSON output enabled only for a node on older firmware, or while the setting is still on, and while it is on the app’s own MQTT proxy also subscribes to the /2/json/ topic and decodes those payloads.

3076.title: Encryption & Privacy
3076.content: Understanding the layered encryption model: . | Channel encryption happens on the mesh before MQTT. If your channel has a PSK, the MQTT payload is already encrypted — the broker and any subscribers see only the ciphertext. | Encryption Enabled (the module setting) decides which copy of the packet the gateway publishes — it is not an extra layer. Leave it on and the broker receives the packet still encrypted with your channel key. Turn it off and the gateway publishes the decrypted packet, so anyone subscribed to the topic reads your messages in the clear. Turn it off only when you own the broker and want plain payloads for a dashboard. | TLS encrypts the TCP connection to the broker itself, preventing network-level eavesdropping. | . 🔒 Security: The default public channel has a well-known key. Messages on the default channel sent via MQTT are effectively unencrypted — anyone can decode them. Always use a custom PSK for private communications.

3077.title: Buone pratiche
3077.content: . | Use channel-level encryption (PSK) on channels that bridge to MQTT | Don’t enable MQTT on a node with no internet access of its own unless MQTT Client Proxy is on (the node queues messages it can’t send and wastes memory) | Use a private broker for sensitive deployments | Be mindful of airtime when downlinking messages from busy MQTT topics — every downlinked message consumes radio airtime on your local mesh | Consider enabling uplink-only if you only need to monitor your mesh remotely without injecting messages back | .

3078.title: Risoluzione problemi
3078.content: MQTT Not Connecting . | Check Wi-Fi — the gateway node must have an active internet connection (Wi-Fi or Ethernet). MQTT does not work over the LoRa radio link itself. | Verify credentials — with incorrect credentials, most brokers fail silently — double-check for trailing spaces. | Firewall — port 1883 (MQTT) or 8883 (MQTT over TLS) must be reachable. Some networks allow only web traffic (ports 80 and 443). | DNS resolution — if using a custom broker hostname, verify the node can resolve it. Try the broker’s IP address directly. | . Messages Not Bridging . | Check uplink/downlink settings — if only uplink is enabled, messages flow from mesh to MQTT but not back. Enable downlink on the receiving gateway. | Channel mismatch — both gateways must share the same channel with the same PSK. A mismatch means messages are encrypted with different keys and appear as garbage. | Topic mismatch — both gateways must use exactly the same root topic. On the public broker, setting a region rewrites a default root to msh/<REGION> (for example msh/US), so gateways in different regions do not meet until you give both the same explicit root. Firmware 2.8.0 and older also rewrite a root starting with msh on a private broker. | Ignore MQTT is on — in a region with a duty-cycle limit, the node turns on Ignore MQTT (LoRa config, Advanced) when you set the region, and then drops every packet that reached it via MQTT. Turn it off on the receiving nodes, not only on the gateway. | OK to MQTT is off — on a public broker a gateway uplinks other nodes’ packets only when the sending node has OK to MQTT (LoRa config, Advanced) on. Your own traffic bridges either way; your neighbors’ does not until they opt in. | .

3102.title: MQTT
3102.content: MQTT bridges your Meshtastic mesh network to the internet, enabling long-range communication beyond radio range.

3103.title: Преглед
3103.content: The MQTT module connects your node to an MQTT broker, allowing: . | Messages to reach nodes on different physical meshes via the internet | Integration with home automation and monitoring systems | Publishing node positions to the public Meshtastic map | Custom data pipelines for logging and alerting | .

3104.title: Как работи
3104.content: [Your Node] → Radio → [Gateway Node with Wi-Fi] → MQTT Broker → [Remote Gateway] → Radio → [Remote Node] . A gateway node with internet access (Wi-Fi or Ethernet) publishes mesh messages to an MQTT topic. Remote gateways subscribed to the same topic inject those messages into their local mesh.

3105.title: Конфигурация
3105.content: Enabling MQTT . | Navigate to Settings → Module configuration → MQTT. | Turn on MQTT Enabled. | Configure the broker connection: | . | Настройка | Описание | По подразбиране | . | Address | MQTT broker hostname. Empty means the public broker | mqtt.meshtastic.org | . | Username | Broker authentication | meshdev | . | Password | Broker authentication | large4cats | . | Encryption Enabled | Publish packets still encrypted with the channel key | Активиран | . | JSON output enabled | Shown only for a node on firmware older than 2.8, or while the setting is still on. See Message Formats | Disabled | . | TLS Enabled | Secure connection to broker | Disabled | . | Root Topic | Base topic for messages | msh, which the node rewrites to msh/<REGION> when you set a region while it uses the public broker | . | MQTT Client Proxy | Relay MQTT through the connected app | Disabled | . | Map Reporting | Report position to public map | Disabled | . Connection Status and Test Connection . The top of the MQTT settings screen shows the status of the relay this app runs: Connected, Connecting…, Reconnecting…, Disconnected, or Inactive. It reads Inactive whenever the app is not relaying, which includes the normal case of a node reaching the broker over its own Wi-Fi or Ethernet. The node’s own connection to the broker is not reported here. When the broker accepts the connection but refuses a subscription, the status names the refused topics and the broker’s reason: Connected, but the broker refused every topic when nothing was granted, or Connected, but the broker refused followed by the topics when only some were. A broker’s access-control list is the usual cause. Test connection probes the broker before you commit the settings to the node, and distinguishes the failure modes: the hostname not resolving, the TCP connection being refused, TLS failing, the attempt timing out, or the broker rejecting your credentials with a reason. Find Topics Near You . The region topic (msh/US) carries every gateway in the region. Find topics near you, under the root topic field, listens to the broker for one minute and lists the narrower roots in use around you, with the number of nodes heard on each. | Near you lists the region, then the country when the broker shows it in use (msh/EU_868/DE), then your state or province and city, named from the node’s position or, failing that, the phone’s location. The phone’s geocoder turns the location into place names; the location itself never reaches the broker. Community roots whose names don’t say where they are (msh/US/DMV) follow when they serve your area, from a directory the app refreshes from the Meshtastic API. | Active topics lists every other root heard. Roots under your state or city come first, then roots in neighboring states, then the rest. | Custom topic takes any root the node accepts: up to 31 ASCII characters, no leading or trailing slash, no + or #. | . The finder only subscribes and publishes nothing. Picking a topic fills in the root topic field, and nothing reaches the node until you save. It needs the LoRa region to be set. Without a location, or on desktop, it still lists the region and every root it hears. MQTT Proxy in This App . If your node has no internet access of its own, it can use the app as its MQTT gateway. Turn on MQTT Enabled and MQTT Client Proxy in the module config. The app then relays MQTT traffic between the node and the broker over your phone’s or computer’s internet connection. The MQTT proxy in this app toggle at the top of the MQTT settings screen shows whether this relay is running and lets you cut it off (or restart it) immediately, without editing and re-saving the node’s MQTT configuration. Default Meshtastic Broker . The community maintains a public broker at mqtt.meshtastic.org. This is intended for general use and testing. When this app relays MQTT for the node, connections to that broker always use TLS on port 8883 even if TLS Enabled is off. That upgrade is the app’s own, and the switch says so. A node that reaches the broker over its own Wi-Fi or Ethernet forces nothing: it uses TLS Enabled as stored, so turn it on yourself or the node connects in the clear on port 1883. For any other broker the toggle decides in both cases. A port written in the address, as in broker.example.com:8884, is kept; without one, TLS uses port 8883 and plain connections use 1883. 🔒 Privacy: Messages on the public broker are readable by anyone subscribed. Always use channel encryption for private communications. Private Broker . За по-добра поверителност и контрол, можете да управлявате свой собствен MQTT брокер: . | Mosquitto (lightweight, open-source) | HiveMQ | EMQX | . Configure your node to point to your private broker with appropriate credentials.

3106.title: Map Reporting
3106.content: When Map Reporting is on, your node periodically publishes a map report to the broker. The report goes out unencrypted, whatever keys your channels use, and carries your node id, long and short name, approximate location, hardware model, role, firmware version, LoRa region, modem preset, and primary channel name. Turning it on opens a consent card. Turn on I agree. and choose a Map Publish Interval of one hour or more — the screen will not save until you do. A slider sets the position precision, and the app shows the resulting accuracy as a ± distance, so you can publish an approximate location rather than an exact one. Reports appear at meshmap.net and similar community map services. 🔒 Privacy: A map report is readable by anyone subscribed to the broker. Leave Map Reporting off if you do not want your approximate location published.

3107.title: Uplink vs Downlink
3107.content: | Direction | Описание | . | Uplink | Messages from mesh → MQTT broker | . | Downlink | Messages from MQTT broker → mesh | . Uplink and downlink are per-channel settings, not MQTT module settings. Open Settings → Channels, tap the channel, and use MQTT Uplink Enabled and MQTT Downlink Enabled. Every channel you want bridged out needs uplink on, and every channel you want MQTT traffic injected into needs downlink on.

3108.title: Message Formats
3108.content: Gateways publish packets as binary Meshtastic protobufs on the /2/e/ topic, which is what node-to-node mesh bridging uses. Firmware 2.7 and older can also publish human-readable JSON on the /2/json/ topic for consumers outside the mesh, such as dashboards and home automation, when json_enabled is on. Firmware 2.8 removed JSON support and ignores the field. The app shows JSON output enabled only for a node on older firmware, or while the setting is still on, and while it is on the app’s own MQTT proxy also subscribes to the /2/json/ topic and decodes those payloads.

3109.title: Encryption & Privacy
3109.content: Understanding the layered encryption model: . | Channel encryption happens on the mesh before MQTT. If your channel has a PSK, the MQTT payload is already encrypted — the broker and any subscribers see only the ciphertext. | Encryption Enabled (the module setting) decides which copy of the packet the gateway publishes — it is not an extra layer. Leave it on and the broker receives the packet still encrypted with your channel key. Turn it off and the gateway publishes the decrypted packet, so anyone subscribed to the topic reads your messages in the clear. Turn it off only when you own the broker and want plain payloads for a dashboard. | TLS encrypts the TCP connection to the broker itself, preventing network-level eavesdropping. | . 🔒 Security: The default public channel has a well-known key. Messages on the default channel sent via MQTT are effectively unencrypted — anyone can decode them. Always use a custom PSK for private communications.

3110.title: Най-добри практики
3110.content: . | Use channel-level encryption (PSK) on channels that bridge to MQTT | Don’t enable MQTT on a node with no internet access of its own unless MQTT Client Proxy is on (the node queues messages it can’t send and wastes memory) | Use a private broker for sensitive deployments | Be mindful of airtime when downlinking messages from busy MQTT topics — every downlinked message consumes radio airtime on your local mesh | Consider enabling uplink-only if you only need to monitor your mesh remotely without injecting messages back | .

3111.content: MQTT Not Connecting . | Check Wi-Fi — the gateway node must have an active internet connection (Wi-Fi or Ethernet). MQTT does not work over the LoRa radio link itself. | Verify credentials — with incorrect credentials, most brokers fail silently — double-check for trailing spaces. | Firewall — port 1883 (MQTT) or 8883 (MQTT over TLS) must be reachable. Some networks allow only web traffic (ports 80 and 443). | DNS resolution — if using a custom broker hostname, verify the node can resolve it. Try the broker’s IP address directly. | . Messages Not Bridging . | Check uplink/downlink settings — if only uplink is enabled, messages flow from mesh to MQTT but not back. Enable downlink on the receiving gateway. | Channel mismatch — both gateways must share the same channel with the same PSK. A mismatch means messages are encrypted with different keys and appear as garbage. | Topic mismatch — both gateways must use exactly the same root topic. On the public broker, setting a region rewrites a default root to msh/<REGION> (for example msh/US), so gateways in different regions do not meet until you give both the same explicit root. Firmware 2.8.0 and older also rewrite a root starting with msh on a private broker. | Ignore MQTT is on — in a region with a duty-cycle limit, the node turns on Ignore MQTT (LoRa config, Advanced) when you set the region, and then drops every packet that reached it via MQTT. Turn it off on the receiving nodes, not only on the gateway. | OK to MQTT is off — on a public broker a gateway uplinks other nodes’ packets only when the sending node has OK to MQTT (LoRa config, Advanced) on. Your own traffic bridges either way; your neighbors’ does not until they opt in. | .

For any other broker the toggle decides in both cases. 3128.title: Map Reporting
3128.content: When Map Reporting is on, your node periodically publishes a map report to the broker. The report goes out unencrypted, whatever keys your channels use, and carries your node id, long and short name, approximate location, hardware model, role, firmware version, LoRa region, modem preset, and primary channel name. Turning it on opens a consent card. Turn on I agree. and choose a Map Publish Interval of one hour or more — the screen will not save until you do. A slider sets the position precision, and the app shows the resulting accuracy as a ± distance, so you can publish an approximate location rather than an exact one. Reports appear at meshmap.net and similar community map services. 🔒 Privacy: A map report is readable by anyone subscribed to the broker. Leave Map Reporting off if you do not want your approximate location published.

3129.title: Uplink vs Downlink
3129.content: | Direction | Beschrijving | . | Uplink | Messages from mesh → MQTT broker | . | Downlink | Messages from MQTT broker → mesh | . Uplink and downlink are per-channel settings, not MQTT module settings. Open Settings → Channels, tap the channel, and use MQTT Uplink Enabled and MQTT Downlink Enabled. Every channel you want bridged out needs uplink on, and every channel you want MQTT traffic injected into needs downlink on.

3130.title: Message Formats
3130.content: Gateways publish packets as binary Meshtastic protobufs on the /2/e/ topic, which is what node-to-node mesh bridging uses. Firmware 2.8 removed JSON support and ignores the field. The app shows JSON output enabled only for a node on older firmware, or while the setting is still on, and while it is on the app’s own MQTT proxy also subscribes to the /2/json/ topic and decodes those payloads.

3131.title: Encryption & Privacy
3131.content: Understanding the layered encryption model: . | Channel encryption happens on the mesh before MQTT. If your channel has a PSK, the MQTT payload is already encrypted — the broker and any subscribers see only the ciphertext. | Encryption Enabled (the module setting) decides which copy of the packet the gateway publishes — it is not an extra layer. Leave it on and the broker receives the packet still encrypted with your channel key. Turn it off and the gateway publishes the decrypted packet, so anyone subscribed to the topic reads your messages in the clear. Turn it off only when you own the broker and want plain payloads for a dashboard. | TLS encrypts the TCP connection to the broker itself, preventing network-level eavesdropping. | . 🔒 Security: The default public channel has a well-known key. 3132.title: Best Practices
3132.content: . | Use channel-level encryption (PSK) on channels that bridge to MQTT | Don’t enable MQTT on a node with no internet access of its own unless MQTT Client Proxy is on (the node queues messages it can’t send and wastes memory) | Use a private broker for sensitive deployments | Be mindful of airtime when downlinking messages from busy MQTT topics — every downlinked message consumes radio airtime on your local mesh | Consider enabling uplink-only if you only need to monitor your mesh remotely without injecting messages back | .

3133.title: Troubleshooting
3133.content: MQTT Not Connecting . | Check Wi-Fi — the gateway node must have an active internet connection (Wi-Fi or Ethernet). MQTT does not work over the LoRa radio link itself. | Verify credentials — with incorrect credentials, most brokers fail silently — double-check for trailing spaces. | Firewall — port 1883 (MQTT) or 8883 (MQTT over TLS) must be reachable. Some networks allow only web traffic (ports 80 and 443). | DNS resolution — if using a custom broker hostname, verify the node can resolve it. Try the broker’s IP address directly. | . Messages Not Bridging . | Check uplink/downlink settings — if only uplink is enabled, messages flow from mesh to MQTT but not back. Enable downlink on the receiving gateway. | Channel mismatch — both gateways must share the same channel with the same PSK. A mismatch means messages are encrypted with different keys and appear as garbage. | Topic mismatch — both gateways must use exactly the same root topic. On the public broker, setting a region rewrites a default root to msh/<REGION> (for example msh/US), so gateways in different regions do not meet until you give both the same explicit root. Firmware 2.8.0 and older also rewrite a root starting with msh on a private broker. | Ignore MQTT is on — in a region with a duty-cycle limit, the node turns on Ignore MQTT (LoRa config, Advanced) when you set the region, and then drops every packet that reached it via MQTT. Turn it off on the receiving nodes, not only on the gateway. | OK to MQTT is off — on a public broker a gateway uplinks other nodes’ packets only when the sending node has OK to MQTT (LoRa config, Advanced) on. Your own traffic bridges either way; your neighbors’ does not until they opt in. | .
