5858.title: TAK Integration
5858.content: Meshtastic integrates with the Team Awareness Kit (TAK) ecosystem, enabling interoperability between Meshtastic nodes and TAK applications like ATAK and WinTAK.

5859.title: Overview
5859.content: The TAK module allows Meshtastic nodes to: . | Share position data in TAK-compatible CoT (Cursor on Target) format | Appear as team members on TAK map displays | Receive TAK PLI (Position Location Information) messages | .

5860.title: Setup
5860.content: Prerequisites . | ATAK (Android Team Awareness Kit), iTAK, or WinTAK installed | Your node’s Device Role (Device configuration) set to TAK or TAK Tracker — this is what makes the TAK module appear in Module configuration at all | Firmware 2.8.0 or newer on the node. Earlier firmware accepts a TAK config write and never stores it, so the app hides the TAK module entry below that version even when the role is set correctly. See Firmware Updates | . ⚠️ Warning: The old Meshtastic ATAK Plugin is no longer part of this path and cannot work. It bridged through the cross-process AIDL API, which was removed in app 2.8.0; the mesh service runs in-process only. Do not install it. Interop runs over the app’s own local TAK server plus the Mesh to CoT Converter, both described in the following sections, with stock ATAK/iTAK/WinTAK. Configuration . Navigate to Settings → Module configuration → TAK (ATAK). The module’s own settings are your TAK identity — there is no separate enable switch here, because the Device Role setting in Device configuration is what turns TAK on. Your node broadcasts this identity, which appears on TAK maps. | Paramètre | Description | Par défaut | . | Rôle | Your operational role within the team: Team Member, Team Lead, HQ, Sniper, Medic, Forward Observer, RTO, or K9 | Default (Team Member) | . | Team | Your team color on the TAK map, one of the 14 standard TAK team colors such as Blue, Red, Cyan, or Green | Default (Cyan) | . Your TAK callsign isn’t a separate setting. The firmware uses your node’s long name. Team colors are the standard TAK team colors, so coordinate with your TAK team to use consistent team assignments. Local TAK Server . The app can also run a local TAK server so ATAK on the same phone, or WinTAK on the same computer running the desktop app, can connect directly without a remote TAK server. The server binds to localhost only (127.0.0.1:8089) and uses TLS with mutual certificate authentication (mTLS), so it is not reachable from other devices on the network. Open Settings → Advanced → TAK Server. These are app settings stored on this phone, which is why they sit next to Firmware Update and Debug Panel rather than under the TAK module config — and why they need neither a TAK role nor firmware 2.8.0. On Android 17 and newer, turning the server on asks for the local network permission it needs to open its socket. If that permission is denied for good, the app turns the server back off and offers to open app settings: . | Enable Local TAK Server — starts the loopback-only mTLS server on port 8089 for ATAK connections from the same device. | Status — under the toggle: Off, Starting TAK Server, Listening on 127.0.0.1:8089 — waiting for ATAK, the count of local client connections, or Unable to start TAK Server. Turn it off and on to retry. | TAK Mesh Channel — selects which Meshtastic channel outgoing TAK traffic is sent on (default: the primary channel, index 0). Incoming TAK traffic is accepted from any channel. Matches the equivalent setting on iOS and in the legacy ATAK plugin. | Mesh to CoT Converter — off by default, and shown under the server toggle. With the server running, this synthesizes a CoT contact for every node in your node database, so ordinary Meshtastic nodes appear on the ATAK map as contacts. This is what replaced the old plugin’s node visibility — without it, only TAK-role nodes show up. When the connected node runs firmware older than 2.8.0, a notice under the switch says that only location and chat messages bridge to ATAK. | Export TAK Data Package — generates a .zip data package that ATAK can import to connect to this server. The share icon in the top bar does the same. | .

5861.title: TAK Roles
5861.content: Nodes configured with TAK-related roles behave differently from standard clients: . | Rôle | Description | . | TAK | For a node paired with an ATAK device. Turns off many routine broadcasts to favor the CoT packet stream. | . | TAK Tracker | Broadcasts TAK PLI automatically, at the interval set by the position configuration, and turns off many routine broadcasts. Suited to unattended position beacons such as vehicles and equipment. | . 💡 Tip: Use TAK Tracker for devices that only need to report position (e.g., a node mounted in a vehicle). Use TAK for devices where users actively participate in TAK operations. CoT (Cursor on Target) Format . TAK messages use the Cursor on Target XML format — a military standard for sharing situational awareness data. Meshtastic converts its internal protobuf messages to CoT format when bridging to TAK systems, so no manual format conversion is needed.

5862.title: Wire Format (V1 / V2)
5862.content: Meshtastic supports two TAK wire formats, chosen automatically based on the connected node’s firmware — no manual configuration needed: . | Format | Compatibility | Features | . | V1 (Legacy) | Firmware 2.7.x and older | Bare protobuf encoding on port 72. Supports position sharing (PLI) and chat (GeoChat) only — shapes, markers, routes, and other typed CoT events are dropped | . | V2 (Current) | Firmware 2.8.0+ | Compact, zstd-compressed encoding on port 78. Adds shapes, markers, routes, aircraft, casevac, emergency, and task CoT types on top of everything V1 supports | . A node still relays legacy V1 packets from older nodes even while running V2 itself, so mixed-firmware meshes keep working.

5863.title: Usage with ATAK
5863.content: Once configured: . | Meshtastic nodes appear as markers on the ATAK map with callsign labels | Chat messages can bridge between mesh and TAK networks | Position updates flow bidirectionally between Meshtastic and TAK | TAK Tracker nodes broadcast PLI automatically — their positions appear on ATAK maps without any ATAK-side configuration | On Android, routes received from the mesh are also saved as a data package (.zip) in Downloads; import it in ATAK to add the route. An update to the same route overwrites its file rather than adding a copy. After the app is reinstalled, the first update to a route saves one renamed copy, and later updates overwrite that. On Android 9 and older the file goes to the app’s own folder under Android/data instead. The desktop app doesn’t save route files | . ℹ️ Note: TAK integration requires specific node roles. Standard client nodes don’t automatically participate in TAK operations — though with Mesh to CoT Converter enabled they still appear on the ATAK map as contacts.

5864.title: Troubleshooting
5864.content: | Problem | Cause | Solution | . | Node doesn’t appear on ATAK map | Wrong Device Role setting, or Mesh to CoT Converter off | Set the node’s Device Role to TAK or TAK Tracker. For ordinary (non-TAK-role) nodes to appear, also enable Mesh to CoT Converter under Settings → Advanced → TAK Server | . | Position updates are stale | GPS fix lost or interval too long | Check GPS status; reduce position broadcast interval in Position Config | . | ATAK shows “disconnected” | The local TAK server is off, or ATAK is pointed elsewhere | Check Enable Local TAK Server is on, and that ATAK is connecting to 127.0.0.1:8089 — re-import the exported data package if unsure | . | Shapes, markers, or routes not bridging | Sending node is on legacy V1 (firmware 2.7.x or older) | Update the sending node’s firmware to 2.8.0+ for V2 wire format | . | CoT data not flowing | Channel mismatch | All TAK nodes must be on the same channel with matching encryption | .

5865.title: Security Considerations
5865.content: 🔒 Privacy: TAK data shares your position and callsign information. The TAK module respects the same channel encryption as other Meshtastic messages — in sensitive environments, use a channel with a non-default key.

5886.title: Overview

5887.title: Setup
5887.content: Prerequisites . | ATAK (Android Team Awareness Kit), iTAK, or WinTAK installed | Your node’s Device Role (Device configuration) set to TAK or TAK Tracker — this is what makes the TAK module appear in Module configuration at all | Firmware 2.8.0 or newer on the node. Earlier firmware accepts a TAK config write and never stores it, so the app hides the TAK module entry below that version even when the role is set correctly. See Firmware Updates | . ⚠️ Warning: The old Meshtastic ATAK Plugin is no longer part of this path and cannot work. It bridged through the cross-process AIDL API, which was removed in app 2.8.0; the mesh service runs in-process only. Do not install it. Interop runs over the app’s own local TAK server plus the Mesh to CoT Converter, both described in the following sections, with stock ATAK/iTAK/WinTAK. Configuration . Navigate to Settings → Module configuration → TAK (ATAK). The module’s own settings are your TAK identity — there is no separate enable switch here, because the Device Role setting in Device configuration is what turns TAK on. Your node broadcasts this identity, which appears on TAK maps. | Setting | Popis | Predvolené | . | Rola | Your operational role within the team: Team Member, Team Lead, HQ, Sniper, Medic, Forward Observer, RTO, or K9 | Default (Team Member) | . | Team | Your team color on the TAK map, one of the 14 standard TAK team colors such as Blue, Red, Cyan, or Green | Default (Cyan) | . Your TAK callsign isn’t a separate setting. The firmware uses your node’s long name. Team colors are the standard TAK team colors, so coordinate with your TAK team to use consistent team assignments. Local TAK Server . The app can also run a local TAK server so ATAK on the same phone, or WinTAK on the same computer running the desktop app, can connect directly without a remote TAK server. The server binds to localhost only (127.0.0.1:8089) and uses TLS with mutual certificate authentication (mTLS), so it is not reachable from other devices on the network. Open Settings → Advanced → TAK Server. These are app settings stored on this phone, which is why they sit next to Firmware Update and Debug Panel rather than under the TAK module config — and why they need neither a TAK role nor firmware 2.8.0. On Android 17 and newer, turning the server on asks for the local network permission it needs to open its socket. If that permission is denied for good, the app turns the server back off and offers to open app settings: . | Enable Local TAK Server — starts the loopback-only mTLS server on port 8089 for ATAK connections from the same device. | Status — under the toggle: Off, Starting TAK Server, Listening on 127.0.0.1:8089 — waiting for ATAK, the count of local client connections, or Unable to start TAK Server. Turn it off and on to retry. | TAK Mesh Channel — selects which Meshtastic channel outgoing TAK traffic is sent on (default: the primary channel, index 0). Incoming TAK traffic is accepted from any channel. Matches the equivalent setting on iOS and in the legacy ATAK plugin. | Mesh to CoT Converter — off by default, and shown under the server toggle. With the server running, this synthesizes a CoT contact for every node in your node database, so ordinary Meshtastic nodes appear on the ATAK map as contacts. This is what replaced the old plugin’s node visibility — without it, only TAK-role nodes show up. When the connected node runs firmware older than 2.8.0, a notice under the switch says that only location and chat messages bridge to ATAK. | Export TAK Data Package — generates a .zip data package that ATAK can import to connect to this server. Turns off many routine broadcasts to favor the CoT packet stream. | . | TAK Tracker | Broadcasts TAK PLI automatically, at the interval set by the position configuration, and turns off many routine broadcasts. Suited to unattended position beacons such as vehicles and equipment. | . 💡 Tip: Use TAK Tracker for devices that only need to report position (e.g., a node mounted in a vehicle). 5948.title: TAK Integration
5948.content: Meshtastic integrates with the Team Awareness Kit (TAK) ecosystem, enabling interoperability between Meshtastic nodes and TAK applications like ATAK and WinTAK.

5949.title: Overview
5949.content: The TAK module allows Meshtastic nodes to: . | Share position data in TAK-compatible CoT (Cursor on Target) format | Appear as team members on TAK map displays | Receive TAK PLI (Position Location Information) messages | .

5950.title: Setup
5950.content: Prerequisites . | ATAK (Android Team Awareness Kit), iTAK, or WinTAK installed | Your node’s Device Role (Device configuration) set to TAK or TAK Tracker — this is what makes the TAK module appear in Module configuration at all | Firmware 2.8.0 or newer on the node. Earlier firmware accepts a TAK config write and never stores it, so the app hides the TAK module entry below that version even when the role is set correctly. See Firmware Updates | . ⚠️ Warning: The old Meshtastic ATAK Plugin is no longer part of this path and cannot work. It bridged through the cross-process AIDL API, which was removed in app 2.8.0; the mesh service runs in-process only. Do not install it. Interop runs over the app’s own local TAK server plus the Mesh to CoT Converter, both described in the following sections, with stock ATAK/iTAK/WinTAK. Configuration . Navigate to Settings → Module configuration → TAK (ATAK). The module’s own settings are your TAK identity — there is no separate enable switch here, because the Device Role setting in Device configuration is what turns TAK on. Your node broadcasts this identity, which appears on TAK maps. | Setting | Опис | Подразумевано | . | Улога | Your operational role within the team: Team Member, Team Lead, HQ, Sniper, Medic, Forward Observer, RTO, or K9 | Default (Team Member) | . | Team | Your team color on the TAK map, one of the 14 standard TAK team colors such as Blue, Red, Cyan, or Green | Default (Cyan) | . Your TAK callsign isn’t a separate setting. The firmware uses your node’s long name. Team colors are the standard TAK team colors, so coordinate with your TAK team to use consistent team assignments. Local TAK Server . The app can also run a local TAK server so ATAK on the same phone, or WinTAK on the same computer running the desktop app, can connect directly without a remote TAK server. The server binds to localhost only (127.0.0.1:8089) and uses TLS with mutual certificate authentication (mTLS), so it is not reachable from other devices on the network. Open Settings → Advanced → TAK Server. These are app settings stored on this phone, which is why they sit next to Firmware Update and Debug Panel rather than under the TAK module config — and why they need neither a TAK role nor firmware 2.8.0. On Android 17 and newer, turning the server on asks for the local network permission it needs to open its socket. If that permission is denied for good, the app turns the server back off and offers to open app settings: . | Enable Local TAK Server — starts the loopback-only mTLS server on port 8089 for ATAK connections from the same device. | Status — under the toggle: Off, Starting TAK Server, Listening on 127.0.0.1:8089 — waiting for ATAK, the count of local client connections, or Unable to start TAK Server. Turn it off and on to retry. | TAK Mesh Channel — selects which Meshtastic channel outgoing TAK traffic is sent on (default: the primary channel, index 0). Incoming TAK traffic is accepted from any channel. Matches the equivalent setting on iOS and in the legacy ATAK plugin. | Mesh to CoT Converter — off by default, and shown under the server toggle. With the server running, this synthesizes a CoT contact for every node in your node database, so ordinary Meshtastic nodes appear on the ATAK map as contacts. This is what replaced the old plugin’s node visibility — without it, only TAK-role nodes show up. When the connected node runs firmware older than 2.8.0, a notice under the switch says that only location and chat messages bridge to ATAK. | Export TAK Data Package — generates a .zip data package that ATAK can import to connect to this server. The share icon in the top bar does the same. | .

5951.title: TAK Roles
5951.content: Nodes configured with TAK-related roles behave differently from standard clients: . | Улога | Опис | . | TAK | For a node paired with an ATAK device. Turns off many routine broadcasts to favor the CoT packet stream. | . | TAK Tracker | Broadcasts TAK PLI automatically, at the interval set by the position configuration, and turns off many routine broadcasts. Suited to unattended position beacons such as vehicles and equipment. | . 💡 Tip: Use TAK Tracker for devices that only need to report position (e.g., a node mounted in a vehicle). Use TAK for devices where users actively participate in TAK operations. CoT (Cursor on Target) Format . TAK messages use the Cursor on Target XML format — a military standard for sharing situational awareness data. Meshtastic converts its internal protobuf messages to CoT format when bridging to TAK systems, so no manual format conversion is needed.

5952.title: Wire Format (V1 / V2)
5952.content: Meshtastic supports two TAK wire formats, chosen automatically based on the connected node’s firmware — no manual configuration needed: . | Format | Compatibility | Features | . | V1 (Legacy) | Firmware 2.7.x and older | Bare protobuf encoding on port 72. Supports position sharing (PLI) and chat (GeoChat) only — shapes, markers, routes, and other typed CoT events are dropped | . | V2 (Current) | Firmware 2.8.0+ | Compact, zstd-compressed encoding on port 78. Adds shapes, markers, routes, aircraft, casevac, emergency, and task CoT types on top of everything V1 supports | . A node still relays legacy V1 packets from older nodes even while running V2 itself, so mixed-firmware meshes keep working.

6015.title: Wire Format (V1 / V2)
6015.content: Meshtastic supports two TAK wire formats, chosen automatically based on the connected node’s firmware — no manual configuration needed: . | Format | Compatibility | Features | . | V1 (Legacy) | Firmware 2.7.x and older | Bare protobuf encoding on port 72. 6016.title: Usage with ATAK

6048.title: Ülevaade
6048.content: TAK moodul võimaldab Meshtastic sõlmedel: . | Jaga asukohaandmeid TAK ühilduvas CoT (Cursor on Target) vormingus | Kuvatakse meeskonnaliikmetena TAK kaardil | TAK PLI (asukohateabe) sõnumite vastuvõtmine | .

6049.title: Seadistamine
6049.content: Prerequisites . | ATAK (Android Team Awareness Kit), iTAK, or WinTAK installed | Your node’s Device Role (Device configuration) set to TAK or TAK Tracker — this is what makes the TAK module appear in Module configuration at all | Firmware 2.8.0 or newer on the node. Earlier firmware accepts a TAK config write and never stores it, so the app hides the TAK module entry below that version even when the role is set correctly. See Firmware Updates | . ⚠️ Warning: The old Meshtastic ATAK Plugin is no longer part of this path and cannot work. It bridged through the cross-process AIDL API, which was removed in app 2.8.0; the mesh service runs in-process only. Do not install it. Interop runs over the app’s own local TAK server plus the Mesh to CoT Converter, both described in the following sections, with stock ATAK/iTAK/WinTAK. Sätted . Navigate to Settings → Module configuration → TAK (ATAK). The module’s own settings are your TAK identity — there is no separate enable switch here, because the Device Role setting in Device configuration is what turns TAK on. Your node broadcasts this identity, which appears on TAK maps. | Seadistamine | Kirjeldus | Vaikimisi | . | Roll | Your operational role within the team: Team Member, Team Lead, HQ, Sniper, Medic, Forward Observer, RTO, or K9 | Default (Team Member) | . | Tiim | Your team color on the TAK map, one of the 14 standard TAK team colors such as Blue, Red, Cyan, or Green | Default (Cyan) | . Your TAK callsign isn’t a separate setting. The firmware uses your node’s long name. Team colors are the standard TAK team colors, so coordinate with your TAK team to use consistent team assignments. Lokaalne TAK server . The app can also run a local TAK server so ATAK on the same phone, or WinTAK on the same computer running the desktop app, can connect directly without a remote TAK server. Server seostub ainult localhostiga (127.0.0.1:8089) ja kasutab TLS-i vastastikuse sertifikaadi autentimisega (mTLS), seega pole see võrgus olevatest seadmetest kättesaadav. Open Settings → Advanced → TAK Server. These are app settings stored on this phone, which is why they sit next to Firmware Update and Debug Panel rather than under the TAK module config — and why they need neither a TAK role nor firmware 2.8.0. On Android 17 and newer, turning the server on asks for the local network permission it needs to open its socket. If that permission is denied for good, the app turns the server back off and offers to open app settings: . | Enable Local TAK Server — starts the loopback-only mTLS server on port 8089 for ATAK connections from the same device. | Status — under the toggle: Off, Starting TAK Server, Listening on 127.0.0.1:8089 — waiting for ATAK, the count of local client connections, or Unable to start TAK Server. Turn it off and on to retry. | TAK kärgvõrgu kanal — valib, millisel Meshtastic kanalil väljaminev TAK liiklus saadetakse (vaikimisi: peamine kanal, indeks 0). Sissetulevat TAK liiklust võetakse vastu igalt kanalilt. Vastab iOS-i ja pärand-ATAK-i pistikprogrammi samaväärsele sättele. | Mesh to CoT Converter — off by default, and shown under the server toggle. With the server running, this synthesizes a CoT contact for every node in your node database, so ordinary Meshtastic nodes appear on the ATAK map as contacts. This is what replaced the old plugin’s node visibility — without it, only TAK-role nodes show up. When the connected node runs firmware older than 2.8.0, a notice under the switch says that only location and chat messages bridge to ATAK. | Export TAK Data Package — generates a .zip data package that ATAK can import to connect to this server. The share icon in the top bar does the same. | .

6050.title: TAK rollid
6050.content: TAKiga seotud rollidega seadistatud sõlmed käituvad tavalistest klientidest erinevalt: . | Roll | Kirjeldus | . | TAK | For a node paired with an ATAK device. Turns off many routine broadcasts to favor the CoT packet stream. | . | TAK jälgimisseade | Broadcasts TAK PLI automatically, at the interval set by the position configuration, and turns off many routine broadcasts. Suited to unattended position beacons such as vehicles and equipment. | . 💡 Tip: Use TAK Tracker for devices that only need to report position (e.g., a node mounted in a vehicle). Kasutage TAK seadmete puhul, mille kasutajad osalevad aktiivselt TAK toimingutes. CoT (Cursor on Target) vorming . TAK- õnumid kasutavad kursori sihtmärgil XML-vormingut – see on sõjaline standard olukorrateadlikkuse andmete jagamiseks. Meshtastic teisendab oma sisemised protobuf-sõnumid TAK-süsteemidega ühendamisel CoT-vormingusse, seega pole käsitsi vormingu teisendamist vaja.

6051.title: Sõnumivorming (V1 / V2)
6051.content: Meshtastic supports two TAK wire formats, chosen automatically based on the connected node’s firmware — no manual configuration needed: . | Vorming | Compatibility | Omadused | . | V1 (pärandversioon) | Püsivara 2.7.x ja vanem | Bare protobuf encoding on port 72. Toetab ainult asukoha jagamist (PLI) ja vestlust (GeoChat) – kujundid, markerid, marsruudid ja muud tüüpi CoT-sündmused eemaldatakse | . | V2 (praegune) | Püsivara 2.8.0+ | Compact, zstd-compressed encoding on port 78. Lisab lisaks kõigele, mida V1 toetab, kujundeid, markereid, marsruute, õhusõidukeid, tsiviillennukeid, hädaolukordi ja ülesannete CoT tüüpe | . Sõlm edastab pärand sõlmedelt pärit V1 pakette isegi V2 kasutamise ajal, seega sega-püsivaraga võrgud töötavad edasi.

6052.title: Kasutamine koos ATAKiga
6052.content: Kui on seadistatud: . | Meshtastic sõlmed ilmuvad ATAK kaardil markeritena koos kutsungi nimega | Vestlussõnumid võivad ühendada kärgvõrgu ja TAK võrke | Asukohavärskendused liiguvad Meshtasticu ja TAKi vahel kahesuunaliselt | TAK jälgimisseadme sõlmed levitavad PLId automaatselt – nende asukohad kuvatakse ATAK kaartidel ilma ATAK poolse konfita | On Android, routes received from the mesh are also saved as a data package (.zip) in Downloads; import it in ATAK to add the route. An update to the same route overwrites its file rather than adding a copy. After the app is reinstalled, the first update to a route saves one renamed copy, and later updates overwrite that. On Android 9 and older the file goes to the app’s own folder under Android/data instead. The desktop app doesn’t save route files | . ℹ️ Note: TAK integration requires specific node roles. Standard client nodes don’t automatically participate in TAK operations — though with Mesh to CoT Converter enabled they still appear on the ATAK map as contacts.

6056.title: TAK Integration
6056.content: Meshtastic integrates with the Team Awareness Kit (TAK) ecosystem, enabling interoperability between Meshtastic nodes and TAK applications like ATAK and WinTAK.

6057.title: Übersicht
6057.content: The TAK module allows Meshtastic nodes to: . | Share position data in TAK-compatible CoT (Cursor on Target) format | Appear as team members on TAK map displays | Receive TAK PLI (Position Location Information) messages | .

6058.title: Einstellungen
6058.content: Voraussetzungen . | ATAK (Android Team Awareness Kit), iTAK, or WinTAK installed | Your node’s Device Role (Device configuration) set to TAK or TAK Tracker — this is what makes the TAK module appear in Module configuration at all | Firmware 2.8.0 or newer on the node. Earlier firmware accepts a TAK config write and never stores it, so the app hides the TAK module entry below that version even when the role is set correctly. See Firmware Updates | . ⚠️ Warning: The old Meshtastic ATAK Plugin is no longer part of this path and cannot work. It bridged through the cross-process AIDL API, which was removed in app 2.8.0; the mesh service runs in-process only. Do not install it. Interop runs over the app’s own local TAK server plus the Mesh to CoT Converter, both described in the following sections, with stock ATAK/iTAK/WinTAK. Einstellungen . Navigate to Settings → Module configuration → TAK (ATAK). The module’s own settings are your TAK identity — there is no separate enable switch here, because the Device Role setting in Device configuration is what turns TAK on. Your node broadcasts this identity, which appears on TAK maps. | Einstellung | Beschreibung | Standardwert | . | Rolle | Your operational role within the team: Team Member, Team Lead, HQ, Sniper, Medic, Forward Observer, RTO, or K9 | Default (Team Member) | . | Team | Your team color on the TAK map, one of the 14 standard TAK team colors such as Blue, Red, Cyan, or Green | Default (Cyan) | . Your TAK callsign isn’t a separate setting. The firmware uses your node’s long name. Team colors are the standard TAK team colors, so coordinate with your TAK team to use consistent team assignments. Local TAK Server . The app can also run a local TAK server so ATAK on the same phone, or WinTAK on the same computer running the desktop app, can connect directly without a remote TAK server. The server binds to localhost only (127.0.0.1:8089) and uses TLS with mutual certificate authentication (mTLS), so it is not reachable from other devices on the network. Open Settings → Advanced → TAK Server. These are app settings stored on this phone, which is why they sit next to Firmware Update and Debug Panel rather than under the TAK module config — and why they need neither a TAK role nor firmware 2.8.0. On Android 17 and newer, turning the server on asks for the local network permission it needs to open its socket. If that permission is denied for good, the app turns the server back off and offers to open app settings: . | Enable Local TAK Server — starts the loopback-only mTLS server on port 8089 for ATAK connections from the same device. | Status — under the toggle: Off, Starting TAK Server, Listening on 127.0.0.1:8089 — waiting for ATAK, the count of local client connections, or Unable to start TAK Server. Turn it off and on to retry. | TAK Mesh Channel — selects which Meshtastic channel outgoing TAK traffic is sent on (default: the primary channel, index 0). Incoming TAK traffic is accepted from any channel. Matches the equivalent setting on iOS and in the legacy ATAK plugin. | Mesh to CoT Converter — off by default, and shown under the server toggle. With the server running, this synthesizes a CoT contact for every node in your node database, so ordinary Meshtastic nodes appear on the ATAK map as contacts. This is what replaced the old plugin’s node visibility — without it, only TAK-role nodes show up. When the connected node runs firmware older than 2.8.0, a notice under the switch says that only location and chat messages bridge to ATAK. | Export TAK Data Package — generates a .zip data package that ATAK can import to connect to this server. The share icon in the top bar does the same. | .

6059.title: TAK Roles
6059.content: Nodes configured with TAK-related roles behave differently from standard clients: . | Rolle | Beschreibung | . | TAK | For a node paired with an ATAK device. Turns off many routine broadcasts to favor the CoT packet stream. | . | TAK Tracker | Broadcasts TAK PLI automatically, at the interval set by the position configuration, and turns off many routine broadcasts. Suited to unattended position beacons such as vehicles and equipment. | . 💡 Tip: Use TAK Tracker for devices that only need to report position (e.g., a node mounted in a vehicle). Use TAK for devices where users actively participate in TAK operations. CoT (Cursor on Target) Format . TAK messages use the Cursor on Target XML format — a military standard for sharing situational awareness data. Meshtastic converts its internal protobuf messages to CoT format when bridging to TAK systems, so no manual format conversion is needed.

6060.title: Wire Format (V1 / V2)
6060.content: Meshtastic supports two TAK wire formats, chosen automatically based on the connected node’s firmware — no manual configuration needed: . | Format | Kompatibilität | Merkmale | . | V1 (Legacy) | Firmware 2.7.x and older | Bare protobuf encoding on port 72. Supports position sharing (PLI) and chat (GeoChat) only — shapes, markers, routes, and other typed CoT events are dropped | . | V2 (Current) | Firmware 2.8.0+ | Compact, zstd-compressed encoding on port 78. Adds shapes, markers, routes, aircraft, casevac, emergency, and task CoT types on top of everything V1 supports | . A node still relays legacy V1 packets from older nodes even while running V2 itself, so mixed-firmware meshes keep working.

6061.title: Usage with ATAK
6061.content: Once configured: . | Meshtastic nodes appear as markers on the ATAK map with callsign labels | Chat messages can bridge between mesh and TAK networks | Position updates flow bidirectionally between Meshtastic and TAK | TAK Tracker nodes broadcast PLI automatically — their positions appear on ATAK maps without any ATAK-side configuration | On Android, routes received from the mesh are also saved as a data package (.zip) in Downloads; import it in ATAK to add the route. An update to the same route overwrites its file rather than adding a copy. After the app is reinstalled, the first update to a route saves one renamed copy, and later updates overwrite that. On Android 9 and older the file goes to the app’s own folder under Android/data instead. The desktop app doesn’t save route files | . ℹ️ Note: TAK integration requires specific node roles. Standard client nodes don’t automatically participate in TAK operations — though with Mesh to CoT Converter enabled they still appear on the ATAK map as contacts.

6065.title: Telemetry & Sensors
6065.content: Meshtastic nodes can collect and share sensor data across the mesh network. Telemetry allows nodes equipped with sensors to broadcast environmental, power, and device health information, visible on the node detail screen and logged over time.

6066.title: Device Telemetry
6066.content: All Meshtastic nodes report basic device telemetry: . | Metrický | Popis | Typical Range | . | Battery Level | Charge percentage | 0–100% | . | Napětí | Battery voltage | 3.0–4.2V (LiPo) | . | ChUtil | % of local airtime in use | 0–100% | . | AirUtil | % of the last hour this node spent transmitting | 0–100% | . | Doba provozu | Seconds since last boot | Varies | .

6067.title: Environment Sensors
6067.content: Supported environmental sensors: . Temperature & Humidity . | Senzor | Teplota | Vlhkost | Tlak | Poznámka | . | BME280 | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | Recommended all-in-one | . | BME680 | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | Adds gas resistance/IAQ | . | SHT31 | ✓ | ✓ | — | High accuracy | . | MCP9808 | ✓ | — | — | Precision temperature | . | LPS22 | — | — | ✓ | Pressure only | . Air Quality . | Senzor | Metrický | Poznámka | . | BME680 | Gas Resistance / IAQ | Volatile organic compounds | . | PMSA003I | PM1.0, PM2.5, PM10 | See Air Quality Metrics | . | SEN55 | PM, Temp, Humidity | Multi-sensor. Its NOx and VOC indices are recorded and included in a CSV export, but are not shown as cards or charts | . | SEN6x | PM, CO₂, Temp, Humidity | Its status register is always exported; when it reports a fault (fan, RH&T, gas, CO₂, HCHO or PM), the fault names appear as a Sensor Status card and on each Air Quality log entry | . Soil . | Metrický | Unit | Poznámka | . | Soil Temp | °C / °F | Reported alongside soil moisture by soil probes | . | Soil Moist | % | Volumetric water content | . Both appear as info cards on the node detail screen, next to the other environment readings. Soil probe and water-quality sonde chemistry (pH, conductivity, salinity, NPK, dissolved oxygen, ORP, turbidity, nitrate, ammonium, oxygen demand, solar irradiance) appears as a Soil & Water row of info cards on the node detail screen once a node reports any of it, and is included in the node database export. It has no chart or log screen, and the row has no request button. Light & UV . | Senzor | Metrický | . | OPT3001 | Ambient light (lux) | . | VEML7700 | Ambient light (lux) | . | LTR390 | UV index | . Weather and Other Readings . | Metrický | Unit | Where it appears | . | Wind speed | km/h or mph | Card and chart. Sensors report meters per second; the app converts to match your unit setting, and the chart uses the same unit as the card | . | Wind direction, gust, and lull | degrees, km/h or mph | Listed with each reading on the Environment Metrics screen; not charted | . | Rainfall, last hour and last 24 hours | mm or in | Listed with each reading on the Environment Metrics screen; not charted | . | Lightning, strikes in the last hour and storm distance | count, km or mi | Card and listed with each reading on the Environment Metrics screen; not charted. From an AS3935 detector. Storm distance is always in km or mi, since the detector resolves whole kilometers | . | Radiace | µR/h | Card and chart | . | Hmotnost | kg or lb | Card only — load cells, such as a beehive scale | . | Vzdálenost | mm or in | Card only — water level, from a distance sensor | . | Dew point | °C or °F | Card only — computed from temperature and humidity | . | 1-Wire temperature | °C or °F | Card and chart, up to eight DS18B20-style probes | . | ADC voltage | V | Card and chart, up to eight raw analog channels | .

6068.title: Metriky napájení
6068.content: Nodes with INA-series power sensors can report: . | Metrický | Popis | . | Napětí | Per-channel voltage reading | . | Proud | Per-channel current draw, in mA | . The node detail screen shows read-only cards for channels 1 to 3. Use the chart button on the Power Metrics row to open the chart screen, which lists a chip for every channel that reported data — up to eight — and charts the one you select. Rename a channel there, in the label field under the chips, to something like Solar or Battery. There is no separate wattage reading; the app charts voltage and current, and does not compute power from them. Useful for monitoring solar charging or battery health on remote nodes.

6069.title: Configuring Telemetry
6069.content: . | Navigate to Settings → Module configuration → Telemetry. | Each metric group has its own enable toggle and its own interval: . | Device Metrics — battery, voltage, uptime, ChUtil, and AirUtil. Its toggle, Broadcast Device Metrics, appears only on firmware 2.7.13 and later. Turned off, the node stops broadcasting these metrics to the mesh but still sends them to the connected app; on older firmware you can change the interval but not stop the broadcast | Environment Metrics — temperature, humidity, pressure and the other sensor readings | Air Quality Metrics — particulate and CO₂ readings | Power Metrics — the per-channel voltage and current readings | . Environment has an extra toggle, Show on device screen, to show its readings on the node’s own screen, and Display Fahrenheit to show its temperatures there in Fahrenheit. Power has Power Screen for the same purpose. | . Choosing an Interval . These are nominal values, not hard schedules. On a congested mesh the firmware automatically backs off to longer intervals based on how many nodes are online, so you do not need to hand-tune them for mesh size. Lengthen them deliberately only to save battery.

6070.title: Air Quality Metrics
6070.content: Nodes with particulate matter or CO₂ sensors report air quality data: . | Metrický | Unit | Popis | . | PM1.0 | µg/m³ | Ultrafine particulate matter | . | PM2.5 | µg/m³ | Fine particulate matter | . | PM10 | µg/m³ | Coarse particulate matter | . | CO₂ | ppm | Carbon dioxide concentration | . CO₂ sensors such as the SCD4x also report their own temperature and humidity, which appear alongside the readings above. From PM2.5 history the app additionally derives an EPA NowCast AQI value. The CO₂ reading is color-coded by severity (Good → Stuffy → Poor → Unsafe → Evacuate). See Node Metrics — Air Quality for the exact ppm bands, colors, and AQI detail. Air quality data can be viewed as info cards on the node detail screen, charted over time, and exported to CSV.

6071.title: Viewing Telemetry
6071.content: . | Navigate to Nodes and select a node. | The Telemetry section lists a row for each metric type — Device, Environment, Air Quality, Power, Host, PAX, and the rest — whether or not this node has reported it. A row fills in with readings, and grows a chart button, once that node has sent that kind of telemetry. An empty row means nothing has arrived, not that the sensor is missing. Soil & Water is the exception: its row appears only after the node reports soil or water readings. | Use the chart button on a row to open that metric’s history, where you can pick a time frame. The Device, Environment, Air Quality, Power, Signal Quality, and Position screens also export their readings as CSV. | .

6072.title: Troubleshooting
6072.content: . | No environment data showing? The remote node needs a physical sensor connected (e.g., BME280 on I2C). Device telemetry (battery, uptime) is always available, but environment metrics require hardware. | Stale readings? Check the reporting interval — very long intervals (7200s+) mean data updates infrequently. Also verify the remote node is still online. | Sensor conflict on I2C bus? Some sensors share I2C addresses. If you have multiple sensors on the same bus, check for address collisions in the node’s serial debug output. | .

6118.title: Power Metrics
6118.content: Nodes with INA-series power sensors can report: . | Metric | Beskrivelse | . | Voltage | Per-channel voltage reading | . | Current | Per-channel current draw, in mA | . The node detail screen shows read-only cards for channels 1 to 3. Use the chart button on the Power Metrics row to open the chart screen, which lists a chip for every channel that reported data — up to eight — and charts the one you select. 6120.title: Air Quality Metrics
6120.content: Nodes with particulate matter or CO₂ sensors report air quality data: . | Metric | Unit | Beskrivelse | . | PM1.0 | µg/m³ | Ultrafine particulate matter | . | PM2.5 | µg/m³ | Fine particulate matter | . | PM10 | µg/m³ | Coarse particulate matter | . | CO₂ | ppm | Carbon dioxide concentration | . 6121.title: Viewing Telemetry
6121.content: . | Navigate to Nodes and select a node. | The Telemetry section lists a row for each metric type — Device, Environment, Air Quality, Power, Host, PAX, and the rest — whether or not this node has reported it. A row fills in with readings, and grows a chart button, once that node has sent that kind of telemetry. An empty row means nothing has arrived, not that the sensor is missing. Soil & Water is the exception: its row appears only after the node reports soil or water readings. | Use the chart button on a row to open that metric’s history, where you can pick a time frame. The Device, Environment, Air Quality, Power, Signal Quality, and Position screens also export their readings as CSV. | .

6122.title: Troubleshooting
6122.content: . | No environment data showing? The remote node needs a physical sensor connected (e.g., BME280 on I2C). Device telemetry (battery, uptime) is always available, but environment metrics require hardware. | Stale readings? Check the reporting interval — very long intervals (7200s+) mean data updates infrequently. Also verify the remote node is still online. | Sensor conflict on I2C bus? Some sensors share I2C addresses. If you have multiple sensors on the same bus, check for address collisions in the node’s serial debug output. | .

The node detail screen shows read-only cards for channels 1 to 3. Use the chart button on the Power Metrics row to open the chart screen, which lists a chip for every channel that reported data — up to eight — and charts the one you select. Rename a channel there, in the label field under the chips, to something like Solar or Battery. There is no separate wattage reading; the app charts voltage and current, and does not compute power from them. Useful for monitoring solar charging or battery health on remote nodes.

6148.title: Configuring Telemetry
6148.content: . | Navigate to Settings → Module configuration → Telemetry. | Each metric group has its own enable toggle and its own interval: . | Device Metrics — battery, voltage, uptime, ChUtil, and AirUtil. Its toggle, Broadcast Device Metrics, appears only on firmware 2.7.13 and later. Turned off, the node stops broadcasting these metrics to the mesh but still sends them to the connected app; on older firmware you can change the interval but not stop the broadcast | Environment Metrics — temperature, humidity, pressure and the other sensor readings | Air Quality Metrics — particulate and CO₂ readings | Power Metrics — the per-channel voltage and current readings | . Environment has an extra toggle, Show on device screen, to show its readings on the node’s own screen, and Display Fahrenheit to show its temperatures there in Fahrenheit. Power has Power Screen for the same purpose. | . Choosing an Interval . These are nominal values, not hard schedules. On a congested mesh the firmware automatically backs off to longer intervals based on how many nodes are online, so you do not need to hand-tune them for mesh size. Lengthen them deliberately only to save battery.

6149.title: Air Quality Metrics
6149.content: Nodes with particulate matter or CO₂ sensors report air quality data: . | Metric | Unit | Description | . | PM1.0 | µg/m³ | Ultrafine particulate matter | . | PM2.5 | µg/m³ | Fine particulate matter | . | PM10 | µg/m³ | Coarse particulate matter | . | CO₂ | ppm | Carbon dioxide concentration | . CO₂ sensors such as the SCD4x also report their own temperature and humidity, which appear alongside the readings above. From PM2.5 history the app additionally derives an EPA NowCast AQI value. The CO₂ reading is color-coded by severity (Good → Stuffy → Poor → Unsafe → Evacuate). See Node Metrics — Air Quality for the exact ppm bands, colors, and AQI detail. Air quality data can be viewed as info cards on the node detail screen, charted over time, and exported to CSV.

6150.title: Viewing Telemetry
6150.content: . | Navigate to Nodes and select a node. | The Telemetry section lists a row for each metric type — Device, Environment, Air Quality, Power, Host, PAX, and the rest — whether or not this node has reported it. A row fills in with readings, and grows a chart button, once that node has sent that kind of telemetry. An empty row means nothing has arrived, not that the sensor is missing. Soil & Water is the exception: its row appears only after the node reports soil or water readings. | Use the chart button on a row to open that metric’s history, where you can pick a time frame. The Device, Environment, Air Quality, Power, Signal Quality, and Position screens also export their readings as CSV. | .

6151.title: Troubleshooting
6151.content: . | No environment data showing? The remote node needs a physical sensor connected (e.g., BME280 on I2C). 6226.title: Power Metrics
6226.content: Nodes with INA-series power sensors can report: . | Metric | Aprašymas | . | Voltage | Per-channel voltage reading | . | Current | Per-channel current draw, in mA | . The node detail screen shows read-only cards for channels 1 to 3. Use the chart button on the Power Metrics row to open the chart screen, which lists a chip for every channel that reported data — up to eight — and charts the one you select. Rename a channel there, in the label field under the chips, to something like Solar or Battery. There is no separate wattage reading; the app charts voltage and current, and does not compute power from them. Useful for monitoring solar charging or battery health on remote nodes.

6227.title: Configuring Telemetry
6227.content: . | Navigate to Settings → Module configuration → Telemetry. | Each metric group has its own enable toggle and its own interval: . | Device Metrics — battery, voltage, uptime, ChUtil, and AirUtil. Its toggle, Broadcast Device Metrics, appears only on firmware 2.7.13 and later. Turned off, the node stops broadcasting these metrics to the mesh but still sends them to the connected app; on older firmware you can change the interval but not stop the broadcast | Environment Metrics — temperature, humidity, pressure and the other sensor readings | Air Quality Metrics — particulate and CO₂ readings | Power Metrics — the per-channel voltage and current readings | . Environment has an extra toggle, Show on device screen, to show its readings on the node’s own screen, and Display Fahrenheit to show its temperatures there in Fahrenheit. Power has Power Screen for the same purpose. | . Choosing an Interval . These are nominal values, not hard schedules. On a congested mesh the firmware automatically backs off to longer intervals based on how many nodes are online, so you do not need to hand-tune them for mesh size. Lengthen them deliberately only to save battery.

6228.title: Air Quality Metrics
6228.content: Nodes with particulate matter or CO₂ sensors report air quality data: . | Metric | Unit | Aprašymas | . | PM1.0 | µg/m³ | Ultrafine particulate matter | . | PM2.5 | µg/m³ | Fine particulate matter | . | PM10 | µg/m³ | Coarse particulate matter | . | CO₂ | ppm | Carbon dioxide concentration | . CO₂ sensors such as the SCD4x also report their own temperature and humidity, which appear alongside the readings above. From PM2.5 history the app additionally derives an EPA NowCast AQI value. The CO₂ reading is color-coded by severity (Good → Stuffy → Poor → Unsafe → Evacuate). See Node Metrics — Air Quality for the exact ppm bands, colors, and AQI detail. Air quality data can be viewed as info cards on the node detail screen, charted over time, and exported to CSV.

6229.title: Viewing Telemetry
6229.content: . | Navigate to Nodes and select a node. | The Telemetry section lists a row for each metric type — Device, Environment, Air Quality, Power, Host, PAX, and the rest — whether or not this node has reported it. A row fills in with readings, and grows a chart button, once that node has sent that kind of telemetry. An empty row means nothing has arrived, not that the sensor is missing. Soil & Water is the exception: its row appears only after the node reports soil or water readings. | Use the chart button on a row to open that metric’s history, where you can pick a time frame. The Device, Environment, Air Quality, Power, Signal Quality, and Position screens also export their readings as CSV. | .

6230.title: Troubleshooting
6230.content: . | No environment data showing? The remote node needs a physical sensor connected (e.g., BME280 on I2C). Device telemetry (battery, uptime) is always available, but environment metrics require hardware. | Stale readings? Check the reporting interval — very long intervals (7200s+) mean data updates infrequently. Also verify the remote node is still online. | Sensor conflict on I2C bus? Some sensors share I2C addresses. If you have multiple sensors on the same bus, check for address collisions in the node’s serial debug output. | .

6327.title: Ilmanlaatumittarit

6331.title: Telemetry & Sensors
6331.content: Meshtastic nodes can collect and share sensor data across the mesh network. Telemetry allows nodes equipped with sensors to broadcast environmental, power, and device health information, visible on the node detail screen and logged over time.

6332.title: Device Telemetry

6334.title: Power Metrics
6334.content: Nodes with INA-series power sensors can report: . | Metric | Beschrijving | . | Spanning | Per-channel voltage reading | . | Huidige | Per-channel current draw, in mA | . The node detail screen shows read-only cards for channels 1 to 3. Use the chart button on the Power Metrics row to open the chart screen, which lists a chip for every channel that reported data — up to eight — and charts the one you select. Rename a channel there, in the label field under the chips, to something like Solar or Battery. There is no separate wattage reading; the app charts voltage and current, and does not compute power from them. Useful for monitoring solar charging or battery health on remote nodes.

6335.title: Configuring Telemetry
6335.content: . | Navigate to Settings → Module configuration → Telemetry. | Each metric group has its own enable toggle and its own interval: . | Device Metrics — battery, voltage, uptime, ChUtil, and AirUtil. Its toggle, Broadcast Device Metrics, appears only on firmware 2.7.13 and later. Turned off, the node stops broadcasting these metrics to the mesh but still sends them to the connected app; on older firmware you can change the interval but not stop the broadcast | Environment Metrics — temperature, humidity, pressure and the other sensor readings | Air Quality Metrics — particulate and CO₂ readings | Power Metrics — the per-channel voltage and current readings | . Environment has an extra toggle, Show on device screen, to show its readings on the node’s own screen, and Display Fahrenheit to show its temperatures there in Fahrenheit. Power has Power Screen for the same purpose. | . Choosing an Interval . These are nominal values, not hard schedules. On a congested mesh the firmware automatically backs off to longer intervals based on how many nodes are online, so you do not need to hand-tune them for mesh size. Lengthen them deliberately only to save battery.

6336.title: Air Quality Metrics
6336.content: Nodes with particulate matter or CO₂ sensors report air quality data: . | Metric | Unit | Beschrijving | . | PM1.0 | µg/m³ | Ultrafine particulate matter | . | PM2.5 | µg/m³ | Fine particulate matter | . | PM10 | µg/m³ | Coarse particulate matter | . | CO₂ | ppm | Carbon dioxide concentration | . CO₂ sensors such as the SCD4x also report their own temperature and humidity, which appear alongside the readings above. From PM2.5 history the app additionally derives an EPA NowCast AQI value. The CO₂ reading is color-coded by severity (Good → Stuffy → Poor → Unsafe → Evacuate). See Node Metrics — Air Quality for the exact ppm bands, colors, and AQI detail. Air quality data can be viewed as info cards on the node detail screen, charted over time, and exported to CSV.

A row fills in with readings, and grows a chart button, once that node has sent that kind of telemetry. An empty row means nothing has arrived, not that the sensor is missing. Soil & Water is the exception: its row appears only after the node reports soil or water readings. | Use the chart button on a row to open that metric’s history, where you can pick a time frame. The Device, Environment, Air Quality, Power, Signal Quality, and Position screens also export their readings as CSV. | .

6338.title: Troubleshooting
6338.content: . | No environment data showing? The remote node needs a physical sensor connected (e.g., BME280 on I2C). Some sensors share I2C addresses. If you have multiple sensors on the same bus, check for address collisions in the node’s serial debug output. | .

6366.title: Air Quality Metrics

6367.title: Viewing Telemetry
6367.content: . | Navigate to Nodes and select a node. | The Telemetry section lists a row for each metric type — Device, Environment, Air Quality, Power, Host, PAX, and the rest — whether or not this node has reported it. Soil & Water is the exception: its row appears only after the node reports soil or water readings. | Use the chart button on a row to open that metric’s history, where you can pick a time frame. The Device, Environment, Air Quality, Power, Signal Quality, and Position screens also export their readings as CSV. | .

6368.title: Troubleshooting
6368.content: . | No environment data showing? The remote node needs a physical sensor connected (e.g., BME280 on I2C). Check the reporting interval — very long intervals (7200s+) mean data updates infrequently. Also verify the remote node is still online. | Sensor conflict on I2C bus? Some sensors share I2C addresses. If you have multiple sensors on the same bus, check for address collisions in the node’s serial debug output. | .
